articles.title: Members Only: Cabal-Core Horror in the 21st Century
articles.author: Soraya Sebghati
articles.description: Salò: Or the 120 Days of Sodom (Pier Paolo Pasolini, 1975). In 2005, during a television interview in Italy, Giuseppe “Pino” Pelosi—AKA “The Frog”—recanted his confession about murdering Pier Paolo Pasolini on a beach in Ostia 30 years earlier. He claimed that it had been extracted by coercion and threats of violence, against both himself and his family (Pelosi was seventeen at the time). He also said that the legendary director’s death was a political killing disguised as a crime of passion—the premeditated and methodical muzzling of a “Dirty Communist.” Sergio Citti, a close friend of Pasolini, contributed to the controversy by suggesting that the filmmaker had been lured to the water under the guise of retrieving stolen reels of film from his transgressive—and, as it turned out, valedictory—magnum opus Salò: Or the 120 Days of Sodom (1975)—a savage critique of his homeland’s then-recent legacy of fascist decadence. “All’s good if it’s excessive,” says a religious figurehead early in Salò, describing both his unchecked fetishism and the M.O. of the film around him. The question of whether Pasolini’s Sadean vision tested the limits of cinematic transgression or transcended them remains open (Buñuel had gotten to Sade first in L'âge d'or [1930]) but the idea of a filmmaker getting too close to the ugly truth about the ruling class and paying for it is more than irresponsible: It’s irresistible. When Stanley Kubrick died before the theatrical bow of Eyes Wide Shut in 1999, the Internet was in its infancy, but whispers of a cover-up persisted—no more absurd, perhaps, than the rumor that Kubrick had faked the moon landing. Eyes Wide Shut (Stanley Kubrick, 1999). On December 19, 2025, the US government released its first major batch of the “Epstein files” to the public, implicating myriad political figures and billionaires in a decades-long global sex trafficking scheme. Despite the overwhelming evidence of a real-life 120 Days of Sodom -situation, not a single US citizen has been arrested in connection with these crimes. Maybe one reason people cling to the myth of artists like Pasolini and Kubrick as tragic, thwarted whistleblowers is that it makes them nostalgic for the possibility that art could actually make a difference. In the 1970s, Pasolini’s filmmaking and journalism represented a viable threat to Italy’s political and religious establishment; by the time Eyes Wide Shut came out, though, Americans had been inundated by allegations of public and private abuse of sexual power by Bill Clinton while his friend Jeffrey Epstein operated an international trafficking empire in the background. “No I’m not going to tell you their names,” says Sydney Pollack’s malign Victor Ziegler to Tom Cruise (playing a different Bill). “If I did, maybe you wouldn’t sleep so well at night”). The nostalgic view of Eyes Wide Shut as the proverbial last film of the 20th century places it in conversation with one that exists at the primal scene of the 21st. People love to throw around the phrase “eerily prescient” when describing genre works that trade in social commentary, as if filmmakers are different from the other artists who call attention to where things are going. There is nevertheless something retrospectively uncanny about Clifton Holmes’ S.O.V. (Shot on Video) classic In the Dark (2000), which came out of nowhere (Chicago) and predicted something of the paranoid tenor and texture of the decade to come. Surveillance, exploitation, and the link of late capitalism to implacable evil: It’s all there, in 240 fps. Holmes’ Raymond Laymon adaptation follows—or more literally stalks—Jane (Kim Garrett), a manic pixie dream librarian whose day-to-day life is shaken up by a strange hand-written note stowed in a copy of Thomas Wolfe’s Look Homeward, Angel . Its author, The pseudonymous Master of Games (MoG), promises her a crisp $50 bill if she can follow his clues to the next missive. Lo and behold, Jane does as she’s told. The amount of money is doubled every time as the degree of difficulty—and personal risk—increases. Is our heroine playing or being played? It’s all fun and games until somebody’s being offered up to strangers as a sex slave. In the Dark (Clifton Holmes, 2000). This month brings the first ever Blu-ray release of In the Dark from Saturn’s Core, but a case can be made that the film’s spell deepens when viewed on YouTube; the low-quality format bolsters the sense of stumbling upon something not meant for consumption. In the Dark feels like a movie that MoG recorded and uploaded himself; Holmes’s aesthetic recalls detective Danny Upshaw’s man-camera technique in James Ellroy’s novel The Big Nowhere in the way it puts the viewer in the driver’s seat (we’re bracing for the crash). MoG exploits Jane, but he also employs her, quite literally by paying her more and more for each stunt. She’s freelancing! But soon Jane joins in on her own exploitation, writing messages on her own body and trying to surveil her own watcher, only to find a message left inside of her; pre-dating the OnlyFans comments and requests model in its own sick way. Soon her own participation turns from gleeful to compulsory. The only way out is to become an MOG herself—to climb the corporate ladder. Her reward resembles nothing so much as the proverbial corner office—a room of her own in a luxurious downtown skyrise. She has her own Jane to boss around; the building’s vastness implies that each of her neighbors has become a Master themselves. The dirty little conspiracy launched in that library is nothing more—or less—than a pyramid scheme. In the Dark is one of one, but it also laid a foundation—modest but solid—for a distinctly millennial subgenre predicated on the same contradictions between social collapse and elite control explored in Salo and Eyes Wide Shut. In these films, more things fall apart below a certain level, the tighter the grip grows at the top. Call it cabal-core, where evil lurks behind closed doors, embedded into the language, structure and aesthetics of bureaucracy itself. (A goofy Hollywood precursor: Taylor Hackford’s The Devil’s Advocate, [1997], itself a parody of Rosemary’s Baby [1968]). If In the Dark doesn’t literally depict corporate environments or characters, it nevertheless approximates and weaponizes the logic of late capitalism; it’s structured as a series of revelations exposing a massive sex trafficking operation of girls and young women. Holmes’s roughness is a byproduct of his low budget, but the use of surveillance-style perspectives anticipates other entries into this unofficial but suggestive microgenre, as does the refusal of closure or catharsis. In cabal-core, the Big Bad is never defeated; instead it subsumes our day-to-day. Nothing Ever Happens. Demonlover (Olivier Assayas, 2002). Our final glimpse of Jane in In the Dark , as a brainwashed plaything wielding a controller, is sobering; the cinematic rabbit hole would only get deeper from there. Master of Games, meet Mangatronics; Oliver Assayas’s nice ’n’ sleazy 2002 film Demonlover puts us in the middle of a twisted web made up of multinational corporations whose portfolios include soft-core pornography and possibly also snuff cinema. Diane de Monx (a steely Connie Nielsen), a lupine exec at Volf Corporation, will do just about anything to further the agenda of whoever’s payroll she is on, even if it means killing a higher-up at Demonlover, Mangatronics’s main rival. During the course of her adventures—as indebted to the erotic espionage of Feuillade as Irma Vep (1996)—she discovers that Demonlover is a front for the Hellfire Club, a dark-web site that creates made-to-order torture porn—but that’s just business. Once Diane is caught for selling corporate secrets and sabotaging deals (and murdering Gina Gershon, a terrible crime indeed) her punishment is a fate worse than death: donning latex and starring in superhero movies. Well, I’m half-kidding. Having gotten rich (and gotten off) on trafficking women, she becomes the product, a helpless fetish object on offer for anybody with a credit card and the gumption to open an onion browser. Which begs the question—is it actually more ethical to ask Grok to generate some “shipper porn” than it is to go to “starznaked.com”? Inquiring minds want to know. Kill List (Ben Wheatley, 2011). Where Demonlover connects us to the future, Ben Wheatley’s 2011 folk-horror inversion, Kill List, is a bridge to the past. The British director’s sophomore feature draws deeply from the imagery of the UK folk horror urtext, The Wicker Man , to elucidate a contemporary set of horrors. Two British Iraq war veterans, Jay (Neil Maskell) and Gal (Michael Smiley), are at a career crossroads. A few years removed from the war that brought them together, they’ve found themselves employed as hitmen; their softer bodies not getting in the way of their usefulness as hardened killing machines. Gal’s mysterious new paramour, Fiona (Emma Fryer), explains over dinner one night that her line of work is “human resources,” and that she explicitly deals with managing “extraneous manpower.” Fiona’s all-business persona really grinds Jay’s wife Shel’s (MyAnna Buring) gears, drawing comparisons over lamb chops to Nazi Germany, especially when the guest also admits she doesn’t identify with the cause of Irish liberation. Jay and Shel, and to a lesser extent Gal, are positioned in opposition to Fiona, as workers (and small business owners!) in fear of being seen as fat to be trimmed from the whole operation. Kill List is divided unevenly and erratically into four chapters, and in its third, we get a glimpse at the Lord Summerisle that we unfortunately deserve. The string-pulling millionaire billed as the Client (Struan Rodger) somehow looks like a Joe Biden/Donald Trump hybrid puppet right out of Spitting Image . Toward the end, Jay and Gal lie in wait for their final target, only to stumble upon a scene straight out of a QAnon fantasy of Bohemian Grove—a virgin girl being sacrificed on an altar of pound notes. Except The Client is not honoring paganism in the face of rapidly spreading Christianity—he’s the very man who hired Gal and Jay in the first place. They were not sent to stop a ritual; they were sent to be part of it, in possibly the most twisted layoff meeting ever imagined. At the heart of both Kill List and Demonlover is some sort of corporate conspiracy related to the violent and sexual exploitation of women—between the Hellfire Club’s pixelated misogynist fantasia and “The Librarian’s” massive archive of homemade samizdat, including some implied kiddie porn—we have two complementary, cautionary fables stories of cogs being eliminated for grinding too close to the truth. Bastards (Claire Denis, 2013). In Claire Denis’s Polanski-ian 2013 neo-noir Bastards , sturdy seaman Marco Silvestri (Vincent Lindon) returns home to Paris to help his sister recover from her husband’s mysterious suicide; he means well, not that it matters. The double-dip recession facing Europe in the early 2010s looms over the story like a Biblical plague, infecting everyone and everything except those who deserve it. At first blush, the motivation behind the suicide is the dearly departed indebtedness to an Epstein-like monster. It turns out the collateral was his daughter, and after an extended fugue of carnage, we get a cosmic and incestuous miscarriage of justice à la Chinatown (1974). From its title on down, Bastards vibrates with rage at individuals and systems—patriarchy distilled into an epithet. Denis’s detached, surveillance style of shooting—her first film on digital, less voluptuous than the vampirism of Trouble Every Day (2002)— and climactic reveal of a repurposed corncob would make Chekov (or its literary source, Faulkner) blush. “Put your love in me,” pleads Stuart Staples on the soundtrack, a perfect and perfectly horrible needle drop in a movie where everything has been perverted. Bastards essays helplessness; Lynne Ramsay’s You Were Never Really Here (2017) imagines a vigilante in order to orchestrate a happy ending: Joe (Joaquin Phoenix), a traumatized veteran who specializes in rescuing sex-trafficking victims. His latest assignment is Nina (Ekaterina Samsonov), the young daughter of US senator Albert Votto (Alex Manette). She’s being held in a makeshift brothel in the middle of New York City; figuratively if not literally near 9 East 71st Street. Ramsay’s adaptation of Jonathan Ames’s novel is grounded and even realistic: Joe has a cellphone, a boss, a handler, his mother to take care of, and the severe PTSD and suicidal ideation that plague his every waking moment. His home is not an aspirational Parisian flat, or even a picturesque British cottage; it’s strewn with family photos and the soapy footprints Joe’s mother leaves behind when she forgets how to bathe herself. You Were Never Really Here (Lynne Ramsay, 2017). Joe’s work is very specialized, but he is wage-dependent; at the same time, it seems that enacting extreme acts of violence upon the people who make the world sick is the only thing that keeps his demons at bay. He rescues Nina fairly early into the film, which points to the other shoe waiting to drop: she is not who we think she is. The revelations come to the viewer via background information (the TV news, secondhand confessions), giving the conspiracy of high-level child-sex trafficking a larger-than-life shadow. That shadow hangs over Ramsay’s narrative affairs, encircling every innocent who had the misfortune of being tangentially involved in Joe’s life. He prepares to go rescue Nina a second time, but we are denied the satisfaction of seeing her captor pay for his crimes; Joe arrives on the scene after Nina has already taken matters into her own hands, the cavalry coming in too late; their bloody victory over the bad guys yields neither catharsis nor change, but further visions of self-annihilating despair. Ari Aster’s polarizing COVID-western Eddington (2025) positions Phoenix yet again as a man on a mission named Joe: not so much the dapper, white-hat sheriff, but an impotent cuck-in-waiting. The film has one foot grounded (maybe too) firmly in COVID-era reality—“hindsight is 2020,” goes Aster’s tagline—and another in the filmmaker’s signature heightened, penny-dreadful comic-book world, yet it somehow feels like the truest representation of the pressure-cooker that was the USA at the height of the pandemic. Again, Sheriff Joe Cross is not the hero we want, but he is probably the one we deserve; having proven ineffectual in his own life—as a husband, a lover, and a boss—he is determined to become a transformational figure. Dismayed by mandatory masking and jurisdictional red tape, he decides to run for office, positioning himself opposite (and to the right) of the town’s handsome, neoliberal cipher of a mayor (Pedro Pascal). Joe’s wife (Emma Stone) isn’t turned on by her husband’s initiative; she’s repulsed even more by his exploitation of her mysterious sexual trauma as a stump speech. She duly runs out on him for the enigmatic, Svengali-esque cult leader Vernon Jefferson Peak (a delightful Austin Butler), who works his magic on her and everyone else in his orbit. One of the tricks up his sleeve: the invocation of ritualistic child molestation as a motivator—a plot point Aster jams into the movie like the wedge issue it is. Vernon exploits those around him using (likely false) memories of having been hunted for sport as a child by powerful men in DC—the same tactic that many at the front of the QAnon movement use to manipulate their base while keeping them from sympathizing with the actual adult women who are also victims of trafficking. Eddington (Ari Aster, 2025). Vernon and the Client in Kill List should exchange numbers, but he isn’t Eddington ’s Big Bad. The real specter looming on the horizon is the SOLIDGOLDMAGIKARP Data Center, in whose name the ensuing horror unfolds. The citizens don’t even notice—they’re too busy taking their cues about the protest from CNN. Joe assures the constituency that Black Lives Matter but also that the fact that some people aren’t sure about that isn’t his fault, specifically; he’s a perfect, unwitting fall guy for the crisis actors masquerading as Antifa supersoldiers, deployed to Eddington to ensure the data center’s erection. Like Kill List , Eddington transforms late into a kind of war movie (crossed with a stand-off western as per the New Mexico backdrop), and Aster shoots these conflicts as plausibly schizophrenic: The enemy is faceless, prolific, and omnipotent. No matter how valiantly Joe fights his unseen opponent (staged like a Looney Tunes climax), it’s no use. He’s shot up, stabbed, and paralyzed, a combination scapegoat and sacrificial lamb; the real winner is a local failson who arrives on the scene in time to get off a single lucky shot and become Kyle Rittenhouse. (Aster’s next movie is supposedly about Charlie Kirk.) Actually, Joe does win: he becomes mayor, living in a state of mute paralysis, unable to even cut the ribbon on the data center. A Pyrrhic victory: Joe gets what he wants because they get what they want. Aster surely loves his secular and sacrilegious rites: one of the ancient pagan rituals not wiped out by Christianity and modernity is that of the sin-eater. The sin-eater is meant to fall on the sword for the sins of another in a metaphorical act of absolution. For instance: Mussolini’s death was a huge turning point in the war for a free Italy, but more importantly it was a massive symbolic win: a public bludgeoning of an effigy of Italian fascism. Of course Il Duce was not the only one responsible, but at the very least the face of the party was hanged. It appears that our sin-eaters for the crimes of Jeffrey Epstein are Ghislaine Maxwell and certain others as we have been denied the satisfaction—however brutal— of watching Jeffrey Epstein face any semblance of justice. It seems at this point we will be denied watching any of his other co-conspirators receive anything close to adequate punishment either. Certainly one thing each of these filmmakers is doing is attempting to make some sort of sense of this darkly farcical landscape we’ve found ourselves in. At this point the (business side of the) art is imitating that morbid side of life. Movies are not banned from wide release (like Ken Russell’s recently restored The Devils was originally in the US) due to their content, but instead due to their being a tax write-off rather than a viable theatrical success (welcome back, Coyote vs. Acme ). This week, news of the Paramount/Warner merger’s passing emerged—a Faustian bargain for those of us living in California, and in truth just one among many, in an industry whose fingers are in everything and rarely clean. But what can you do? You can put your head down and doom-scroll through it; if you’re Paul Walter Hauser, you can wear a “KUBRICK DIDN’T KILL HIMSELF” T-shirt to a premiere. Perhaps art doesn’t have the power to cut an empire down at the knees anymore, but there’s still something to be said for movies that have teeth and use them to bite you know what. Rage is a powerful tool, and at its best cabal-core channels that feeling, beyond comfortable numbness or fashionable despair. There’s something at stake in these movies, burning or otherwise; a flicker of resistance in the dark.

articles.title: Pirating the Pirates
articles.author: Devan Scott
articles.description: Home video release images from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Sergio Leone, 1966). Clockwise from top-left: Arrow Video (4K UHD, 2025), Kino Lorber (4K UHD, 2021), MGM (4K Blu-ray, 2014), MGM (DVD, 1998). “ People who alter or destroy works of art and our cultural heritage for profit or as an exercise of power are barbarians, and if the laws of the United States continue to condone this behavior, history will surely classify us as a barbaric society. ” —George Lucas, 1988 “ To me, it [the original Star Wars trilogy] doesn’t really exist anymore. It’s like this is the movie I wanted it to be, and I’m sorry you saw half a completed film and fell in love with it.” —George Lucas, 2004 Vancouver, 2011 : My then-roommate Willa Ross and I are at our wit’s end in one of Simon Fraser University’s characteristically antiseptic editing suites, having just spent the weekend hacking together three distinct copies of Sergio Leone’s 1966 western The Good, the Bad and the Ugly , all illegally ripped. The film had fallen victim to an MGM “restoration” in the early 2000s: Scenes Leone cut were reinstated, inflating the English-language runtime from 161 to 179 minutes, with Eastwood and Wallach dubbing the missing dialogue and a soundalike standing in for the late Lee Van Cleef. The mono soundtrack, meanwhile, had been reworked into a surround mix with jarringly modern gunshot effects. This “extended” cut was the only version commercially available for nearly a decade, an all-too-common fate in an era of revisionist studio reworkings. Our goal was simple: undo this butchery. We planned to combine sound from an out-of-print 1998 DVD (an approximation of the 1967 international release) with video from a recently imported Blu-ray of the Italian cut. After successfully navigating the various pitfalls of late-2000s home video ripping, our hopes were dashed by a catastrophic realization: The Italian cut was even more dissimilar to the international cut than the extended cut, the infamous torture scene entirely restructured and various shots missing heads and tails. We gave up for nearly a decade. *** Publicly accessible versions of major works of cinema are often wholly inadequate for reasons as diverse as the resultant shortcomings. A major studio’s home video arm might “expand” a film, remix a monaural audio track, wipe away digital grain, oversaturate or oversharpen the image, or even change the aspect ratio for the sake of an attractive sticker promising a new-and-improved experience. At other points, low budgets and corporate apathy lead to corners being cut. Spencer Draper—best known as the Damn Fool Idealistic Crusader on YouTube, where he reviews the technical and historical aspects of digital releases with a rigor usually reserved for scholarly peer review—characterized the attitudes of negligent studios harshly in my recent interview with him: “‘Oh, you got a problem? The Kino [an American boutique label] disc is defective? So what. So what if it uses a defective Paramount master with frozen grain and [has] problems throughout.’ [The studios] don’t care that any given audio file is 30 years old and the channels are reversed.” Sometimes, this persists for decades: Every copy of Once Upon a Time in the West (1968)released since its 1984 reconstruction has featured a major soundtrack mistake during the end credits brought about by a botched attempt to fix another error introduced in 1970, one example that particularly rankles Draper. This is where boutique labels come in—companies that independently license and release archival titles, in something like the spirit of Criterion’s founding aim: to gather significant films from around the world and present them as close to a filmmaker’s intent as possible, in the best technical condition available. Outfits like Arrow, Kino, and Eureka operate on a version of that premise. What any given label actually restores versus what it merely receives is a separate question, running a wide spectrum. Sometimes a label might receive a fully mastered digital file and find themselves contractually obliged to release it as-is; at other times, they might receive raw digital scans with partial or no cleanup; or they might be required to source, scan, and restore a film by themselves. James Flower, director of production at Arrow Films, a British boutique label renowned for its rigorous approach to preservation, raises a different culprit for historical inaccuracies: living filmmakers. The revisionist impulse is nearly as old as cinema—from Charlie Chaplin modernizing his silent classics in later years to Wong Kar-wai radically altering the color grading, aspect ratios, and soundtracks of his back catalog for a 2021 Criterion box set. In his note accompanying this set, Wong Kar-wai justified his alterations with a simple philosophy: “No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man.” However, this revisionist approach often leaves release-accurate versions unavailable to historians and audiences alike. In our interview, Flower recalled a director enamored with a digital aesthetic “wanting his films to look sleek and modern and degrained, with oversaturated colors that would not have been achievable photochemically.” Flower suggested including both the revised cut and a historically accurate version, but the director vehemently refused. Facing a deadline, Arrow acquiesced. “For me, he was vandalizing his own work,” says Flower. *** Home video release images from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Sergio Leone, 1966). Clockwise from top-left: Arrow Video (4K UHD, 2025), Kino Lorber (4K UHD, 2021), MGM (4K Blu-ray, 2014), MGM (DVD, 1998). Vancouver, July 2019. Radicalized by a disheartening screening of the official MGM masters of Leone’s Dollars trilogy at a local cinematheque, Willa and I resume work on our cobbled-together cut. We now have better raw materials: a new Blu-ray with far superior picture quality, and an old LaserDisc with an uncompromised mono track. A decade of expertise (I have become a colorist and Willa an editor), alongside a decade of technical progress in editing tools available for independent filmmakers, enables us to properly process them. A local repertory cinema programmer catches wind of this, and a plan is hatched: book an official Digital Cinema Package from MGM and swap it out with our homebrew copy for a public screening. A magical evening ensues: It was as if we were seeing the film for the first time, smuggled before a live audience. After the screening, I’m approached by a man with an attitude that screams “so you think you know a thing or two, huh?” It turns out his attitude is warranted: He enthusiastically informs me that he’s spent years on his own far superior reconstruction—a 4K scan of a well-preserved IB Technicolor print of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly . *** Home video release images from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Sergio Leone, 1966). Clockwise from top-left: Arrow Video (4K UHD, 2025), Kino Lorber (4K UHD, 2021), MGM (4K Blu-ray, 2014), MGM (DVD, 1998). While digital tools have evolved, this pattern of unofficial preservation is by no means new. It’s the reason F. W. Murnau’s Nosferatu (1922) survives: after Bram Stoker’s widow won a 1925 copyright suit, a German court ordered every print to be destroyed, but copies slipped past German jurisdiction and circulated for years as unauthorized bootlegs. Similarly, Kevin Brownlow’s reconstruction of Abel Gance’s Napoléon (1927) began as an illicit teenage hobby. Starting in 1954, he spent decades tracking down fragments and duplicating fragile, rights-encumbered prints to keep them from disappearing—essentially a massive fan edit, eventually completed with Gance’s own participation. The most famous retrospective cinematic alteration was committed by George Lucas with massively controversial Special Editions of the original Star Wars trilogy—and the subsequent unavailability of unaltered versions in anything resembling acceptable quality. Both Draper and Flower cite the 2004 DVD release and emergence of communities such as the one found on OriginalTrilogy.com as key personal entrees into the world of fan preservation. Draper jokes that “I’ve learned more from George Lucas than anyone ever because he made certain choices that I didn’t agree with, so I started digging!” Starting in the mid-2000s, he took an active role on various forums, contributing wherever he could: “They eventually made a sub-thread about preservation efforts, which was everybody capturing VHS tapes and laserdiscs and trying to upscale LDs and sync other audio tracks. One thing led to another as the preservation scene grew out of one little thread.” Eventually, two distinct projects emerged. Petr “Harmy” Harmáček’s “Despecialized” edition, a Frankenstein’s monster cobbled together from various official releases, came first. Next was Team Negative1’s Project 4K77, which used homebrew 4K scans of 35mm theatrical prints to create accurate bootlegged digital copies. Both projects remain freely available to anyone willing to jump through some trivial internet hoops. When an informal network of amateurs questions the work of industry standard-bearers, it is rarely a matter of raw technical superiority but rather a fundamental difference in constraints. While restoration entities often operate on strict budgets and tight deadlines, preservationists can spend years cross-referencing decades of older releases. This is not to say fan efforts are infallible—debates in online forums about accurate color grades spurred by the recent influx of amateur 35mm scans of release prints demonstrate how certain elements remain moving targets—but for objective elements like editorial cuts, missing frames, or unaltered audio, historical reference materials generally leave little room for debate. Furthermore, fans operate entirely outside the structural limitations that thwart even skilled industry technicians. A professional lab might make all the right archival choices only to have those compromised by a revisionist director or a studio’s marketing needs. Fans, in contrast, answer to no one but themselves, which has let them accomplish what studios with exponentially more resources and infrastructure haven’t: banding together to preserve and disseminate historically accurate versions of some of the most beloved films in history—an end-run around the rights and financial issues that hold legitimate enterprises back. Flower notes: “We don’t always have the time or budget, or even the legal right, to do multiple versions. Fans don’t have those restrictions. They can do as many variations as they want, and that’s fine.” As of this writing, Project 4K77 features dozens of audio tracks and a file size exceeding 100GB: both impossible on any commercial Blu-ray release, and unfeasible for online distribution via legitimate channels. Beyond Star Wars , an illicit cottage industry has sprung up to patch the holes in any given film’s digital representation. Of particular note is the “remux” community, dedicated to seamlessly stitching together the best video and audio streams from different releases without any generational loss of quality. Want a version of Stop Making Sense (1984) in which you can freely select every soundtrack mix ever released? You won’t find it on the official A24 disc; you have to turn to a remux circulating on a few highly exclusive private torrent websites. The original 5.1 mix of Master and Commander (2003) married to the new 4K transfer? Remux. Dr. No (1962) with audio that hasn’t been scrubbed of all its detail? Remux. Draper sees this pooling of resources as an incredible service: “Somebody’s already done a great job of the work you were going to do yourself.” His thoughts quickly turn, however: “We’re all worried about the crackdown coming at any point. Put your hood on, look over your shoulder, go to the back door video speakeasy and give the secret recognition code.” The elephant in the room: Legally, this is piracy. Under Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, merely breaking a Blu-ray’s digital lock to rip the video files is a federal violation, regardless of intent. The law makes no distinction between mass-distributing a movie for profit and preserving the historical record. To take part in these preservation projects is to take on significant legal risk, with admonishments from rights holders and cease-and-desist letters being common. Flower sees copyright law as a double-edged sword for film preservation. Though intellectual property rights—and the resultant studio-mandated limitations—hold Arrow back from certain actions that would be theoretically possible otherwise, these same rights in many ways ensure their income: “We have to protect our interest as well as that of the rights holders that have entrusted their films to us. We spend a lot of money on licensing and restoring. I certainly don’t think that copyright is something that should be abolished, unless someone can think of another commercial framework that would allow us to invest in the work we do.” Yet he maintains that there is a place for piracy-based preservation: “It comes down to who is financially benefiting from these things. In terms of using a physical copy and then manipulating it or finding another use for it beyond just watching it, that is a gray area that I’m personally more inclined to be generous towards.” A sort of “pirate’s code” has emerged among these communities: an attempt to create a parallel set of norms in a context in which the strict definition of “legal” can no longer operate as a guiding principle. “You have to own a physical copy of at least one version of any given film,” says Draper. “We’re not trying to make any money out of this. Don’t make your own bootleg copies and throw them on eBay, or throw them on Twitter of all places.” Nevertheless, the clandestine nature of these efforts weighs on Draper: “It would be nice if there was at least a little bit more recognition of unofficial preservation efforts. I feel like there’s a gigantic weight about to come crashing down on me at any second because, heaven forbid, I bought another twenty laserdiscs and captured audio tracks and bought VHS tapes on eBay to compare audio captures to fix the bad audio they didn’t care about the first time around.” *** Home video release images from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Sergio Leone, 1966). Clockwise from top-left: Arrow Video (4K UHD, 2025), Kino Lorber (4K UHD, 2021), MGM (4K Blu-ray, 2014), MGM (DVD, 1998). Vancouver, December 2020. While cooking dinner in my apartment, I get a call from a California number. Must be a scam. Then an email: “Read your profile on National Post . I work in mastering and want to talk to you guys about The Good, The Bad and the Ugly .” Apparently, word of our pseudo-legal screening had gotten around. So began my semi-official involvement in film preservation. I roped in Willa and, most importantly, Benji Heran—the man who had accosted me after our screening of the film the year prior—and Jordan Krug, the other party responsible for their remarkable bootleg restoration of the film which would prove to be the main editorial reference point of every subsequent release. What ensued was a months-long collaboration to turn the drastically underfunded 2021 Kino Lorber release of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly from a disaster-in-waiting to the best home video release of the film since the 1990s. Doing so involved much chicanery: Benji and Jordan supplied ripped LaserDisc audio that became the release’s main track, while Blake Blasingame—who deserves the lion’s share of credit for this release’s strengths—fulfilled his contractual obligation for a surround mix by simply placing that mono track into a 5.1 container with extremely mild panning effects. When a high-up Kino figure made a Blu-Ray.com thread to read the room on whether to include the international cut, Willa and I made dummy accounts and anonymously badgered him into making our preferred version the primary feature. The result was a release that—despite a highly compressed turnaround time, virtually nonexistent budget, and compromised source materials—was nonetheless a largely accurate approximation of the 1967 international cut of the film in reasonably high fidelity. At last. *** Flower had been leveraging the fan community’s knowledge to assist with various releases for some time prior to his work on Arrow’s release of Leone’s Dollars trilogy. “That ultimately winds up being a regular part of my research process; I go, ‘What have the fan restorers done? Can we pre-empt them from having to [fix the release] by bringing that fix into an official space if we’re allowed?’ Just recently with Mortal Kombat [1995], I happened upon a capture of an original DTS cinema mix that walloped the 5.1 audio on the prior Blu-Ray, so I was like, ‘Well, we’ll just use that!’ That’s me pirating the pirates, I guess.” Because labels like Arrow, Criterion, and Eureka release dozens of films a year, their researchers are by necessity generalists. “As much as I would love us to have intimate knowledge with every film that we work on, we’re usually not in that position,” says Flower. This is where he reaches out to amateur experts. “Brandon Bentley—who does a lot of stuff on the Hong Kong cinema side—started out literally as an amateur. His work is so good that I see him as a colleague; he’s the person we turn to when we want to digitally recreate photochemical credits.” Flower compares his process in an official capacity with Arrow to his early days trawling internet forums: “When I came to work for Arrow, I was bringing a lot of awareness of the methods of fan preservationists on the torrent sites. When it came time to officially create different versions of things—the big box set of the Gamera films—it’s the same methodology. It’s just in an official capacity by sheer dint of the fact that we have the license for the film and I’m not working with a DVD rip, I’m working with a ProRes [a professional video codec] master.” *** Home video release images from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Sergio Leone). Clockwise from top-left: Arrow Video (4K UHD, 2025), Kino Lorber (4K UHD, 2021), MGM (4K Blu-ray, 2014), MGM (DVD, 1998). In May 2024, I met James—along with other key figures at Arrow—on a video call in which Benji, Jordan, Willa, myself, and eventually Spencer, were officially brought in as consultants on Arrow’s forthcoming release of the Dollars trilogy. The expertise of the amateur enthusiast community was, at long last, aligned with an officially sanctioned organization with the resources and patience to make a fully realized, historically rigorous release happen. No internet trolling of label heads or NDA-breaking was necessary. The process took a very leisurely and considered year. And we still used the LaserDisc audio. While drafting this article, I checked my usual private torrent site for the latest copy of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly . The 4K Arrow release is on there, in all its 89gb glory, with the Italian track that Arrow was unable to secure the rights to and every single commentary track ever released—including those not present on the Arrow disc—all muxed in. The cycle continues.

articles.title: Movie Poster of the Week | The Posters of the 1976 New York Film Festival
articles.author: Adrian Curry
articles.description: French grande for Small Change (François Truffaut, France, 1976). Design by Jouineau Bourduge. Another year, another Truffaut, another Fassbinder, another Visconti, another Renoir revival. The 1976 New York Film Festival—which ran from October 1 to 17—was nothing if not true to its brand. But the 14th New York Film Festival, programmed by Richard Roud, Susan Sontag, Richard Corliss, Charles Michener, and Roger Greenspun, was still a relatively small affair, showcasing just eighteen features and eleven shorts. It was also still a defiantly Euro-centric program, top heavy with French cinema. Both the opening- and closing-night films were French (François Truffaut’s Small Change and Eric Rohmer’s The Marquise of O , respectively) and there were four other French features in the mix along with an Agnès Varda short. There were three films from Germany, two from Italy, and one from Switzerland. But whereas the previous year there were no films from Asia, the 1976 fest branched out with films from India (Satyajit Ray’s The Middleman , 1975), Hong Kong (King Hu’s A Touch of Zen , 1971) and Japan (Nagisa Ōshima’s In the Realm of the Senses and Akira Kurosawa’s Japanese-Russian co-production Dersu Uzala , 1975). The 1976 NYFF is full of great films, but not as many out-and-out masterpieces as in other years. In the world at large, cinema seemed to have taken a step back after the banner year of 1975 (which was so chock-full of barnstormers that Morgan Neville made a documentary about it last year ). In my piece on the 1975 festival I listed all the major movies that were playing in commercial theaters in New York the weekend that the NYFF began (concluding “Who needs a film festival?”). In 1976 it was a different story. The biggest ads in The New York Times on October 1, 1976, were for the boy-and-his-dog weepie Where the Red Fern Grows , a Jack Lemmon film ( Alex & The Gypsy ), an Italian film starring Marcello Mastroianni ( Sunday Woman ), a Dennis Hopper western ( Mad Dog ), a Giancarlo Giannini romp ( How Funny Can Sex Be? ), a Redd Foxx comedy ( Norman…Is That You? ), a horror movie ( Burnt Offerings ), and a compilation film of “the most hilarious, brilliant scenes in film history” called All About Us: America at the Movies —none of which I had ever heard of before I scrolled through the Times’ archives. The only two high-profile films I did know were Alan Parker’s Bugsy Malone and Martin Ritt’s The Front . But buried among the smaller ads are more promising signs of life in Victor Erice’s The Spirit of the Beehive (1973), Barbet Schroeder’s General Idi Amin Dada: A Self-Portrait (1974), Peter Watkins’s Edvard Munch (1974), Paul Verhoeven’s Keetje Tippel (1975), and—in its “10th Smash Week”—Bertrand Tavernier’s The Clockmaker of St. Paul (1974). Also, opening five days later at the Ziegfeld, and seemingly having its very first New York showing, was Andrei Tarkovski’s Solaris (it had played at the Chicago Film Festival in November 1972 but had seemingly been passed over by the NYFF that year). But Lincoln Center had Truffaut, Rohmer, Rivette, Kurosawa, Fassbinder, Francesco Rosi, Marcel Ophuls, Satyajit Ray, and Nagisa Ōshima. Sadly, 50 years on, only two of the NYFF Class of 1976 are still with us: Wim Wenders (31 then, 81 now, and with a new film this year, From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor ) and Barbara Kopple (now 80, also with a new film this year: Union Town ) whose world premiere of Harlan County U.S.A. was one of the two sensations of the festival. Alexander Kluge, whose Strongman Ferdinand was in the 1976 edition, passed away on March 25 of this year at the age of 94. The other sensation of the festival didn’t actually play at the festival. Ōshima’s famously sexually explicit In the Realm of the Senses was seized by customs officers who were in attendance at its press screening, and confiscated for alleged obscenity. It had to be replaced at the last minute with Ōshima’s 1971 film The Ceremony . Apparently this is the only time in NYFF history that they have been unable to show a scheduled film. A judge later ruled that the film had been improperly detained (the story made the front page of The New York Times ) and the Film Society screened it at MoMA in December, honoring New York Film Festival ticket stubs. This governmental prudishness is surprising when you see that there were ads for porn movies in The New York Times in those days, films like In the Heat of the Knight and two seemingly unrelated pornos called Alice in Wonderland: An X-Rated Musical Fantasy and Through the Looking Glass (pull quote: “Hard core pornography at its best. A ‘Marnie’ like mystery and the ‘Exorcist’ with incest. Ladies, you’ll like it.”) I’ve tried to find the most interesting poster for each film that played in the 1976 festival. The highlights include Jerzy Flisak’s Polish poster for his countryman Walerian Borowczyk’s The Story of Sin (1975), Averardo Ciriello’s Italian in medias res cliffhanger for Dersu Uzala , and Satyajit Ray’s own type-centric collage for The Middleman . The only feature film that I couldn’t find any poster for was Fassbinders’s Fear of Fear (1975), which was made for television and seems to have never had a theatrical release. The posters are shown below in the order in which the films played in the festival. Artists and designers are credited where known. Italian 2- foglio for Ossessione (Luchino Visconti, Italy, 1943). US one sheet for Jonah Who Will Be 25 in the Year 2000 (Alain Tanner, Switzerland, 1976). Japanese poster for In the Realm of the Senses (Nagisa Oshima, Japan, 1976). Art by Susumu Masukawa. Japanese poster for The Ceremony (Nagisa Oshima, Japan, 1971). French poster for Kings of the Road (Wim Wenders, West Germany, 1976). Art by E. Watcker. US poster for The Memory of Justice (Marcel Ophuls, France, 1976). Italian 2-foglio for Dersu Uzala (Akira Kurosawa, Japan/USSR, 1975). Art by Averardo Ciriello. French poster for Illustrious Corpses (Francesco Rosi, Italy, 1976). Design by Jouineau Bourduge. Polish poster for The Story of Sin (Walerian Borowczyk, Poland, 1975). Art by Jerzy Flisak. French poster for Surreal Estate (Eduardo de Gregorio, France, 1976). German poster for Strongman Ferdinand (Alexander Kluge, West Germany, 1976). Hong Kong poster for A Touch of Zen (King Hu, Hong Kong, 1971). Indian poster for The Middleman (Satyajit Ray, India, 1975). Design by Satyajit Ray. French poster for Duelle (Jacques Rivette, France, 1976). French poster for Nana (Jean Renoir, France, 1926). French poster for Harlan County, U.S.A. (Barbara Kopple, USA, 1976). French grande for The Marquise of O (Eric Rohmer, France, 1976). Design by René Ferracci. Official poster by Allan D’Arcangelo for the 14th New York Film Festival. Full-page advertisement for the 14th New York Film Festival in the New York Times on Sunday, September 12, 1975. At these links, you can see my previous New York Film Festival flashbacks to 1963 , 1965 , 1968 , 1969 , 1971 , 1972 , 1973 , 1974 , 1975 and 1988 .

articles.title: Rushes | Venice and TIFF Announce Awards, Paramount Settles Antitrust Lawsuit, “Cliff Booth” Trailer Drops
articles.author: Notebook
articles.description: Get in touch to send in cinephile news and discoveries. To keep up with our latest features, sign up for the Weekly Edit newsletter and follow us @mubinotebook on X and Instagram . NEWS Woman Unknown (May el-Toukhy, 2026). The Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival announced its list of winners . May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown (2026) won the Golden Lion and Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love (2026) won the Grand Jury Prize. Meanwhile, Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s La Bola Negra (2026) won the People’s Choice Award at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival. Paramount CEO David Ellison has resolved the antitrust lawsuit filed by twelve states opposing the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, paving the way for the merger to go forward. The news has prompted mixed reactions from the industry : while the DGA, SAG-AFTRA, and IATSE broadly support the settlement, the WGA still believes the merger to be a mistake. Meanwhile, former commissioner of the FTC Alvaro Bedoya and actor Mark Ruffalo believe that California Governor Gavin Newsom and Attorney General Rob Bonta caved to pressure from Ellison, who threatened to leave California if the merger failed. After Universal Pictures initially expressed reservations about releasing Alex Gibney’s Musk (2026) , a documentary about the controversial tech mogul, due to the impending Paramount-WBD merger and possible political pressure, they are now holding internal talks to push forward with its distribution . Universal bought the international rights to Gibney’s four-hour film back in 2023, which recently premiered at Venice amidst legal threats from Musk himself. NAZA (2026) will receive a theatrical release in New York City on September 30 before expanding to Los Angeles the following week ahead of a national rollout. The film’s release arrives on the heels of Israeli culture minister Miki Zohar’s threat to revoke the citizenship of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor citing treason and IDF chief of staff Eyal Zamir’s order for a legal review of the film to possibly bring a lawsuit against the filmmakers, describing their work as an “attack on the State of Israel.” DEVELOPING Carlito's Way (Brian De Palma, 1993). John Leguizamo is set to join Joseph Kosinski’s Miami Vice ’85 as the main villain opposite Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler in a new cinematic take on the ’80s NBC crime drama. REMEMBERING The Battle of Chile (Patricio Guzmán, 1975-79). Jeremy Thomas has died at 77 . The son of filmmaker Ralph Thomas, the British producer got his start working as an assistant editor for films like Family Life (1971) and The Harder They Come (1972) before eventually serving as sole editor on Ken Loach’s A Misfortune (1973), an adaptation of an Anton Chekhov short story for television, and Phillipe Mora’s documentary Brother, Can You Spare a Dime? (1975). Though he first produced the Dennis Hopper-starring Australian film Mad Dog Morgan (1976), Thomas gained international prominence with his next production, Jerzy Skolimowski’s The Shout (1978), which won the Grand Prix at Cannes and was the first feature released under his independent production company Recorded Picture Company. RPC went on to produce a number of acclaimed films by directors such as Nicolas Roeg, David Cronenberg, and Takashi Miike. Thomas won the Oscar for Best Picture for producing Bernardo Bertolucci’s The Last Emperor (1987), which led to a decades-long collaboration with the Italian filmmaker. He went on to be the Chairman of the British Film Institute between 1992 and 1997 before directing his sole feature All the Little Animals (1998). “An entrepreneurial spirit is an important element of being a producer, some sort of inner workings that is pushing you forward,” said Thomas . “Because there are a lot of knockbacks and you have to wear a sort of armour so you can continue believing in your films when everybody around you is telling you: ‘Don't do that.’” Patricio Guzmán has died at 85 . After working for two years at an advertising studio in Madrid, the Chilean documentarian directed his first film, El primer año (1972), a survey of the first year of Salvador Allende’s socialist government, which garnered the attention of French filmmaker Chris Marker. Marker later supplied Guzmán raw film stock from the United States to help film his epic documentary The Battle of Chile (1975–79), which chronicled the fall of the Allende government in real time, ending on the day of General Augusto Pinochet's coup. The footage was smuggled out of the country and the film was completed in Havana after Guzmán went into exile in November 1973 following his illegal detainment by the Pinochet government. Guzmán continued making documentaries in Spain and France before returning to Chile in 1997 to direct Chile, Obstinate Memory (1997), his follow-up to The Battle of Chile about the country’s political amnesia surrounding the military dictatorship. His post-millennium work includes The Pinochet Case (2001), about the failed attempt to prosecute the former dictator, Salvador Allende (2004), a portrait of the politician’s rise to power, and a late-career trilogy about the Andes. His final film My Imaginary Country (2022) was about the youth revolt in Santiago between 2019 and 2020 and the lingering consequences of the protests. “Memory has a gravitational force,” Guzmán told Notebook in 2010 . “Cinema suffers without memory in the same way that history suffers without memory. Science would also suffer without memory. The human race suffers. The absence of memory produces a global suffering.” Gerrit Graham has died at 77 . The American actor is best known for his collaborations with filmmaker Brian De Palma, appearing in four of his films: Greetings (1968), Hi, Mom! (1970), Phantom of the Paradise (1974), and Home Movies (1979). He also costarred in such beloved cult classics like Donald Cammell’s Demon Seed (1977), Robert Zemeckis’s Used Cars (1980), and Alex Cox’s Walker (1987). Graham’s career extended into writing, including cowriting the Disney film The Prince and the Pauper (1990) and a lengthy songwriting collaboration with vocalist and guitarist Bob Weir, penning lyrics for the Grateful Dead as well as multiple Weir side projects. Describing him as a “scene-stealer par excellence,” Edgar Wright paid tribute to the actor’s performance in Phantom of the Paradise , saying that he’s “a constant joy, from his unforgettable line readings to those insane dance moves.” RECOMMENDED READING Night on Earth (Jim Jarmusch, 1991). “This issue is dedicated to westerns made at the margins, produced with little means and made from the scraps of the studio system: cheap programmers of Poverty Row, seventy-minute features of cowboys with guns ablaze on the backlot. These were films that exploited leftover sets, recycled plotlines ad nauseam, and made use of filmmakers and actors idling between major projects or exiled from the studios proper. At once popular and peripheral, they were the morass upon which American cinema was built, the crude oil that fueled an empire. However, they also exist in another lineage, one that includes the films of Luc Moullet, Paul Vecchiali, Larry Cohen, and any other filmmaker who made art with a poverty of means. Embodying all that is criminal and beautiful in the history of cinema, the B western tells the story of its medium.” The editors of the Narrow Margin Quarterly explain the impetus behind their fourth issue , The Western: From B – Z , featuring writing on Andre de Toth, Budd Boetticher, John Wayne, and more. “Look, I think you could look at my life and go: I like standing on the edge of a cliff physically and metaphorically. Meaning, I look at life as an adventure, and I always have, my whole life. I want to understand people. I want to understand life and cultures. We’re looking at life. I wonder: Who are those people? How do they feel? Do they think the way I do? Do they laugh at the same thing? How do I connect with them? And I didn’t want to just be a tourist. I wanted to go make movies there because I also find you really get to know people when you create with them. Everyone has a different subjective reality of what they think about life, about people. And there is common ground in humanity, and I’m looking for that common ground.” For GQ , Zach Baron interviews Tom Cruise for the magazine’s cover story and attempts to break through his elusive shell before the release of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger (2026). “Her biography was catnip. She grew up (for a while, anyway) in a commune. Her godfather was Timothy Leary, the counterculture icon infamous for advocating for psychedelic drugs. She suffered from insomnia and called Al Pacino in the middle of the night to talk. She chose ‘Ryder’ as a stage name because her father’s Mitch Ryder and the Detroit Wheels album was playing when the producer called to ask how she should be credited; apparently ‘Horowitz’—her birth name—was assumed to be less than ideal. Was all the talk about Ryder being ‘smart’ a coded way of acknowledging that she was Jewish? Or was it only a way of acknowledging that she had brown hair?” For the Metrograph Journal’s Cracked Actor column, Christine Smallwood unpacks Winona Ryder’s career and how she offered an alternative to the typical Hollywood “it girl.” “The filmmakers’ tightness of form extends to a similar elegance of its metaphors—the memory palace was a Greek mnemonic device, revived to more extensive use in the Renaissance (notably by Italian hermetic scholar Giordano Bruno, one of the major dramatis personae of Crowley’s Aegypt books) in which the practitioner would conjure a familiar environment and then methodically ‘place’ pieces of information in certain locations there to be more easily recalled later. What if the world itself was a memory palace that contained everything that had ever happened and we just needed the right tools to see it?” For Reverse Shot, Jeff Reichardt reviews Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s “singular and strange” debut feature Chronovisor (2026) and the enduring allure of research as a gateway to discovery. RECOMMENDED EVENTS Faluyi (Ayo Akingbade, 2022). Luxembourg, through November 15: The Casino Luxembourg presents The Day of the Mantis , an immersive film installation by artistic duo M+M (Marc Weis and Martin De Mattia) containing three stereoscopic 3D film installations featuring praying mantises and stick insects. Los Angeles, through February 27: The Marciano Art Foundation presents Tacita Dean: FILM , a reprisal of the British European artist’s 2011 installation that takes the form of an enormous 35mm film strip. New York, September 24 through January 3: The New Museum presents Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony , the first US museum survey exhibition of the video artist’s career, which endeavored to “find new visual forms to capture the rhythm and realities of Black life in America.” Zurich, September 26 through January 10: The Kunsthalle Zürich presents Crossing , the first institutional solo exhibition outside the UK by London-based artist Ayo Akingbade, featuring two new productions juxtaposed with the artist’s earlier works that explore urbanism and architecture. RECOMMENDED VIEWING Netflix presents a trailer for David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026), a standalone sequel and spin-off to Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood (2019) written by Quentin Tarantino with Brad Pitt reprising his role as the title character. data-height="natural"> Sony Pictures Classics presents a trailer for Bitter Christmas (2026), Pedro Almodóvar’s tragicomedy about a commercial director’s tumultuous long weekend and a filmmaker’s attempt to adapt it to the screen. data-height="natural"> Neon presents a trailer for Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden (2026) about a caretaker’s relationship with a terminally ill theater director, starring Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto. data-height="natural"> NYFF64 presents a trailer for My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (2026), the second part of Julia Loktev’s documentary about a group of independent Russian journalists living in exile in the wake of the Russo-Ukrainian war. data-height="natural"> Film Movement presents the new 4K restoration of Zhang Yimou’s Raise the Red Lantern (1991), which will be released in theaters on the 35th anniversary of its release. data-height="natural"> RECENTLY ON NOTEBOOK The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). “It needs virtually no introduction. Fifteen years after its world premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the 2011 Toronto International Film Festival, The Raid (2011) has so shaped the landscape of contemporary action cinema that it’s birthed its own prepositional descriptor: ‘like The Raid’ adorns sundry headlines to describe any action film featuring some combination of a single-location setting, gritty atmosphere, barbarous bloodletting, and no-holds-barred mixed martial arts.” In the latest entry in The Action Scene column, Jonah Jeng revisits Gareth Evans’s The Raid (2011) on its fifteen anniversary and the lasting influence of its kinetic filmmaking. “A movie is expected to explain itself on some level. We agree to be nudged along by the crafty and creative individuals who make it easier for us to follow and understand. But this process also entails our unconscious filling in all the blank spots between the projector and the screen (suggesting presence) and those between individual still images (suggesting motion). This adds up to a form of collaboration we can all accept with pleasure, a creative form of acquiescence that we simply experience as moviegoing.” Jonathan Rosenbaum explores the beauty of elusive cinema and the way that absences in clarity unites the audience and filmmaker. “Late into this horrifying confessional, a soldier admits he’s helped carry out a genocide, and another that he doesn’t see much of a difference between Israel and Nazi Germany. As their words echo in this sepulchral night, Abraham and Szor linger on the buildings around them. Behind their windows, life in Tel Aviv goes on as normal: people sleep, do yoga, run on treadmills, watch Netanyahu announce the army has blocked trucks carrying humanitarian aid into the Strip. It’s at these interludes that NAZA reminded me of The Zone of Interest (2023)—incidentally, Jonathan Glazer here served as executive producer—another incendiary vivisection of the banality of evil, and all the lies we tell ourselves to deny it and carry on.” Leonardo Goi reports from the 2026 Venice Film Festival and examines some of the films in the lineup including Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU (2026), Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , and Mariano Llinás’s Life of Jorge Luis Borges (2026). “Watching films at a festival produces a peculiar form of misremembering. By my third day in Locarno, the films I had seen were beginning to bleed into one another. Through the sheer density of images, a morning motif folded into an evening silhouette, and a line of dialogue acquired the phantom inflection of another film. In memory, the consecutive dissolves into the simultaneous. I found myself drawn to films that seemed to work with this instability—pulling experience apart, rearranging the debris, and holding those disparate fragments up to the light.” In partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, Notebook presents a series of correspondences from burgeoning writers on the ground. WISH LIST Cold Water (Olivier Assayas, 1994). Assayas on Assayas , a book-length conversation between the French filmmaker and critic Jean-Michel Frodon that is “a springboard for an expansive exploration of cinema, memory, literature, politics, travel, and the creative process,” is available to purchase from Sticking Place Books. EXTRAS Mulholland Dr. (David Lynch, 2001). Amanda Karkoutly details Lynchian landmarks around Los Angeles , including the Big Boy Diner, the Doheny Mansion, and his grave at the Hollywood Forever cemetery.
