articles.title: Toronto Filmmaker Survey: Just One Moment
articles.author: Daniel Kasman
articles.description: Tender Loving Care (Mike Leigh, 2026). Courtesy of Joseph Lynn. Midway through the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), Canadian prime minister Mark Carney hosted the Canadian Investment Summit, which had its opening gala at the Art Gallery of Ontario. Bringing together business people from more than 30 countries with the stated aim of accelerating investment in the country which has been beset by trade conflicts with the United States, the event also galvanized a range of community groups with diverse objections to protest the summit, which then brought hundreds of police officers and vehicles to the area just north of the festival center. Meanwhile, just south of that center another new business summit was being held: an inaugural industry market at TIFF. But despite the fraught condition of the film industry, the atmosphere wasn’t of turmoil and opposition but of engineered optimism. The big news at the festival this year wasn’t a new premiere, or what won the People’s Choice Awards (confusingly, the "international" winner was the English-language Elisnore , but the main award-winner was Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s Spanish-language La bola negra ). It wasn't even a controversy over a film rejected from or accepted into the program ( see last year’s report ). Rather, it’s the expansion of business. Or at least, expansion in the hope for more business. Like Cannes with its Marché (since 1959) and Berlin with the European Film Market (1979) before it, TIFF has officially added a industry-focused market, held simultaneously with its large public event that is often characterized as a “people’s festival.” Despite this reputation—or, in fact, perhaps because of it—with its sprawling program, courtship of stars, and territorial focus on premiere status, the festival has for decades attracted international film business, albeit in a more informal manner. Launched with a C$23 million investment, “TIFF: The Market” is a pricey and insistent new trade conference intended both to reclaim some of the deal-making visitors and perceived industry might lost since the pandemic, as well as provide new opportunities for local and international attendees to meet, finance, and sell more films. (Presumably some business might very well take place at and during movies screened at the festival, as a new policy, shown before press and industry screenings, grants permission to use mobile devices, thus sanctioning attending bozos to disturb everyone in the auditorium.) New for the festival this year: Explicit permission to use mobile devices during screenings for press and industry attendees. But what really brings people to TIFF is not the action behind the scenes, but what’s on all those big screens, glowing white in the dark in anticipation of new revelations. The dauntingly large program—always a challenge to parse as much for press as for regular festival-goers—certainly did what the festival does best: bring together excellent highlights from earlier festivals. From Berlin’s competition came Angela Schanelec’s My Wife Cries (all films 2026 unless otherwise noted), whose white, bourgeois, European milieu in Berlin belies its increasingly intense and touching dissection of social and gender relationships, rendered through the director’s mysterious storytelling paths and luminous long takes. Beginning a week before Toronto was the Venice Film Festival, from which the Canadian fest imported Shinya Tsukamoto’s unflinchingly primal anti-war film, Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? , which featured an devastatingly anguished performance by Rodney Hicks as a Vietnam veteran tortured mind, body, and soul by PTSD and guilt over wartime killings. Another gem from Venice was Rami Kodeih’s expertly-crafted debut Furies , about two sisters driven by a confluence of Lebanon’s banking crisis and a medical emergency to rob a bank. And from Telluride came Mike Leigh’s possibly (but hopefully not) final film, Tender Loving Care , a story fundamentally dedicated to all the women who work so hard to fix our broken world (including one played with sublimely comic poignancy by Kate O'Flynn). Notable highlights curated from Cannes included Marine Atlan’s beautiful, fresco-like, Critics’ Week-winning debut La gradiva , about a trip of high schoolers visiting Naples and encountering their own transformative version of the city so memorably seen in films from Rossellini’s Journey to Italy (1954) to Gianfranco Rosi’s Pompei: Below the Clouds (2025). Sandra Wollner’s Everytime , the Un Certain Regard winner, evolves from a deceptively quotidian domestic drama to an evocation of grief’s eerie, lingering affliction. Another German standout, The Dreamed Adventure , Valeska Grisebach’s long-awaited follow-up to 2017’s Western , is an engrossing and unclassifiable Bulgaria-set drama mixing unpredictable tensions between local gangsters, an archeological dig, and middle-aged female desire. And speaking of desire, Géssica Généus’s vibrant Marie Madeleine colorfully reinvents the Biblical character for a modern-day Haiti in which evangelical fervor and earthly longing are so close they verge on combustion. For its own premieres, the festival made at least one significant programming gaff, giving the spotlight to Zack Snyder's morally repugnant The Last Photograph , a Trumpian vigilante fantasy of righteous paramilitary intervention into a depraved and lawless Third World nation. But TIFF also presented some truly excellent premieres, including sophomore director Yoon Dan-bi’s soulful and delicately imagined small-town coming-of-age tale of first love, The World Before , a showcase for both the director (between this and her 2019 debut, Moving On , clearly a major voice in new Korean cinema) and teenage lead Sim Su-bin, in a star-making performance. And Tamil director Karthik Subbaraj’s Dorothy , a blood-brother melodrama of inseparable village hoodlums, should get a prize for its tremendous volte-face, shifting from a story of violent masculinity to one confronting gender acceptance, showing just how radical mainstream filmmaking can be when directed with vigor and dedicated to transformative storytelling. *** As we did earlier this year in Berlin , in order to spotlight the range of impressive films at TIFF this year, I’ve surveyed filmmakers across the festival’s programs, asking them to select a memorable image or moment from their own film and describe why it is particularly special to them. Some directors chose a moment that forms the crux of their entire movie; others zeroed in on an image that surprised them beyond even their own conception. One tells of an analog discovery that impacts the whole style of the film, while others pinpoint the creation or the meaning of a moment that only they, behind the scenes, could reveal. While some of the answers below may even make you feel like you need to see the film to fully understand them, but that’s perfectly okay. We aim to showcase how different artists choose to reflect on their work and share what they value, from the filmmaking process all the way through to the final film. If the answers inspire you to watch (or rewatch) their films, that’s all the better. Rehearsals for a Revolution (Pegah Ahangarani, 2026). This photograph is the reason the film exists. For most of my childhood it was another page in my parents' album. My mother and father sitting close together, his arm around her shoulder, a small framed picture held between them. I would look for a second and turn the page. Then I was told the story. The man in the frame is Davoud, my parents' close friend. My parents and Davoud were young revolutionaries who lost their belief once the crackdown on opposition groups began. A few years after the 1979 revolution Davoud was executed as a political prisoner. Before this photograph, that frame held a picture of Khomeini, smiling kindly. That was the image the state published. So they removed the founder of the system that killed their friend and put Davoud in his place. Now I see what I could not see before. My father has made himself smaller than he is. A faint smile on both their faces, and inside it, vulnerability, guilt, grief. They are looking into the lens. The frame is turned the same way, toward us. The dictator erased him and wanted him forgotten. They kept him in the frame. I also notice the plant in the corner, its pink flowers. Loss and continuing, in one image. Hope is itself a form of resistance. Without its story, this is a family photograph. With it, a document that contradicts the official narrative. Dictators can erase people from history. We can bring their images and stories back, and give them a place in our collective memory. That is what I want my films to do. — Pegah Ahangarani, Rehearsals for a Revolution (Centrepiece) Masao Adachi Takes a Passport Photo (Kamal Aljafari, 2026). On the second day of shooting, Shida-san, the elderly woman who ran the photo studio, wanted to print Masao Adachi's passport photo. The machine broke, and the printer made an error and printed the photo in red—it was an ink issue. Suddenly, she didn't know what to do and started talking to Neo Sora, the cameraman on the film, asking him for help. He left the camera, keeping it running, and stepped into the frame, and while he was trying to help her fix the issue, the tripod—which was a bit loose—let the camera drift and pan on its own, leaving the frame, showing the colorful photos of children, and slowly coming to rest at the edge of the studio door, where the street could be seen. During this time, Shida-san was telling him that she didn't know how to deal with the issue, since it was usually her late husband—the photographer, who had passed away a year earlier—who handled things, and that she was worried the company that produced the paper and ink for the old printer might shut down. I sat there with the producer Aiko Masubuchi, looking at the camera moving alone. We looked at each other and smiled. This accident basically made the film. It gave answers to all the questions that might have arisen about the characters and who they are—questions that fiction films would have answered superficially. Life gave the answers. It is the kind of cinema I deeply believe in: allowing oneself to be guided by what unfolds once the decision has been made to make a film with real people in real places. Reality is always more interesting than the idea one has of it, as Masao would say. — Kamal Aljafari, Masao Adachi Takes a Passport Photo (Wavelengths) The most important moment for me is the scene in which Kristine Froseth’s face gets destroyed. Every time I watch it, I am fascinated by it and I get the shivers. It’s so operatic and unhinged. The way it builds from her character being ill and pining for her husband, to her face morphing into a monster’s face, to the way she finds her rage at last. And just on a visceral level it’s so magnificent, with all the reds and golds, and the teal castle walls, and the dreamlike quality of the bedroom, and the swelling score, and the stabbing, and the blood. Kristine was channeling real hurt and rage—I have never in my life seen anything like it. I don’t know where she pulled that emotion from, but it was a very deep and dark place. At the end of the scene, she was standing there with blood streaming down her yellow satin gown and down her legs, and she had to leave the set for a few minutes to gather herself because she was sobbing so hard (so was I). I could watch this scene a million times and never get tired of it. I don’t mind saying that I think it’s one of the best scenes in cinema. — Anna Biller, The Face of Horror (Midnight Madness) Nobody's Violence (Denis Côté, 2026). Among the exhilarating moments in the making of Nobody’s Violence , I remember the adventure of finding the film’s visual look in Super 16mm. I had long discussions with cinematographer Vincent Biron. I wanted to create something nonchalant, impure, and dirty. Naturally, he went looking for a somewhat vintage solution. He showed me YouTube clips about a German film stock called ORWO. During a visit to the Berlinale, he went out and bought 100 or 200 feet of it to run some tests. The look turned out to be extraordinary, and we very quickly decided to shoot a good part of the film on that stock. Then, some time before the shoot, a certain fear began to set in: exposing ORWO is rather unpredictable. The solution, then, was to shoot all the nights and interiors on Kodak and keep ORWO for the day exteriors. This marriage of two film stocks was as worrying as it was exciting. I knew I was playing with fire, and I could see the terror in Vincent’s eyes. On one side, we had the fairly smooth comfort of Kodak; on the other, the unpredictable, dirty, extraordinarily vintage solution of ORWO. We even had a drone shot, inevitably captured on video. In the end, the color-grading stage became a wonderful playground, and we are proud of our great impure adventure. — Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence (Wavelengths) Clarissa (Arie Esiri, Chuko Esiri, 2026). Jamil McGinnis’s book All Paths Lead Home opens with a comment made by Camille Billops to bell hooks that touched me profoundly: “Put all your friends in [your art], everybody you loved, so one day they will find you and know that you were all here together.” Those nearest and dearest to us feature as Clarissa’s party guests in the climax of the film. — Arie Esiri, Clarissa (Special Presentations) I want to talk about a scene between Marie Madeleine (Gessica Généus) and Sister Melody (Melissa Mildort). Marie Madeleine is leaning on a wall at the entrance to an outdoor church, watching the church women singing, and thinking her own thoughts. Melody comes up and surprises her, asking if she would like to join the church gathering. Marie Madeleine declines and goes back to the brothel on her own side of the street. I profoundly love that scene, even though it’s not necessarily a scene that would attract attention. I love the softness of it. It makes you wonder what religion could have been to the world if there was this softness in the way they share their spiritual values with those around them. What if, you know? The second thing I love is the proximity of two drastically different choices cohabiting a space without necessarily clashing with each other. The simplicity of this moment is really changed with silence—a dense silence that carries a lot of unspoken emotion. — Gessica Généus, Marie Madeleine (Centrepiece) There are so many moments that feel important to me for different reasons in At Night— it’s hard to choose! Perhaps the bar scene, with all the women talking, all the women listening to each other, is the one I’d pick. It’s inspired by a scene in Bette Gordon’s Variety (1983) featuring her friends—artists and sex workers—in a bar talking. The bar scene in my own film is so fascinating to me, so prismatic, it manages to hold many different points of view with relative tenderness, at the same time as maintaining a kind of tension. Like another favorite scene, the shop scene, it doesn’t try to flatten out the group’s asymmetry or difference of opinion; rather, it stays with it: what’s oppressive for one woman is liberating for another. I love how the scene manages to hold that complexity. Ben Rivers’ camera work is also formidable in this regard. He had the courage to stay put—to keep the camera trained on characters not speaking, on characters as they listen—and the effect is that, as a viewer, you’re watching people listening, which puts you too in the position of listener. This is what makes the scene so tender and open. The star of this scene to my mind is the character called Kátia. From a white feminist perspective, what she says is deep. She pulls us all up. In many ways, stretching beyond this scene even, Kátia does this repeatedly. She’s like a heartbeat. — Beatrice Gibson, At Night (Wavelengths) There is an image that appears three times in the film: one showing the small garden of a suburban home, as seen from a window. The first time, it’s a photograph being filmed, hanging on the wall of the main character’s apartment—David’s—depicting this view: down in the garden, a woman is holding a child in her arms and looking toward the camera. It’s David’s mother, holding David when he was a child. The second time, the same photo is being looked at by Malia, now trapped inside David’s body: she looks at this photo, which should be intimate and evocative of memories for this body, but is completely foreign to her. The third time we see this garden, it is David—himself trapped inside a woman’s body—who opens the window of what used to be his childhood bedroom and looks down at the view. The garden has aged; his mother is no longer there; there are no children anymore. It is a scene that embodies the indescribable sense of exile in which the characters are immersed—a sense of loss that lies at the heart of what the film seeks to express. A ghostly presence hovers over these three visions: that of the person who likely took the original photo—David’s father, who has long since passed away.” —Arthur Harari, The Unknown (Special Presentations) In the second half of the film, the main character, Fátima (Luisa Ahl Laabiad), goes to one of the local fishermen’s houses and discovers that a tragedy has occurred. It’s a very intimate scene, portraying a deeply painful moment. When shooting it, we were afraid that the emotion might be overshadowed if we took an overly descriptive or informative approach. Therefore, during the shoot and later in the editing, we gradually began to remove elements and layers, simplifying the scene while keeping it legible. Eventually, by stripping the scene back to its essential elements, we were able to amplify its emotional core. Without using dialogue, without even focusing on the tragedy itself, we direct the attention instead to the emotion evoked by the characters’ gaunt faces and the atmosphere of the room. The heavy silence, broken only by the sound of a distant sea, made the scene more intense than any dialogue could have. — Helena Girón, Samuel Delgado, The Fortunate Isles (Discovery) There are many moments in Furies that I remember fondly, one being the “pirate scene” earlier in the film. Our two main characters—Dalia (Maria Nakouzi) and Maro (Rym Mroue)—are playing pretend with Maro’s 8-year-old son, Ali. Amidst Lebanon’s devastating economic crisis and corruption-fueled electricity outages, they’ve transformed their living room into an arena for fantasy, imagination, and adventure. It’s a moment of escapism amidst unimaginable socioeconomic turbulence. This moment is directly inspired from my childhood. During long electricity outages, sometimes with war waging outside, my family and I would build pillow-forts and tents and turn the entire home into a playground-slash-movie set. Imagination was an act of resilience, just like it is for Maro, Dalia, and Ali in our film. I knew early on that I wanted to film the play pretend scene unapologetically like an action scene. The camera is completely immersed in the fantasy that these characters have created for themselves, as opposed to spectating or watching them at a distance. Approaching it like an action scene makes the moment feel visceral, character-centered, and alive, so you as an audience member are right there with them. You’re a part of this family now. This scene celebrates the sheer resourcefulness of these two women—how, with just a few neon lanterns and a couple household basics, they create a whole universe for this little boy. Those same neon lanterns and sources of light later reappear during the heist, transforming from tools of play and innocence into tools of rebellion and survival. The very same light that fuels their escape from reality ultimately enables their fight to survive it. —Rami Kodeih, Furies (Centrepiece) It would have to be the moment when Fujino (Furi Nanase) starts running on roads between the rice fields in the rain: that moment is when Fujino life begins. — Hirokazu Kore-eda, Look Back (Special Presentations) All of a Sudden (Ryusuke Hamaguchi, 2026). It is impossible for me to choose one particular scene from my own film as something special. None is more privileged than another; every moment in my films derives its value only from its relationship with, and mutual support of, all the other moments. Every moment is equally important. I would be very happy if audiences could experience the film in that way as well. — Ryusuke Hamaguchi, All of a Sudden (Special Presentations) For me, it’s a moment early on, when a village woman defends the young girl under siege in this small village, by declaring that she’s a “rebel,” not a “bandit.” Immediately after, we have a shot from behind of the senior officer on site, walking with purpose to exterminate this rebel. He stops in his tracks, and demands to know who said that. The line of villagers remain silent, as does the officer nearby who knows who said it, but says nothing. What means so much to me is the musical score here. A slight push of dread underneath it all. The mildest version of it. Something that just nudges us to focus on this moment, but also step outside of it. To contemplate that this isn’t just a scene unfolding—it’s indicative of the world we’re in today. Words, expression, outbursts of raw emotion, must all be tempered. Each one can be an infraction, and even get you killed. And yet, we’re immersed in this world of Phoolan, of people so far down the economic ladder, who have the courage to risk their lives to say, and do, what they feel is righteous. And the magic of this moment did not come from me as a writer/director. It came from what the actors and on-set crew did, from what my editor snipped together, from what my composer felt and responded to, and from what my sound designer enhanced and elegantly got out of the way of. It’s everyone’s synergy, and it all converges into a moment the viewer will miss if they’re folding laundry or cooking while watching this. —Richie Mehta, Phoolan (Special Presentations) There is a frontal shot of the prisoners, in the police station, sitting down, and some of their heads appear chopped off by the framing. It is a copycat image from Jorge Cedron's work in the clandestine 1973 film Operación Massacre . The 2009 novel Glaxo is kind of an homage to the 1957 book Operación Masacre , and with that layer, we paid tribute to a lesser-known gem of Argentine film. The heads chopped by framing, while reshooting just as Cedron did, found a meaning I had not felt as an audience member. It is strange, and compelling in this case, to look directly through somebody else's frame. — Benjamín Naishtat, Glaxo (Special Presentations) It's the last scene of the film that I find affects me the most. I realized watching it in the cutting room after we shot the film that it is here where the film becomes most personal to me. A young man who has experienced loss and love and death and the bleakness and the joys of these dark years, and of youth, finds himself alone at a bar, a survivor, not sure whether to go forward or to give up, to seek love, or pleasure, or not to, and in that moment—finishing a beer, taking the last sip and considering what's behind him, and ahead—he gets the courage to go on, to get up, to join these other men on the dance floor, and to dance. I knew that doubt, that fear, that hope, that possibility then and I still know it now. — Ira Sachs, The Man I Love (Special Presentations) Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? (Shinya Tsukamoto, 2026). At the end of the film, the protagonist, Allen Nelson, delivers a message to the audience: “War causes terrible suffering, but it also makes people commit terrible acts of violence. It can happen to people from any country, to any kind of person. It could be you. It could be your own beloved child.” When I made this film, there was one thought constantly on my mind: I wanted to bring Allen back to life once again—the man who came to Japan and shared with us his own experiences of war. Although the protagonist of this film is an American, what I wanted to convey is that becoming a perpetrator of violence is not something that belongs to any one country or nationality. Under the circumstances of war, it can happen to anyone, regardless of where they come from. In this final scene, Allen recalls a precious moment he experienced on the battlefield: the memory of warm water. Amid the horrors of war, that small but deeply meaningful memory comes back to him. — Shinya Tsukamoto, Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? (Special Presentations) Everytime (Sandra Wollner, 2026). There is a moment I think many of us know: after a long night, you climb onto a roof or a hill or some other slightly forbidden place and watch the sun come up. You take terrible pictures of it, and of course they fail completely. They cannot hold the moment, only prove that it happened. The sun as a mess of a few orange pixels. In Everytime , we watch two teenagers on a rooftop in Berlin after such a night. They have taken something, they are listening to music, talking about the day, the sun, the seagulls, all kinds of things. We see them from an almost impossible distance, and yet we hear them very close. Their chitter chatter has the lightness of a first, cautious love, every word so careless, as if there were still billions of words ahead of them. The girl gets up, takes those same bad, precious pictures: of him, of herself, of the sun. Then something shifts. She looks directly toward us, or through us, as if she has seen something behind the camera. Or as if, in some strange way, has seen herself from afar. Vague premonitions of death, a dream within a dream, a déja vu, or, more to the point, a feeling that, in this infinitesimal moment, life is all it will ever be. That was one of the first images. — Sandra Wollner, Everytime (Centrepiece) The World Before (Yoon Dan-bi, 2026). There is a scene where, after deciding to go to the seaside with Dujae (Kim Eo-jin), Jin (Sim Su-bin) does sit-ups alone and checks herself out in the mirror. It's a bit silly, suddenly working out because she's going to the beach with someone she likes, but for Jin it's actually quite serious. In front of the mirror, Jin's lips stay closed, but I laid in the sound of her breathing hard. It's a sound that could never actually be heard at that moment. I wanted that breath to hover right at the viewer's ear, almost like ASMR, so that just for this instant, the audience could feel as close as possible to what Jin is sensing. Being conscious of Dujae, Jin looks closely at her own body for the first time. Wanting to be seen by someone makes her see herself in a new way too. Then, right in the middle of this, her younger sibling catches her in the act. I love this scene. For Jin, it's a very private and significant moment, but to anyone else watching, it might look a bit funny. That's the kind of film I wanted The World Before to be. — Yoon Dan-bi, The World Before (Platform) Fire Flies (Zhang Lu Xinyuan, 2026). For some time, shooting footage that would later become Fire Flies , I followed my friend Yin through the darkness in the mountain, almost blinded by the glowing DV screen, barely able to see the trail. I listened to her footsteps and used the image as a guide, like some kind of cybernetic human. Then came the moment when Yin crouched down and began stirring the bushes with her flashlight. I froze and knew: a film existed here. She murmured a question that blurred imagination, delusion, and sensory experience, reminding me of a childlike intensity of focus and a bubbly sense of in-betweenness. —Zheng Lu Xinyuan, Fire Flies (Wavelengths)

articles.title: Toronto Dispatch: The War Against Memory
articles.author: Michael Sicinski
articles.description: Life of Jorge Luis Borges (Mariano Llinás, 2026). Words mean things, but that meaning is always changing. Sometimes those changes are organic, a gradual movement that is driven by the changing needs of speakers. But sometimes those changes are engineered from above, to serve the needs of those in power. After years of algorithmic censorship, we now see words like “unalive” or “le$bean” replacing their antecedents even in conversation, even if only ironically. (As if to prove the point, the plot of the new film by Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence , manages to hinge on the issue of assisted suicide without ever uttering the s-word. It’s as if the film anticipates the language that will be deleted from many online reviews.) It is an embarrassing cliche to describe an authoritarian gesture as Orwellian, but using technology to eliminate words and concepts from our consciousness cannot really be described in any other way. The word “memory” has undergone a significant shift over the past twenty years. Do you remember memory? More often than not, people now use the word to describe the capacity for digital storage, not the human ability to recall people, things, and events. This evolution seems quite deliberate. Virtually every innovation by Big Tech works to externalize the memory of the world, to delete it from our brains and store it somewhere where it can always be erased, should it become troublesome. Tools for convenience, when designed for the profit of the few, inculcate habits that dull our minds. But more than this, the offloading of consciousness onto the digital realm sets the stage for whole-cloth revisionism. Digital knowledge does leave a trace, a footprint deep in the code, but it is legible only to a select few. But it isn’t a palimpsest. A fully digital archive lacks reminders, the partial erasures and strikethroughs and overwriting, that one finds in physical culture, as well as in our memories. Instead, it allows for a wholesale find/replace function – instantaneous, possibly permanent change. (One man can rename a body of water for petty, jingoistic reasons, and suddenly, there is it.) So memory, if shared, is a site of resistance. But of course there are many different ways to externalize memory. Artwork is one such way. It allows humans to memorialize facts and objects, thoughts, and experiences that are inconvenient, to actively prevent erasure and to share evidence among and between human minds, away from the top-down imperatives of late capitalist meaning-making. In this sense, an artwork can serve as an alternative archive, collating histories and ideas for preservation. Artworks often exist within institutions, which include museums and film festivals like the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF). These institutions sometimes gatekeep, but crucially they also preserve. In addition to preserving individual art objects, they can also make space, preserving the very possibility for sustained attention. Right-wing strategist and former filmmaker Steve Bannon has described the need for reactionary political actors to “flood the zone,” to bombard the populace with more information, and more horror, than it is possible to mentally assimilate. This is a process that militates against memory by fragmenting attention. But artworks have a unique ability to focus our attention, to create a clearing for analysis and understanding. Art can be higher ground, a beachhead from which to establish new tactics. In recent years, many experimental film works have exhibited an archival impulse. This has taken different forms, including the documentary exploration of archival processes, as seen in Jessica Sarah Rinland’s films, or the exploration of personal histories as a form of material culture, something we find in films as diverse as Payal Kapadia’s A Night of Knowing Nothing (2021), Sophy Romvari’s Still Processing (2020), and the work of British-Nigerian artist Onyeka Igwe. And of course Chronovisor (all films 2026 unless otherwise mentioned), one of the year’s most fascinating films, is about the research process, the accumulation of clues from old documents and dusty tomes, as a way to present contra-power histories that may have been hiding in plain sight. Wavelengths, TIFF’s programming section for unconventional, artist-driven filmmaking, has long been an oasis for what Scott MacDonald has called “a critical cinema,” works that interrogate social structures as well as the conditions of their own making. In a variety of ways, many of the films presented in TIFF’s 2026 Wavelengths edition engage with the question of memory and the archive. Some of them, like Mariano Llinás’s brilliant, sprawling biography of Jorge Luis Borges, are in part about the process of delving into the archives and unearthing meanings that can only be derived from material history. Much of Life of Jorge Luis Borges (all titles 2026 unless otherwise noted) consists of Llinás and literary scholar Ernesto Montequín examining manuscripts and ephemera in order to piece together exactly how Borges became a transformative figure in world literature. In addition to traveling to places that were significant in Borges’s development—a library, a café, a hotel, a city block—we see the two men comparing artifacts to the descriptions of them that Borges wrote in his work. A children’s book with drawings of tigers (not by Borges, alas), or a literary magazine with a jade-green cover (alluded to in the story contained therein), and dozens of handwritten drafts are all rigorously examined, as Llinás films Montequín’s excitement as if they were making an unboxing video for YouTube. The Borges papers exemplify the seductions of the archive, showing that no matter how well you know a given subject, it is always possible to be surprised and amazed. Electric Fragments No. 1: Rom (Uomini) (Yervant Gianikian & Angela Ricci Lucchi, 2001). While some archival records augment and amend our knowledge of figures we already know quite well, others stand as evidence of otherwise ordinary lives. The commitment to archival exploration as a means of historical retrieval is seen most vividly in Electric Fragments No. 1: Rom (Uomini) (2001) by the late filmmaking team of Yervant Gianikian (who passed away this July) and Angela Ricci Lucchi (who died in 2018). Rom (Uomini) is one of a series of short films that exemplify the couple’s filmmaking ethos. They collected home movies, official government films, and other cinematic marginalia in order to consider the cultural history and ideologies contained therein. Their method could scarcely be simpler: present the film as-is, apart from slowing it down, tinting it, and adding an unobtrusive soundtrack. As opposed to numbers two and three in the Electric Fragments series (which deal with colonialism in Vietnam and the covert sexualization of women in public, respectively), Rom (Uomini) is gentle and offers the viewer lowkey revelations from a not-so-distant past. It is taken from home movies shot in a Romani camp in Italy, and as the subtitle tells us, we are simply watching human beings: a family playing around outside, acting silly, and loving each other. One refrain in the film is the image of a baby sleeping on the ground, and a man, presumably the child’s father, placing his fedora over the baby’s face to shield them from light and noise. Gianikian and Ricci Lucchi understand that this footage is both unremarkable and priceless, probably one of the only extant records that these people and their community ever existed. It is to the great credit of Wavelengths’ programmers, Jesse Cumming and Andréa Picard, that they showcase older, underseen films like this one, along with the TM , a lyrical 1974 work by Japanese Fluxus composer Takehisa Kusogi. The Black Box Is Orange (Yuula Benivolski, 2026). Among the other films playing in Wavelengths, the political potential of the archive is demonstrated most unequivocally in Yuula Benivolski’s debut feature, The Black Box Is Orange . Composed like an essay film but also incorporating diaristic elements, Black Box finds the Russian-born Canadian returning to her childhood of Shlomi, a rundown border town in Israel. Benivolski uses her own family photos along with official military images to articulate how Shlomi was built on the land that was once the Palestinian village of al-Bassa. The Israelis have done everything they can to erase al-Bassa, but its material existence persists, in disused railroad tracks, a concrete slab in a forest, and the continued existence of a building that has withstood decades of sustained ordnance. In her own family photos, as well as images found in the archives of Israel’s Ministry of Defense, Benivokski compiles evidence of al-Bassa’s existence. Benivolski identifies a single home on a high hill, one she remembers from her childhood and that keeps appearing in both family snapshots and official military images. In a place where the landscape is constantly being destroyed and rebuilt in order to erase any traces of Palestinian life, this structure remains like a silent witness. In its combination of personal memory and official records, this chapter of the film, titled “The Little White House,” recalls the best work of Harun Farocki or the documentary work of Israeli filmmaker Amos Gitai. “The Little White House” would be one of the year’s best films on its own. But Benivolski surrounds it with different kinds of discourse, with the viewer asked to consider how these registers of information bounce off one another. In one segment, Benivolski tells the story of a Palestinian family whose home is repeatedly raided. Handful by handful, the soldiers steal pictures from the family’s photo album, and Benivolski learns that the Israeli Ministry of Defense contains a massive archive of such stolen photos, classifying them according to their own internal categories. As we see a series of still images of Palestinians and Israelis going about their lives (which includes the frequent wearing of gas masks), Benivolski asks us to consider the dehumanization implicit in this disciplinary archive. Forever...Forever (Johann Lurf, 2026). While Belivolski’s film is explicitly political, there are, of course, more idiosyncratic forms of memory, ones in which the sociopolitical meanings remain implicit. Some films are less concerned with producing an objective record than in generating a visceral impact by looking at the world in unusual ways. Such films are records not of the thing itself, but the affective relationship between the filmmaker and their subject. In a sense, what is meant to be preserved is the experience of looking at a person, place, or thing. Johann Lurf’s hypnotic Forever…Forever is a record on one very specific place in Austria, the Ottenstein Reservoir in Austria. For this 20-minute film, Lurf shot footage from the exact same angle for nearly two years. There is a body of water in the foreground, a bridge over the water, and two shores covered in trees. Forever…Forever is the type of film that could hypothetically be made anywhere. If you pay close enough attention to a given place for a long enough span of time, it is inevitable that changes will occur: changes in season, in light, in activity. But as Lurf demonstrates, the reservoir is a unique location. It represents an engineered space that contains water, an artificial construction in the landscape. From his chosen angle, Lurf fills most of the frame with water and the reflected sky. The bridge is dead center, like a bowtie holding the image together. Using time-lapse photography, Forever…Forever details the cycles of time as observed from this single spot. The sun rises, it sets, the moon comes out, and it sets in turn. The trees accumulate snow, their leaves change. Using an accelerating timeframe, as the timelapse increasingly condenses more time into fewer 65mm film frames, Lurf presents a document of what the naked eye cannot see. Much like Michael Snow’s La région centrale (1971) or certain films by the late Tomonari Nishikawa, Forever…Forever is a testament to deep observation. It shows us that any place participates in the general, cosmic movement of the planet while also maintaining its radical particularity. The Address Book (Mustafa Uzuner, 2026). Like Lurf’s film, two short films in the program pay close attention to very specific objects, suggesting the ways that people go about preserving cultural heritage against destruction. Mustafa Uzuner’s The Address Book is a simple film that shoots the pages of an address book, in order, one after the other. The method recalls Hollis Frampton’s filmed script Poetic Justice , or better yet Heinz Emigholz’s page-by-page presentation of his notebooks in the Basis of Make-Up series. The Address Book preserves a delicate object and offers it for display. Specific names and numbers tell us that the book’s owner is part of the New York art world, but when we learn that it belonged to Joseph Cornell, an additional layer of meaning emerges. Cornell, after all, exemplifies the artist as magpie, collecting and assembling nondescript bits of detritus and memorabilia in sculptural showcases. Uzuner’s film performs much the same function. Cornell was a filmmaker as well as a sculptor, composing his works using excerpts from science films, newsreels, and, in the case of his most famous film, Rose Hobart (1936), clips of the titular actress from her role in East of Borneo (1931). Uzuner combines these tendencies, “encasing” Cornell’s personal artifact on celluloid. La Prospettiva (1653) (Ben Russell, 2026). La Prospettiva (1653) by Ben Russell is a gentle observational recording of the process of physical preservation and upkeep. The film gazes down the length of the Colonnade at the Palazzo Spada in Rome, watching carefully as two workers clean the dust from its arch and walls. This is one of Russell’s simplest and most poetic films, recalling Friedl vom Gröller’s cinematic haikus of European life. Drawing on the vernacular of structural films like Serene Velocity (1970) and, indeed, Wavelength (1967), Russell optically takes us into the colonnade, turning the portico into a bounded yet infinite space. As the title tells us, Russell is considering the way that Baroque space, designed by Borromini, plays tricks with our perception, tweaking the Albertian optics of the Renaissance and making the space less rational, more haptic and experiential.In a way, La Prospettiva forms an intriguing diptych with Russell’s other film from this year, Another Earth . That film is organized around a blitz of doomscrolling on an iPhone, imparting a sense of claustrophobia and despair. The phone, after all, takes all of human life and reduces it to the consumable optics that photography inherited from the Renaissance. By contrast, La Prospettiva tells us that certain things can endure for centuries, that the world contains great mysteries, provided there are people willing to care for them. Ghazal-e Sorkh (Maryam Tafakory, 2026). One of the festival’s most powerful films, Ghazal-e Sorkh by Maryam Tafakory, speaks very directly to the engineering of memory through public spectacle as well as active suppression and destruction. Where Tafakory’s recent films have involved a feminist and queer counter-reading of the history of Iranian cinema and media, Ghazal-e Sorkh engages with governmental propaganda, specifically the cult of personality around Iran’s last shah, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi. Framed around the story of her own father’s arrest for attending a protest in 1974, Tafakory’s film details the mass suppression of books and authors under the Shah’s dictatorial rule, which he was able to wield in no small part due to the support of Western capitalist nations. Tafakory tells the viewer about others who protested in 1974, including a group of young women poets who were killed. Ghazal-e Sorkh does not need to remind the viewer of the 2022 murder of Jina (Mahsa) Amini by Iran’s morality police. The film trusts us to recognize that fascism takes many forms but that misogyny remains constant. Tafakory goes on to list numerous books that were banned by the Shah’s cultural institutions, noting the reasons given for their suppression. As always, the forces that engage in censorship understand what “free speech” liberals conveniently forget. Words are dangerous, and books represent the precarious archive of revolutionary speech. Tafakory has prepared a damning document that memorializes both the Shah’s tyranny and the West’s political and financial incentives for ignoring it, particularly when compared with the demonizing of the 1979 revolution. We see the Shah’s lavish, decadent 2,500-year celebration of the Persian Empire, attended by fawning heads of state from around the world. And as a final, poignant twist of the knife, Tafakory interpolates fragments from the Shah’s propaganda film, Flame of Persia (1971), narrated by none other than Orson Welles. The message is clear: no one, no matter how politically astute, is above being lured astray by flattery and money. Microcosmic Orbit: Encased (Danaya Chulphuthiphong, 2026). Archival knowledge is unstable, something that must itself be guarded from attack. Generative AI doesn’t simply erase human history. It is used to create deceptive histories out of decontextualized sounds and images. A film that speaks directly to this, 09/05/1982 , premiered in the 2025 Wavelengths program and was one of the most important films of last year. In it, directors Camilo Restrepo and Jorge Caballero present supposed documentary footage, both audio and video, of the violent aftermath of an unrising in an unspecified Latin American nation. As the film continues, anomalies accrue and eventually we realize we’ve been duped. The filmmakers used generative AI to fabricate very convincing archival evidence of a historical event that never took place. 09/05/1982 is precisely about the danger posed to historical knowledge, including material artifacts of the past, by tools that have been designed to inculcate false consciousness. A similar point is made, although in a somewhat different register, by Danaya Chulphuthiphong’s Microcosmic Orbit: Encased , from this year’s program. Where Restrepo and Caballero demonstrate the possibility of media manipulation, Microcosmic Orbit is about the artificial preservation of the natural world, which can also entail manipulation and deception. Beginning with shots of people swimming in a lagoon, Chulphuthiphong uses close-ups and distorted angles to confuse the viewer regarding what we are actually seeing. Some of the plants and mosses we witness are artificially grown, kept in terrariums. As with several other films discussed above, Microcosmic Orbit takes us behind the scenes as workers in a natural history museum organize and arrange plants, rocks, and lichens to produce exhibits that mimic “nature” but are not in fact natural formations. Chulphuthiphong reveals the process whereby “nature” is manicured, manipulated, and preserved. The irony is that “nature” would not be an object to preserve were it not for the human race’s endless reshaping of the earth, and the eradication of the very flora on display in this natural history museum. In a sense, the exhibition space in Microcosmic Orbit presents the natural world like an argument: edited, assembled, and exhibited as a metonym, an example of something beyond itself. Chulphuthiphong also demonstrates the ways that cinema can participate in this argumentative process. This is a vital reminder. Memory isn’t neutral. It is subject to engineering, even by seemingly benign institutions. As so many of these films demonstrate, archival knowledge is partisan because those instigating enforced forgetting are also partisan. Filmmakers, then, must become archivists, because archivists represent a guerilla force in the war against memory.

articles.title: The Action Scene | “The Raid” at 15
articles.author: Jonah Jeng
articles.description: The Action Scene explores the form, history, and visceral power of action cinema through its set pieces. Clockwise from top-left: The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011), Merantau (Gareth Evans, 2009), The Raid 2 (Gareth Evans, 2014), The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). It needs virtually no introduction. Fifteen years after its world premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the 2011 Toronto International Film Festival, The Raid (2011) has so shaped the landscape of contemporary action cinema that it’s birthed its own prepositional descriptor: “like The Raid ” adorns sundry headlines to describe any action film featuring some combination of a single-location setting, gritty atmosphere, barbarous bloodletting, and no-holds-barred mixed martial arts. The film’s seismic success—along with that of its sequel—jump-started global interest in its director, its stars, Indonesian action cinema, and, building on the popularity of Thai martial arts movies from the previous decade, Southeast Asian action cinema more generally. It all began in 2007 when Welsh director Gareth Evans, shooting a documentary in Indonesia on the local martial art pencak silat , visited a silat school in the province of West Sumatra specializing in Silek Harimau , or “Tiger style.” Impressed by the physicality and presence of one of the students, Iko Uwais, Evans approached him with an offer to make a movie. Conceived and pitched to financiers as a vehicle for “reclaiming” silat and launching Uwais as a star, their first project, Merantau (2009), marked a pointed departure from silat ’s local association with cheap, antiquated, often fantasy-based and VFX-infused television programs. 1 Centering on the indigenous tradition of “merantau,” in which young men leave their families to venture out into the world, acquiring experience and knowledge, the film aimed for a certain authenticity, rooting its choreography in actual Silek Harimau moves and their practical application. Despite moments of extravagance—for instance, a high-fall off of construction scaffolding filmed in a single take, the floatiness of the descent exposing the use of wires—the fight scenes are largely grounded, eschewing the acrobatics seen in other martial arts pictures. Iko Uwais and Yayan Ruhian fight using Silek Harimau in Merantau (Gareth Evans, 2009). As a screen-fighting form, silat ’s movement profile comprises what Evans describes as an interplay between “fluidity” and “aggressiveness”—between flowing maneuvers and sharp contact points, 2 Silat ’s percussive snap evokes the knee- and elbow-heavy Muay Thai and Muay Boran popularized by Tony Jaa—a key predecessor for Uwais as a Southeast Asian martial arts star who broke onto the international scene. But whereas Jaa’s fight scenes from the 2000s often decelerate dramatically around big stunts—slow-motion and overlapping editing, which replays part of the stunt from a different angle, appear in abundance— Merantau displays an aesthetic of perpetual motion, each strike flowing into the next with minimal pausing or posing between hits. In an interview about The Raid 2 (2014), Evans notes how he and his team “never loop[ed] a shot, showing it more than once. [It was] only that one moment and in real time” 3 —a practice that emerged almost fully formed with Merantau . Unable to get funding for his second, more ambitious film, which would go on to become The Raid 2 , Evans pitched The Raid as an interim project, the now-legendary single-location premise initially proposed as a cost-saving device. The Raid intensifies—and reworks— Merantau ’s principles of realism and perpetual motion when a police squadron is tracked as it raids a drug lord’s apartment complex, and the officers are forced to fight for survival when discovered. Once more, there is minimal slow motion and overlapping editing, generating the impression of a real-time onslaught (“it’s just ‘attack, attack, attack’” 4 ). Silat does appear, but as part of a medley of other martial traditions; for example, the squadron captain Jaka, played by national Judo champion Joe Taslim, executes grappling and throwing maneuvers that play to the actor’s strengths. If Merantau ’s realism references an existing archive of silat moves, The Raid ’s realism feels more “universal,” subordinating “proper” martial arts form to the desperation of a kill-or-be-killed scenario, in which any maneuver from any tradition is fair game if it helps the fighter survive. This universalism was carefully orchestrated; in Uwais’s words, “we concentrated on making a silat movie that we could export to other countries.” 5 Although still a platform for spreading awareness for silat and Indonesian culture, The Raid minimizes a focus on silat ’s relationship to local tradition and national heritage, leaning instead into action-movie iconography that would be legible to an international audience. Synergy between camera, cutting, and choreography in The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). Among the film’s most celebrated realist flourishes is the handheld camerawork by cinematographers Matt Flannery and Dimas Imam Subhono, which sprints the tightrope between clarity and chaos. Indebted to the Jason Bourne movies directed by Paul Greengrass and the broader 2000s trend for frenetic, “documentary-style” cinematography (Evans has also cited Romain Gavras’s 2010 music video for M.I.A.’s “Born Free” as a primary influence 6 ), the camera pitches from room to room alongside combatants, conferring a sense of breakneck immediacy. However, unlike the Bourne films and their offshoots, in which the combination of jumpy editing and unsteady framing often transforms the image into an impressionistic frenzy, in The Raid choreographic beats are clearly communicated through clean continuity editing, emphatic insert shots, and gaze-directing tilts and pans, sustaining a sense of geography and intricate cause-and-effect. This balancing act incorporates the best of both worlds: the immersiveness of the embodied camera, which seems to place the viewer in the scene (a pseudo “first-person,” more “subjective” kind of perspective), and the vicarious thrill of seeing other bodies do extraordinary things (a “third-person,” more “objective” type of presentation). This latter aspect—the lucid display of skilled bodies in spectacular combat—was especially central to the film’s success, particularly in the West. After a decade of rampant CGI and Bourne-style impressionism, many viewers found The Raid ’s practical stuntwork and clean visual presentation to be a blast of fresh air: a return to real bodies, real stunts, and real physical stakes (in this sense also, the film followed in the footsteps of Jaa and the Thai action cycle of the 2000s, which hinged on a sense of “authentic” physical action). Yet another kind of realism, working in the film’s favor. Over the next few years, films like Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol (2011), John Wick (2014), Mad Max: Fury Road (2015), and Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation (2015)—all of which were similarly marketed and received as a “return of the real,” marked by legibly filmed practical stunts—also premiered to widespread acclaim. There are moments in the movie when filmmaking and choreography seem to alchemically fuse, as if each were tailor-made for the other. Multiple examples appear in a brawl between Taslim’s Jaka and the drug lord’s top enforcer, Mad Dog (Yayan Ruhian, a silat instructor and demonstrator who makes a brief but memorable appearance in Merantau ). The fight commences with a fusillade of blows, captured in medium shots. Cut to a split-second wide shot of Mad Dog launching himself in the air, his momentary weightlessness underlined by the frame opening up, inducing a similar feeling of airiness and levitation in the viewer. Once contact is made, the shots tighten and accelerate again, as if bombarding us with blows as well. Seconds later, a three-shot combo shows Jaka ducking low in frame to evade Mad Dog’s punch (first image below); Mad Dog kicking toward the camera as Jaka dodges frame-left (second image); in the same shot, Jaka ducking again to evade Mad Dog bending his leg back (third image); then Mad Dog extending his leg into another kick (fourth image), which connects with Jaka’s face in close-up (fifth image). A thrilling three-shot combo in The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). Without being literally “from” either Jaka’s or Mad Dog’s point-of-view, these trio of shots nonetheless approximate it: In the first shot, Mad Dog’s punch arcs forward, almost like we’re throwing it ourselves, while the kick in the second shot seems to nearly strike us, as if we were the intended target. The framing brings us as close to the fighters as they are with each other, heightening a sense of claustrophobia and physical danger. Despite this, the match-on-action cutting and center-framing—the focal point of each shot occupies the same visual region as the preceding shot’s, saving the viewer from having to search the frame—makes the action supremely easy to follow across cuts. The fight scenes in The Raid can grow exhausting, even tedious, so relentlessly does blow after blow rain down within homogenous rooms and hallways. Moment to moment, however, there’s an ongoing synergy between the framing, editing, and choreography, which complement each other so well that, often, it’s easy to lose oneself in the flow of violence, forgetting the filmmaking choices that shape this flow. The Raid 2 contains similarly propulsive passages, but it also cranks up the baroque artifice. Opening with a static long shot of a grassy field that decelerates the first film’s run-and-gun pacing to slow-cinema extremes—“I wanted to tell the audience, ‘this is not Raid 1 ’’’ 7 —the film picks up mere hours after the original ended, observing as Uwais’s cop-protagonist Rama goes undercover to bring down a crime syndicate. From there, the formal and narrative flourishes proliferate. Bird’s-eye framing presents a mud-caked prison riot as a writhing, indistinguishable mass of bodies, like some medieval painting of hell. When a character is thrown through a window, the camera somersaults with him and lands on its “back,” the frame turned upside down. Two characters—a sibling duo, one wielding a bat, another a pair of hammers—feel like they stepped straight out of an anime, and, despite dying gruesomely as Mad Dog in the original film, Ruhian inexplicably returns in a minor role. Innovative vehicular action in The Raid 2 (Gareth Evans, 2014). If The Raid is focused and contained, The Raid 2 is swing-for-the-fences epic action cinema, sprawled across more than two years of story time and seemingly half of Jakarta and with whiz-bang filmmaking to match. The film’s celebrated car chase is a prime example of the latter. Circumventing a host of resource limitations—as Evans notes, Indonesia lacks the infrastructure for vehicular action, such as the means to easily secure a stretch of road and redirect traffic, 8 and budgets tend to be a fraction of Hollywood’s, curbing the possibility of large-scale property destruction 9 —the sequence is a feat of innovation. Sandwiched between thugs in the backseat, Rama starts punching and kicking every which way, the film switching to an overhead shot of the car’s interiors, laid out like a design blueprint. As the fight continues, the film cuts between two planes of action—the scuffle in Rama’s car and bumper-car chaos involving a trailing vehicle—and the choreography abounds with (literal as well as figurative) swerves. A henchman, knocked halfway out a car window, cracks his head against a passing semi, leaving a bloody spot on the trailer paint. Dodging a kick, Rama rakes the assailant’s leg across shards of glass from a previously broken window. In the film’s formal showstopper, a long take travels between three moving vehicles by threading through the windows—the result of stuntmen literally handing off the camera like a football. Top: The Night Comes For Us (Timo Tjahjanto, 2018). Above: Jailbreak (Jimmy Henderson, 2017). Since the series’ resounding success, the cast and crew have branched out, plying their trade around the world and indelibly shaping the landscape of contemporary action filmmaking. Uwais and his trusted stunt crew—the “Uwais Team”— have designed action for a range of works, including indie sci-fi actioner Beyond Skyline (2017), the highly underrated Mile 22 (2018), and the Grand Guignol, horror-adjacent one-two punch of Headshot (2016) and The Night Comes For Us (2018), helmed by Timo Tjahjanto, Evans’s heir apparent in hyper-violent Indonesian action cinema. Uwais stars in all four of these and has appeared in numerous others, such as Triple Threat (2019), The Expend4bles (2023), and Timur (2025), his directorial debut. Evans has pivoted away from Indonesian-language projects and silat choreography but retained his signature, blistering visual style, as seen in Havoc (2025) and the first season of Gangs of London (2020–). Ruhian and Cecep Arif Rahman of The Raid 2 make a cameo appearance in John Wick: Chapter 3 (2019), a series that has become a showcase of action cinema’s who’s who, spanning the likes of Donnie Yen, Scott Adkins, Mark Dacascos, Hiroyuki Sanada, and Jung Doo-hong. Indonesian representation within this context feels like a veritable induction into action cinema’s hall of fame. A comparable feeling of significance attends Ruhian’s and Taslim’s inclusion in The Furious (2026) , which similarly assembles some of contemporary action cinema’s leading talent, both behind and in front of the camera. Additionally, the Raid films have helped raise the international profile of Southeast Asian action in general. Films like the Cambodian Jailbreak (2017), the Filipino BuyBust (2018), and the Malaysian Wira (2020) were clearly inspired by the narrative and aesthetics of the first Raid especially, whereas the whirligig dance between camerawork and choreography in the Vietnamese Furie (2019) and Furies (2022) feels reminiscent of The Raid 2 . In retrospect, The Raid 2 ’s geographical expansion of the original’s scope—from a single apartment complex to various corners of Jakarta—feels like extratextual foreshadowing. Since 2011, the series’ stars, filmmakers, and silat -style combat have left their mark well beyond Indonesia’s borders; in the new millennium, only a handful of martial arts films— Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000), Ong-Bak (2003), John Wick —can claim a comparable level of international reach and renown. Inextricably woven into the DNA of contemporary action cinema, the Raid series continues to shape the genre’s evolving textures and sensibilities over a decade out, its influence showing no sign of abating. 1. “Interview: ‘The Raid: Redemption’ Director Gareth Evans Talks His Realistic & Brutal New Action Film,” Complex , March, 20, 2012, https://www.complex.com/pop-culture/a/complex/interview-the-raid-redemption-director-gareth-evans. 2. “Interview: ‘The Raid: Redemption’ Director Gareth Evans Evans Talks His Realistic & Brutal New Action Film.” 3. Peterseim, Locke. “Interview: The Raid 2 Director Gareth Evans And Star Ike Uwais,” Open Letters Monthly, April 3, 2014, https://www.openlettersmonthlyarchive.com/hammer-and-thump/interview-the-raid-2-director-gareth-evans-and-star-iko-uwais. 4. Peterseim. 5. articles.title: Defending the Elusive
articles.author: Jonathan Rosenbaum
articles.description: Last Year in Marienbad (Alain Resnais, 1961). 1 Although it’s seldom acknowledged, one of the supreme pleasures of movies is the confusion and uncertainty often prompted by the beginning of a story, when we’re not yet fully tuned in to what’s going on. As in our sleeping dreams, a sense of infinite possibility stretches before us. That seemingly limitless vista soon disappoints once it is foreshortened into something real and recognizable, such as a place, an environment, a mood, a character, a theme, a genre, or a plot. Yet without these comfortable anchors, something that resembles prenatal bliss envelops our ignorance, and the fact that we can imagine almost anything makes the start of a film with all of its possibilities seem peculiarly and even exclusively ours. This is another way of saying that the less we know about something, the more our imaginations and expectations can come along to fill in the gaps. So the pleasure I’m talking about is a kind of shameless narcissism, albeit one that feels healthy because of its spur to our creative impulses. 2 Father Mother Sister Brother (Jim Jarmusch, 2025). Courtesy of MUBI. It’s also seldom acknowledged that cinema is interactive, becoming a collective experience even when we’re alone thanks to our phones, social media, and other tools used to convey our impressions afterwards. But because illusions of presence and motion are generated by viewers providing continuity to still frames as they’re being projected, with ourselves as the links between a projector and a screen, this means that the “movie” exists only inside us, even if we prefer to think of it being located elsewhere. A movie is expected to explain itself on some level. We agree to be nudged along by the crafty and creative individuals who make it easier for us to follow and understand. But this process also entails our unconscious filling in all the blank spots between the projector and the screen (suggesting presence) and those between individual still images (suggesting motion). This adds up to a form of collaboration we can all accept with pleasure, a creative form of acquiescence that we simply experience as moviegoing. Thanks to Jim Jarmusch’s minimalism, we partially become engaged with the title characters of his 2025 film Father Mother Sister Brothe r by speculating on some of the details about them that the director chooses to exclude. An inability to fill these gaps may produce boredom, but a capacity to participate effectively means becoming Jarmusch’s fellow artist, an ideal spectator, making the title characters ours as well as his. 3 The Wind Will Carry Us (Abbas Kiarostami, 1999). Some of cinema’s finest artists—Erich von Stroheim, Alfred Hitchcock, Orson Welles, Stanley Kubrick—manage to entertain as well as provoke us. Some, such as theatrical and literary-minded Patrick Wang and hyperactive Romanian gadfly Radu Jude, are better equipped to get us to think creatively, while others—I’d pick Steven Spielberg—deal more with our passive reflexes, and with feelings more than thoughts. Similar distinctions can be made between moviegoers, some of whom might shift from being passive viewers of Spielberg’s Disclosure Day (2026) to active viewers of Jude’s Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World (2023) or Wang’s A. Rimbaud (2026). Some of the fiercest debates among cinephiles tend to be about which filmmakers and which moviegoers belong in each category. “I want to give an audience a hint of a scene. No more than that,” Welles told an interviewer in 1938, a year before the stage and radio director flew to Hollywood to become a filmmaker. “Give them too much and they won’t contribute anything themselves. Give them just a suggestion and you get them working with you. That’s what gives the theatre meaning: when it becomes a social act.” Sixty-five years later, when I was writing an essay about Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami—famous as a storyteller for his missing pieces and withheld information—it seemed appropriate to start with this quotation. It is this social act—the viewer interacting with the work’s ambiguities—that is created when Kiarostami refuses to explain why the protagonist of Taste of Cherry (1997) wants to die by suicide (or even whether or not he succeeds), and when the protagonists of And Life Goes On (1992) and Through the Olive Trees (1994) fulfill their own monomaniacal missions. Similar experiences keep us engaged with Wellesian mysteries, starting with “Rosebud” in Citizen Kane (1940), even (and especially) after they remain unsolved for Welles’ characters, obliging us to determine what they might mean. And by the time Kiarostami made The Wind Will Carry Us (1999), his last feature to be shot on film (and for me his richest) before he switched to video, his compulsion to omit certain things extended to keeping many of his characters partially or wholly off-camera—not to create mysteries about them but to keep them from distracting or diverting us. The advantage of most mystery stories that are eventually resolved for audiences and characters alike is something we like to call “closure”—the satisfaction that comes from settling a nagging question, thus leaving us free to forget this particular story and to embark on another one. But if we’re denied this satisfaction and the nagging questions remain—as in Michelangelo Antonioni’s L’avventura (1960), where the film’s starting protagonist, Anna (Lea Massari), inexplicably disappears from the story and her absence is never resolved or explained in the remainder of the film, in spite of all the efforts of other major characters to find her. This understandably made many viewers feel cheated—the film was roundly booed when it premiered at the Cannes Film Festival—but the aftereffects of this frustration remained and became part of the film’s haunting theme. It wasn’t a film one could easily forget a week later, because its mysteries lingered, becoming in effect mysteries about life and existence and what remains unknowable about them. Indeed, one could argue that solving mysteries is the first step to forgetting them. In the movies, solvable mysteries are thus part of an entertainment model already predicated on consumption, digestion, and a comforting sense of oblivion after reaching a conclusion. But having an unsolved mystery stuck in your craw, part of an aesthetic model, requires creative adjustments. 4 The Asthenic Syndrome (Kira Muratova, 1989). Welles, Antonioni, and Kiarostami were hardly alone in using absences to spark an audience’s participation. Robert Bresson often used sounds to replace images, and Carl Dreyer reinvented the spatial coordinates of certain scenes in The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928) and Ordet (1955) as they unfolded in order to provoke our personal investments in their plots. In Ordet , the camera’s seeming encirclement of two seated characters talking, a troubled adult and a trusting little girl, without ever moving behind them creates an unconscious miracle, one that we aren’t even supposed to notice, in order to prepare us to accept a conscious miracle soon afterwards. Provoking our unconscious collaboration is a guiding principle for many such filmmakers, including such disparate names as Jacques Tati, Alain Resnais, Michael Snow, Jacques Rivette, James Benning, Béla Tarr, Kelly Reichardt, Pedro Costa, and Patrick Wang. The transgressive Soviet and post-Soviet filmmaker Kira Muratova turned a story about one character into a film that another character was watching in her 1989 masterpiece The Asthenic Syndrome . And Radu Jude keeps us readjusting to an ever-shifting environment of hypocrisies and contradictions by interrupting his own social critiques to explore a particular setting, inserting a literary quotation à la Jean-Luc Godard, or injecting a character’s alternative avatar, in Bad Luck Banging or Loony Porn (2021) and Do Not Expect Too Much from the End of the World , films as comically unsettled as their titles. Another Muratova ploy for displacing her viewers while replacing her protagonists comes in her final feature, Eternal Redemption: The Casting (2012), where one encounters the same lines of dialogue spoken by different actors in different settings. One can be irritated about or titillated by (or both) the meaning of this before discovering that the fictional director of these scenes died before completing a film, leaving the producers befuddled about what to do with this footage. One can share their befuddlement and/or reflect that Muratova might have been anticipating her own death in 2018. You might say that to make this movie ours, we have to do something more than imbibe it. In short, we must embrace its mysteries in order to complete it, and bring our life experiences to enhance and inflect its elusiveness.
