articles.title: Venice Dispatch: The Garden of Forking Paths
articles.author: Leonardo Goi
articles.description: NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, 2026). To watch my first film at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, I wore a VR headset. I say “watch” when the more accurate verb would be “experience,” at least going by the fest’s preferred vocabulary for what goes down on Lazzaretto Vecchio, an island a stone’s throw away from the Lido. Once used as a checkpoint for Holy Land pilgrims, and then—after the plague reached the lagoon in 1423—a leper colony, it is, in 2026 AD, now home to the virtual reality sidebar. The architecture has barely changed through the centuries. Dotting the high-ceilinged corridors that used to house the city’s moribund, festival guests can find various booths, each promising its own immersive experience: a multi-sensory journey through the sounds and visuals of David Bowie’s world, a trip to the Galápagos narrated by Margot Robbie, a chance to relive the first expedition that climbed Mount Everest in 1953, Sherpas in tow. I’ve been coming to Venice for twelve years, but busy screening schedules on the Lido have always made my trips to Lazzaretto all too brief;; this time too I could only carve an hour on my first day. What I saw, however, made it difficult to watch anything else. Directed by Faiz Abu Rmeleh and Karen Manor, Raj’in (We Shall Return) (all titles 2026 unless otherwise noted) documents the ethnic cleansing of West Bank Palestinians by Israeli settlers and armed forces. It alternates 360-degree footage of life under occupation with 2D phone clips bearing witness to the invaders’ violence—unnameable brutalities perpetrated against men, women, children, and animals, each video screening while the rest of your visual field is cloaked in darkness. Headset on, eyes and ears physically unable to turn away from all those horrors, the immersive, you-are-there approach was perfectly suited to the film’s design. By bridging the gulf between people made to suffer those unspeakable depravities and outsiders watching them at a remove, Raj’in doesn’t just render the ongoing genocide against the Palestinians unnervingly vivid, but re-humanizes its casualties, at a time when mainstream news coverage tends to write them off as cold statistics. I kept thinking about this all through my time on the Lido, and especially when Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA premiered in the official competition. Mostly, I thought about an interview artistic director Alberto Barbera gave just days prior, hinting that the film was given a late slot because he didn’t want politics “to become the only topic of conversation at the festival, overshadowing the other movies.” It felt like a decision unworthy of an event whose prerogative should be to invite debate—no matter how difficult—not recoil from it. NAZA wasn’t just one of the official competition’s standouts, but one of the edition’s most consequential entries. Shot in the aftermath of October 7, it gathers testimonies from 24 Israeli intelligence officers in an attempt to reckon with the genocide in Gaza: the measures taken to erase an entire people, and the narratives the perpetrators peddle to justify those atrocities. Filmed at night and on rooftops scattered all around Tel Aviv’s affluent city center, the documentary unfurls as a string of conversations between Abraham and his subjects, their faces and voices digitally altered to protect their identities, so that while the director remains visible—aglow in the chalky light spilling out of nearby buildings—his interviewees are shrouded in impenetrable darkness. That’s a fitting choice for a film that’s often unbearable to watch. NAZA , named after the acronym used by Israeli officers to denote the collateral damage left by IDF strikes, only shows the consequences of these attacks at the very end, with clips recording the aftermath of an air raid on the Strip. It’s a devastating coda, but so is everything else that precedes it. There is something terrifying about the ease with which these soldiers embraced the narrative that “there are no innocent people in Gaza,” and saw themselves as part of a system that required no moral judgment, just successful and ruthless decision-making (“the goal was quantity, not quality,” an officer says in reference to strikes where the NAZA dwarfed the number of Hamas targets). Late into this horrifying confessional, a soldier admits he’s helped carry out a genocide, and another that he doesn’t see much of a difference between Israel and Nazi Germany. As their words echo in this sepulchral night, Abraham and Szor linger on the buildings around them. Behind their windows, life in Tel Aviv goes on as normal: people sleep, do yoga, run on treadmills, watch Netanyahu announce the army has blocked trucks carrying humanitarian aid into the Strip. It’s at these interludes that NAZA reminded me of The Zone of Interest (2023)—incidentally, Jonathan Glazer here served as executive producer—another incendiary vivisection of the banality of evil, and all the lies we tell ourselves to deny it and carry on. Imperium (Sergei Loznitsa, 2026). NAZA was only one of several astonishing documentaries in an edition where works of non-fiction largely outshone their fictional counterparts. For another indelible case in point, there was Sergei Loznitsa’s Imperium , a sprawling, three-hour travelogue across the USSR patched together from forgotten footage recorded by an Italian crew between 1970 and 1973. The material—presumably intended as filler for a more conventional doc—is the sort of stuff Loznitsa’s archival projects have long homed in on: glimpses of life in Soviet Russia where crowds take precedence over individuals, and quotidian activities are resurrected with voracious curiosity. As befits the director’s MO, there are no talking heads or title cards, save for the geographical coordinates orienting us along a journey that starts in Moscow and stretches to the farthest ends of the Union. An empire projecting a delusion of homogeneity is here revealed as something much more permeable and syncretic. Buddhist monks in orange robes and blue-tinted shades strolling around temples in Kalmykia; Christians flocking to centuries-old churches in Armenia; women boasting their traditional clothes somewhere in Turkmenistan; models strutting with their Italian-style coats in Riga. A miraculous alchemy binds the original directors to the man editorializing their material several decades later. The Italians didn’t just provide Loznitsa with a time machine spanning 60-plus hours of footage, but also shared his keen eye for incongruous images, wherein the cultural uniformity flaunted by Moscow is routinely complicated by endemic symbols and traditions. The result is a riveting snapshot of a bygone world that never feels didactic. Imperium doesn’t need to spell out the collision between “then” and “now” for you to realize just how different Putin’s Russia looks from this eminently strange and polyphonic milieu. And like the director’s finest, it exemplifies Loznitsa’s ability to reanimate the past, and turn archives into living, breathing things. DAU (Ilya Khrzhanovsky, 2026). One of the negative talking points around the official competition was the inclusion of what’s already gone down as a kind of film maudit , DAU , from the Russian Ilya Khrzhanovsky. To be clear, and notwithstanding the statement Barbera issued on the eve of the festival, the worry here is not the director’s passport. It’s that the film, a rallying cry against totalitarianism, was made by an artist who reportedly embraced the same tyrannical means he purported to attack. The story behind the project’s genesis is nothing short of incredible. In 2006, then 29-year-old Khrzhanovsky pitched a biopic of famed Soviet physicist and Nobel Prize winner Lev Landau, received money from the EU funding body Eurimages with Swedish and German support, and then proceeded to construct his own Synecdoche, New York (2008) in Kharkiv, Ukraine. Between 2008 and 2011, over four hundred non-professional actors lived inside a 42,000-square-foot replica of a Soviet-era research institute. They played versions of themselves transposed to USSR lifestyles, so fastidiously recreated that everything—down to the food served and clothes worn—was made to mirror the period. Khrzhanovsky’s bid for authenticity bordered on madness: real former KGB officers were cast as the film’s fictional KGB guards; some of the thugs terrorizing the institute’s staff were actual criminals (among them Russian fascist Maksim Martsinkevich, who’d be convicted of murder and found dead in his cell in an apparent suicide in 2020); and outsiders wishing to visit the premises had to hand over their electronics and wait for hours to obtain visas. Inside, however, those who’d signed up for “the experiment”—as a 2019 trailer euphemistically called it—were subject to all kinds of psychological and physical abuse. Participants could be arrested, rough-handled, stripped naked, while sexual scenes were often non-simulated (Albina Kovalyova, whom Khrzhanovsky had hired as the project’s official chronicler, has described life at the institute in a hair-raising exposé at The Telegraph ). Crucially, there were no scripts. “Over seven-hundred hours of [the residents’] reactions to these extraordinary circumstances were recorded,” per the trailer, and out of that gargantuan material Khrzhanovsky spawned features, series, an exhibition at the centre Pompidou in Paris, and now, at long last, a biography of the man who triggered this entire folly into being. Does the film itself live up to its insane backstory? I’m still not sure. Of all the features to have graced the festival circuit (see the original 2019 Dau , or 2020’s Degeneration and Natasha , all three unveiled at the Berlinale during the era of festival director Carlo Chatrian), this one feels closer to the biopic Khrzhanovsky must have shopped around to get cash in the mid-2000s (i.e. bold, but not too bold to scare potential backers). It’s a chronological if elliptical look at the man’s life that kicks off in 1928, when Dau (Teodor Currentzis) is a promising physicist roaming the streets of Leningrad, and wraps with the scientist on his deathbed 40 years later. Dau’s a genius, but the only measure of his greatness comes from the praise colleagues and sycophants readily pile on him. In other words, we must trust he is one, for Khrzhanovsky is much less interested in his day-to-day routine than in his inveterate womanizing, and in keeping with the real-life Landau, Currentzis screws his way through DAU as a cad whose experiments spill from the lab to the bedroom, much to the chagrin of his devout wife Nora (Radmila Shchogolieva). Like J. Robert Oppenheimer, Landau would be recruited by his country’s military-industrial complex to help in the nuclear arms race; like 2023’s Oppenheimer (with which Khrzhanovsky’s portrait would make for a singular double bill), DAU rests on a friction between a work made of long chats and Khrzhanovsky’s febrile filmmaking. All throughout, the writer-director intersperses existential debates (“are we scientists moral leaders or technicians creating models of destruction?”) with sequences where sounds and visuals burst forth with such assaultive force as to suggest a film undergoing some kind of seizure. I’ll remember DAU not for its hero’s marital struggles or the vast chunks in which Khrzhanovsky’s epic borders on melodrama, but for these dizzying moments: a masked ball with guests donning the most sinister costumes while a brass band plays with deafening vigor around them; a couple of scenes that look like optical illusions—one where Dau and his mentor stand atop an iron grate suspended several feet about the ground, their silhouettes arranged in a way that blurs your sense of foreground and background, another where the two schlep up a hill at a 45-degree angle while the slope is flattened into the horizontal axis, so that their bent backs seem to defy logic. Khrzhanovsky recruited Lol Crawley as one of his cinematographers, and at its most stunning, DAU evokes the same muscular energy of another film shot by the Englishman, The Brutalist (2024). Like Brady Corbet’s, Khrzhanovsky’s portrait of a genius strains for images worthy of his grandeur, and the few times it achieves them, the effects are breath-taking. Bucking Fastard (Werner Herzog, 2026). “Muscular” is a descriptor that’s long been tossed at Werner Herzog, whose Bucking Fastard was another highlight in an otherwise underwhelming official competition. In it, siblings Kate and Rooney Mara star as sisters who dress, move, and talk like one—a double act loosely inspired by the real-life case of the late Freda and Greta Chaplin, the only known twins who spoke synchronously. It’s the kind of wacky real-life story Herzog has orbited his entire career. The Chaplins rose to fame in the 1980s after they were convicted of stalking their next-door neighbor, a truck driver they’d become obsessively besotted with. In the writer-director’s riff, the man’s a wealthy Lothario played by Orlando Bloom, and the film kicks off in a surreal vein redolent of Yorgos Lanthimos before swelling into a more romantic fairytale. It’s not just the sister’s act that feels uncanny; everything does. Shot by Peter Zeitlinger, Herzog’s cinematographer since the mid-1990s, Bucking Fastard traffics in sweeping, unbroken sequences, most of them shot on a gimbal, and there’s an intoxicating effect to the floating camerawork that leaves the whole thing hanging in a kind of dream space—long before a third act that sees the siblings dig a tunnel through a mountain that legend says will lead them from rural Ireland to the faraway Orkney Islands. Herzog’s first fiction foray since 2019’s Family Romance, LLC , Bucking Fastard is often ridiculous, but it’s so committed to the bit and so earnest about its love for the eccentric duo as to become strangely hypnotic. Possible Love (Lee Chang-dong, 2026). I wonder what Herzog might have to say to Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), the moneyed filmmaker who saunters into Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love fueled by the haughty belief that “documentaries are a powerful means to inspire others.” Ye-ji is making a film about South Korea’s troubled workforce which will center on Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) and her husband Ho-seok (Sul Kying-gu), a factory worker who lost his job after his company was bought by a US private equity firm. The thematic affinities with Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (2025) are hard to miss: together, the two features make the case for unchecked neoliberalism as a plague shattering the country’s social fabric. But where Park couched his film as a farce, Lee sustains a far more harrowing register. So traumatized is Ho-seok by the loss of his gig he doesn’t just shudder at the idea of letting Ye-ji interview him, he cannot bring himself to join a therapy group with other former coworkers. Lee, who wrote the script with Oh Jung-mi, shows a perceptive eye for the dehumanizing effects of late-stage capitalism. Possible Love isn’t just a fierce critique of Ye-ji’s predatory project and the misery porn she’s after, but a testament to the ways the atomizing, cut-through logic so ingrained in our economic order makes it impossible to dream up alternative realities, how it renders things like “workers’ solidarity” hollow slogans. The lucky employees who kept their jobs after the restructuring are referred to as “the living,” those who didn’t “the dead,” and Ho-seok—who used to call his colleagues “brothers,” went on strike with them, and watch them turn their backs on him once the cops showed up at the picket line—is effectively grieving over the death of a family. Nothing in Possible Love is more lacerating than a therapy session in which a fellow “dead” wonders if her present sadness is the price she’s paying for a happiness she was never supposed to feel. Still, this is no dirge, and if Lee’s film can skirt miserabilism that’s credit to Jeon’s performance. Her turn as Mi-ok—the crowning jewel in a work that towers high above anything else in this year’s official competition—suggests a woman who gradually wakes up to the malevolent schemes of her interviewer, and in the final act, as Ye-ji and her rich husband invite Mi-ok, Ho-seok, and their ten-year-old son to spend a few days at their seaside mansion, all the rage Possible Love accrued along the way finally detonates. The doc-within-the-film conceit gives cinematographer Kim Ji-yong a chance to seesaw between different coverage: static shots for Ye-ji’s footage, handheld for Lee’s; as the director lingers on Mi-ok at the climax, actress and film strike a near-molecular symbiosis: it’s as though the fervor she radiates made the frames vibrate. Musk (Alex Gibney, 2026). Early into Possible Love , the two couples are having dinner at a high-end restaurant when Mi-ok—class differences and social anxieties all but evaporate thanks to unhealthy amounts of soju—says Ye-ji’s husband looks like Steve Jobs. Never mind that’s patently not true: the tech guru “looked free,” she says dreamily, “like he could solve all our problems.” The words rattled around in my head all through Alex Gibney’s Musk , a near four-hour closeup that says less about the richest man on Earth than it does about our readiness to hail figures like him as prophets. The operative question here is not who is Elon Musk, but how could he assume so much power, and why did we all decide to hand it to him. Predictably, Gibney could not land a tete-à-tete with his subject, leaving Musk to summon a second-hand portrait sketched by reformed disciples and longtime skeptics. It also resorts to deep-fake technology to stage talking head-style segments where a digitally-created Musk spouts some of the deranged stuff he’s said in public, a choice that befits the fake persona he’s nurtured and opportunistically tweaked through the years. That said, it’s hard to shake off the feeling that Musk amounts to little more than an extended newsreel, most of it familiar but no less infuriating for that. We begin in the late 1990s, when Elon was an IT dork at the helm of Zip2—a tech company that provided city guides and maps to newspapers—and wrap today, the man so immured in his obscene wealth and delusions of extraterrestrial colonialism as to look and sound like an alien himself. Gibney wants to chip away at the idea of Musk as a genius, and doesn’t need to look too hard for evidence: multiple failed launches at SpaceX, fatal bugs in Tesla’s autopilot tech, to say nothing of the cancerous results of his anti-deficit crusade as head of DOGE. Far from “the world’s greatest inventor,” as throngs of adoring Silicon Valley bigwigs insist he is, Musk suggests he might instead be the world’s greatest salesman, a fraud whose myth has been inflated by media conglomerates all too willing to kowtow to his demands. Life of Jorge Luis Borges (Mariano Llinás, 2026). Gibney’s is a meandering and necessarily incomplete portrait, a good way to think about the festival’s best: Mariano Llinás’s Life of Jorge Luis Borges . Anyone familiar with the filmmakers collective Llinás co-founded—Pampero Cine—will know the group’s penchant for restlessly inventive, sinuous narratives. From Llinás’s magnum opus, La Flor (2018) to Laura Citarella’s Trenque Lauquen (2022) and, more recently, Alejo Moguillansky’s Endgame (2025), what unites different Pampero Cine productions is a seditious belief that films could turn into games, and viewers into co-conspirators actively partaking in their directors’ efforts to subvert storytelling conventions. Seen in this light, Llinás’s biography is not just an illuminating closeup, but a phenomenal manifesto of the collective’s idea of cinema, so open to fissures and digressions as to become, to borrow from the literary titan himself, a garden of forking paths. As he did in La Flor , Llinás outlines the rules of his game right at the start: Life , he tells us in voiceover, came to being once a foundation handed him exclusive access to a treasure trove of relics: manuscripts, drawings, books, and all sorts of other inestimable documents that belonged to Borges. And Llinás, aided by scholar Ernesto Montequín (a Sherlock Holmes to the filmmaker’s Watson), turns to them as clues in his quest to sketch a portrait of the man. That the pursuit is hopeless is the point. Life makes no claim to coherence or completeness, as every object Llinás trains his gaze on beckons him into a maze of bizarre conjectures and coincidences, and the film—not unlike one of Borges’s short stories—becomes a kind of labyrinth, sending director and Montequín around the world in hopes to uncover more about the writer through the places that haunted him, and vice versa. I’m not sure I could ever do justice to the extraordinary vitality Life communicates, or the contagious fever Llinás’s literary forensics transmit. (What a year this is turning out to be for book and film lovers; watching the two men work their way through Borges’s writings, convinced they might yield the most astounding secrets, I kept flashing on Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s Chronovisor , another film that treats texts as oracles). I suspect much of that effervescence has to do with the director’s willingness to welcome mistakes and imperfections instead of shying away from them. Life is littered with scenes another filmmaker might have disposed of as errors: we hear Llinás complain, offscreen, that the shots we’re seeing are “amateurish,” “out of focus,” “corny,” “cliché”. But he still includes them, and in his hands, they give the film the rare feeling of something that’s inventing itself as you watch, and you, the spectator, the illusion to not just witness but take part in that creation. No film I saw this year energized me quite like this. So I turned to the web for my own search. As it happens, Borges visited Venice once, in 1984, when he was already blind, an octogenarian travelling with a woman he’d fallen hopelessly in love with, and would be his wife for a few months only before his death in 1986. There’s a picture of them standing under the cloister of the former monastery in San Giorgio Maggiore, another island, like Lazzaretto, sitting between the Lido and San Marco. The convent is now home to the Giorgio Cini Foundation, a cultural center that resolved, in 2011, to honor the 25th anniversary of Borges’s passing by creating a maze inside the monastery’s walls out of 3250 boxwood plants. “This labyrinth-garden is not about getting lost,” said a review online, “but about finding a dimension of pure beauty.” I’m not sure that’s what I found when I got there. A storm was just leaving Venice; dark clouds chased each other over the lagoon and the boxwood quivered in the wind. My phone died. I wandered about trying to get a feel of the place, but it looked like an empty tourist trap. I’m not convinced Borges would have found a dimension of pure beauty there either. But in the days that followed, I kept going back to that trip, the maze—Borges’s and Llinás’s. Even now as I type, almost a week since that screening, I can feel my senses heightened, my mind agog, primed for all manner of mysteries and revelations. How rare, and how thrilling, to come across a film that can invite you to look at the world anew.

articles.title: Survival Tactics: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
articles.author: Dylan Adamson
articles.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year’s participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this final installment, three critics explore how “tendenko,” a Japanese term that implies isolating to survive a tsunami, resonated across the program. “We live in a state of apocalyptic fetishism,” a radio announcer proclaims in Ann Oren’s Objet A (2026), and the slate of films at Locarno this August did little to dissuade its spectators of this assessment. As has been everywhere observed in recent years, the constant sounding of the alarm has become the 21st century’s room tone, and film festivals are not situated on high enough ground to be safe from tsunami-like waves of crisis. Locarno, for its part, engaged with the apocalypse in a number of ways: Some films got up on soapboxes, others languished in despair, and a select few films and film-related events proffered solutions for living through this dire state of affairs. Objet A (Ann Oren, 2026). Manhunt (2026) premiered the same day the TIFF lineup was announced, sans Manhunt , and Canadian director Wayne Wapeemukwa introduced his film by praising the megaphone Locarno affords its artists: “Whereas Locarno programs boundary-pushing cinema, TIFF programs silence.” Taking inspiration from a murder spree perpetrated by two teenage boys in Northern British Columbia in 2019, Wapeemukwa’s second film lies somewhere between Taxi Driver (1976), Gummo (1997), and Elephant (2003) . While its actors take a bracingly improvisational approach, Manhunt is unfortunately burdened with a well-rehearsed diagnosis for teen violence, pinning it on a melange of video games, incel ideology, and capitalist realism. The slippery slope from mediated to IRL cruelty weighs heavy on Manhunt ’s mind. (“Like and subscribe,” one boy says before an execution.) But it is, in all, too credulous of the fire-and-brimstone promises of the online right, its provocations bearing the politics-of-concern of a teen internet-safety awareness. The film aims to offend—and I admit to being as obediently shocked and appalled as many of the elderly Swiss women I spoke to on my way out of the screening—and suffers from an eagerness to make its point in all-caps, with the ending taking place amid a literal forest fire. I’m not saying silence is a virtue, necessarily, but perhaps a little restraint would be nice. When confronted with the end times, a polemical approach can be tempting. Entering the festival, my uninterrogated preconception of the Hollywood Blacklist (the subject of this year’s retrospective, curated by Ehsan Khoshbakht) was that a number of writers of well-intentioned and limply directed social-problem pictures had been barred from working in Los Angeles for a few years. To my relief, the program disproved this prejudice again and again. Force of Evil (1948), Ruthless (1948), and He Ran All the Way (1951) each conjured forceful, disparaging visions of modern American life, which demonstrated greed and ambition as structuring forces in American society. That said, a grandstanding approach held sway in some films: Character after character in Smash-Up: The Story of a Woman (1947) decries the horrors of alcoholism; The Sound of Fury (1950) was burdened with an academic coda explaining the pitfalls of mob rule; even Chaplin’s otherwise laid-back A King in New York (1957) lends a pulpit to an annoying child asserting his right to read Marx without having to self-identify as a Communist. As the water pulls back for the tsunami—be it the rise of McCarthyism, inceldom, or ecological disaster (in Objet A , the characters must learn to love a Björk-like character named “Gaia”)—there is an understandable desire to make one’s meaning crystal clear. Yet, after a title card somewhat gratingly announces a “post-postmodern persistence parable,” Nicolaas Schmidt’s September Afternoon (2026) is content merely to feel the storm winds, announcing nothing. Once a family has arrived at a beach for a picnic, Schmidt spends 30 hardly interrupted minutes observing the patriarch attempting to pin down a small beach tent against rising winds, while an instrumental take on Billy Idol’s “Eyes Without a Face” loops endlessly on the soundtrack. Schmidt’s 70-minute vibe-piece felt more oriented to the gallery than the cinema, but at least its method was specific to the audiovisual format: observing rather than declaring the apocalypse. It goes unstated that we’re living through this, and that it’s often relatively boring; the work of “why” and “how” is left up to the viewer. September Afternoon (Nicolaas Schmidt, 2026). At a certain point, I started to hope the festival could move on from apocalyptic fetishism toward apocalyptic pragmatism. It was perhaps a damning comment on that morning’s cinematic offerings (the less-than-tempting press conference for Ketticè , in the international competition) that the room for the FIPRESCI-sponsored discussion panel “A World Without Film Critics” was packed to the gills, but here, at last, was a sincere inquiry into the possibility of life in this afterworld, if only for one part of the festival community. As was pointed out in the conversation, the "world" indicated by the attention-grabbing title—one without critics—might not look too different from the one we currently find ourselves in. In many ways, we are already in that reality. Panelists Diego Cepeda, Sona Karapoghosian, and Laura Staab, along with moderator Christopher Small, discussed in sober terms what precisely has been lost, and what might still be salvaged from the wreck. What emerged was a vision for a film-critical practice more comfortable (or at least less uncomfortable) at the margins. If tendenko tells us to leave the wave-wrecked beach, we film critics have not listened, have stayed with the wreckage of cinema. But perhaps we can—unlike the beachgoers in September Afternoon —shift our little tent to a more sheltered area. In this light, Hong Sang-soo’s Nowhere to Lay My Eyes (2026) emerged as the film of the festival. Kim Min-hee stars as Sang-hee, an experimental filmmaker and port employee visiting her family on Jeju Island, attempting to make a case for her marginal art practice to her mother who only wants her to have financial stability. The film is inseparable from Hong’s other works, his quietly indefatigable mode of working. But where his other films tend toward the apolitical, this script acknowledges the dire state of the world, making a reference to the genocide in the Middle East (although he does not name it as such). Like his best work, Nowhere to Lay My Eyes talks its way around something unspoken, culminating in a stunning final laptop screening of Sang-hee’s flower films. What Hong’s characters can’t communicate in words, but what is communicated all the more powerfully by the film is the worthiness of persistence in an ever-shrinking niche. Let us forsake headline-grabbing pronouncements, embrace marginality, and attempt to weather this storm. — Dylan Adamson *** While tendenko was specific to the world of Ana Vaz’s Hanabi (2026), the term kept reverberating in my mind as I watched this year’s Locarno retrospective. From the 1940s to the 1960s, Hollywood filmmakers faced censorship for suspected ties to communism. Some kept working, but on smaller projects or under pseudonyms. Others were jailed or, under the threat of imprisonment, fled the United States. In line with tendenko , those fugitive filmmakers made a bid for survival, often resolving to be on their own. Meanwhile, various characters in their films were also isolated—but by remorse, greed, addiction. In Cy Endfield’s The Sound of Fury (1950), loneliness emerges from feelings of guilt. Howard Tyler (Frank Lovejoy) has moved with his family from Boston to California and is looking for a job. As his desperation escalates, he turns to a life of crime and becomes distant from his wife—unable to face her, unable to face himself. Endfield plunges us headlong into this feeling through his filmmaking choices. Howard is framed in close-ups, his face pained with contrition. As he withdraws into an abyss of his own making, Endfield amplifies his isolation. Irony gains momentum: Howard is tempted to play away from home, leaving his pregnant wife and child alone, but it is he, subsumed with regret, who is alone. If being an accomplice to a crime was a compromise he made to survive, then it also, paradoxically, chips away at his survival. The Sound of Fury (Cy Enfield, 1950). © Courtesy of Park Circus-Paramount. That tension recurs in Edgar G. Ulmer’s Ruthless (1948). The film’s protagonist, Horace Vendig (Zachary Scott), was abandoned by his father at birth and grew up blinded by ambition, eventually becoming a wealthy trader. He regards isolation as a refuge, using it as a coping mechanism and seeming to believe it is the only way he can live. Ulmer crowds the film with characters who are fond of Horace, but Horace sees them only as so many ladders for climbing up the social ranks. His self-isolation is a bleak version of tendenko : his selfishness, tantamount to drowning others in order to save himself. That this antihero is enterprising but, as the title has it, so ruthless, is his tragic flaw. In Stuart Heisler’s Smash-Up: The Story of a Woman (1947), alcoholism isolates Angie Evans (Susan Hayward). She is a singer who resorts to liquid comforts after her marriage falls apart and insecurity creeps in. As her husband becomes famous, Angie shuts herself in her house—the vastness of which underscores how much she shrinks in confinement. Days leak into nights through Heisler’s montage, mirroring Angie’s confusion as her husband turns increasingly hostile. It’s a cautionary tale that warns us against withdrawing from the world. If tendenko can be translated as “each person for themselves,” then these films illuminate that tendency in human behavior—and do so in a way that might, by contrast, highlight an alternative possibility. One can survive on one’s own, it’s true. But to live, to really live, one needs community—or at least a hand to hold. — Ishita Sengupta *** We’d been warned by our editor not to fall too vaguely into the porousness of the word tendenko . Yet I tend to find porousness generative, and the more I looked into the term’s meaning, the more it seemed that consensus on how to interpret it was fraught, even in Japanese. Though it can be translated “to each on their own,” and refers typically to the safety measure of isolating in a tsunami so as to maximize chances of survival, that quick act of self-preservation is also understood to build confidence in other people (evacuation is possible), and an embrace of the term has been argued to reduce survivor’s guilt. After I first heard tendenko in Hanabi , I was fascinated by that complexity, and wanted us to take the word out of its context to consider broader themes of isolation. In this year’s Locarno retrospective, there was a battle between individualism and socialism. In the international competition, loneliness was a consequence of modern alienation for some, while solitude was a coping mechanism for others. The French proverb chacun pour sa pomme translates as “every man for himself” and transliterates as “every man for his apple.” It would have made a witty title for Jules Dassin’s Thieves’ Highway (1949), in which a truck driver heads north from Fresno to San Francisco to sell a load of apples. The film depicts the lives of truckers not only as lonely, but as physically demanding to the point of being exhausting; the protagonist is constantly struggling to stay awake while on the road. As with most films in the festival’s Hollywood Blacklist retrospective, a socialist message is smuggled into this story: Workers are called upon to renounce personal profit, recognize the value of unions, and aspire to a collective freedom. Thieves' Highway (Jules Dassin, 1949). But that vision of society doesn’t come easily. Almost every cast and crew member of Thieves’ Highway was born outside of the United States, and between the film’s production and its narrative, an accurate picture of America forms: Everyone is welcome, but only if they’re willing to compete against each other. “You can’t trust nobody these days,” one of the film’s characters says. At every opportunity, cheats backstab and sabotage each other in order to make a dime. This is tendenko as brutal personal interest amid the swallowing waves of capitalism. Why stick your neck out for another guy when there is an extra buck coming your way to help you survive? A slick-looking angel of death in Denis Côté’s Nobody’s Violence (2026) had me lingering on the meaning of the Spanish word mira , “to look.” Côté’s frequent collaborator Larissa Corriveau stars as Mira, who performs assisted suicide with a mysterious powder. She is also a witness, someone who sees. Through wide, long-distance shots, her work is framed dispassionately; she looks death in the eye with each assisted suicide, but maintains her own emotional distance. Is she running away from something? Is she experiencing burnout? While the film allows Mira moments of tenderness—on the road with her dog, she seems almost happy—Côté offers no back story, tells us little of who she really is. Nobody's Violence (Denis Côté, 2026). Few languages have a translation for the English term “burnout,” yet it’s a word that is foreign to no one today. In Sarah Leonor’s D’ici là (2026), the protagonist has decided to become a recluse in the neighboring mountains of his French village. He’s completely at odds with society, exhausted by its bureaucracy. When his friend comes to find him, he tricks her into thinking he’ll come home, only to escape before dawn, deeper into the forest. Meanwhile, another character in the film is attempting to track down a wolf—an animal that perfectly exemplifies tendenko . When wolves disperse, becoming lone creatures, it’s usually in a bid for survival. D’ici là ends with Weyes Blood’s song “Seven Words,” the lyrics of which express a desire for freedom from a romantic relationship: “In time we’ll both be free from this ball and chain.” The song arrives at a vanishing point here. What comes after a break-up’s waves? After survival: What next? —Matilda Hague

articles.title: Cut and Spliced: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
articles.author: Catherine Weng
articles.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year’s participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this second installment, four critics muse on cinema’s ability to splice disparate fragments together. They touch on ecstatic New York sirens, self-preservation in Iran and Palestine, performances that bear the weight of passing time, and an actress’s descent into two-faced delirium in Rome. We hear in Sans soleil (1983) that “Nothing sorts out memories from ordinary moments. It is only later that they claim remembrance, when they show their scars.” This is how I feel about memories all the time. What lingers in my mind most vividly are the seams between memories; in films, I like the joints that crack open to let imagination slip inside. I am writing this the evening after the festival has ended. On my walk back to my hotel, our nightly haunt, Pardo Bar, remains lit, yet the crowd has vanished. From my room, I look down on the Piazza Grande, once bustling but now standing relatively empty as staff quietly clear away rows of black and yellow chairs. Where blanks start to form, memories rush in. I sort through these echoes, finding a way to splice fragments of the past together. Ana Vaz’s Hanabi (2026) weaves street footage of Tokyo and the Tohoku region together with a voiceover that reads entries adapted from Yoko Hayasuke’s Journal of a Radioactive Brain , capturing the everyday reality of living in the aftermath of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and Fukushima nuclear disaster. In that these journal entries primarily use an intimate second-person address, the film might evoke Sans Soleil , in which a female voiceover reads letters from an unseen man—her voice almost rewriting the images and reshaping how we interpret the past. In Hanabi , the “you” becomes a bridge between the writer and the narrator, the narrator and the listener. At times when that insistent “you” summoned me into the frame, I felt awkwardly self-conscious and irritated. It later dawned on me that this discomfort was, perhaps, the point: to strain toward empathy, to confront a vital boundary, to realize the impossibility of experiencing a memory or inhabiting a body that is not your own. Hanabi occupies various thresholds: between “I” and “you,” between Brazil and Japan, between entries written on a discontinuous timeline. In moments of audiovisual separation or audio interference—as when the non-diegetic beeping of a radiation monitor displaces the natural environmental sound—Vaz foregrounds the unsmoothness of the splice. Where objectivity falls short, collective historical trauma is written in private, personal terms, and artful intervention finds its footing. Siren Island (Isa Hesse-Rabinovitch, 1981). Courtesy of Cinémathèque suisse. Like Hanabi , Isa Hesse-Rabinovitch’s Siren Island (1981) makes disjunctive use of montage. It pieces together sequences the director shot with a group of women, primarily in New York, and opens on an image of a woman at the water’s edge, reciting a passage from the Odyssey in which Odysseus sails past the sirens’ island. Throwing us into the midst of the hero’s journey, the film continues in an unpredictable, nonlinear mode. I thought, in one scene, of Julia Kristeva’s theory of “women’s time” as cyclical, spiraling. In a room of many mirrors, a woman tries on dress after dress; the footage plays in reverse and it gives the garments an eerie life of their own: leaping into the air, crawling up to wrap around the body. Queer and feminine imaginaries proliferate throughout the film. Through jagged match-cuts and double exposures of rhyming images, blooming flowers mirror singing lips mirror pulsing labia; curving caves echo the contours of the womb. Hesse-Rabinovitch does not see the sirens’ song as a fatal trap set for men. Instead, she reclaims it for the sirens and their shape-shifting stream of consciousness. In its defiantly irrational splices, her film refuses patriarchal narratives, removes Odyssean wax from the ears, and invites us to listen in ecstasy. I like those wild, rapid-fire edits, yet I find as much joy in quiet, lingering images that stretch my body’s sense of time. In Umair Bilal’s As Light as Air (2026), which depicts a pilgrimage to Sehwan, a Sufi town in Pakistan, time is often suspended. A colorful, vital scene suddenly drains of color and freezes into a static image, or, conversely, a black-and-white still slowly saturates with rich hues and springs to life. Rather than disguising transitions, the film reveals and amplifies them. In one scene, double exposure merges an image of a tranquil sea with crowded streets of pilgrims; in another, a man whirling overlaps with a fairground ride giving off a neon glow. Shirtless men beat their chests and chant in yet another powerful scene, with the camera clinging closely to their bodies. The hypnotic intensity becomes almost suffocating until the film abruptly, briefly cuts to a negative still of the men’s backs, all scarred with blade marks, while the chanting rushes on uninterrupted. These splices continuously pull us in and out of the trancelike state of the pilgrimage: at times, in the thick of the ritual; at others, jolted out of it, reminded of where we stand as viewers, and how we watch. I have watched for scars, leaps, enjambments, and now other sounds and images are falling into the cracks of these transitions: running beneath the scorching sun between screenings, grabbing quick food, drinking mediocre coffee. I know I will remember this August in Locarno. Or rather, I will remember those sounds and images that have been spliced together. “They have substituted themselves for my memory. They are my memory.” Catherine Weng *** “Stay in the moment. Not everything needs to be recorded.” Every film screened at Locarno this year was preceded by this warning against media piracy. Juxtaposed with some of the works screened at the festival, that benign, functional message rang ironic. A surprising number of films—two of which stood out—incorporated fragments that owed their existence to someone recording “the moment.” Take, for instance, the opening shot in Bani Khoshnoudi’s short Elegy for the Forgotten, on an Endless War (2026). A vertical phone recording shows several groups of people running or limping toward the camera; in the background, a suspension bridge is engulfed in clouds of dark smoke. It is, as the subsequent intertitle reads, an “Iranian home movie.” Drawing on the violent protests that erupted in response to worsening living conditions in Iran, and the national instability caused by the US–Israel attacks, the film traces and stitches together comparable moments in Iranian history. Elegy for the Forgotten, on an Endless War (Bani Khoshnoudi, 2026). Through photographs from the past and videos of the present, Khoshnoudi’s film elaborates on different modes of propaganda fabrication and contrasts them with images of real suffering. An anonymous thumb scrolls through low-resolution videos of deceased people of all ages piled in the streets. An anonymous hand flips through the pages of “The Imposed War, Defence vs. Aggression,” the official Iranian records on the 1980–88 Iran–Iraq war. Alternating between succinct Farockian ideas—“Images change meaning, depending on who uses them and when,” reads one intertitle—Khoshnoudi otherwise adheres to an elusively poetic voice. While temporally disparate, the film’s sutured-together fragments stress the similarities between the Iraqi invasion four decades ago and today’s conflict. In a manner vaguely reminiscent of Maryam Takafory’s work, Khoshnoudi concatenates 16mm images of flowers with video recordings of women mourning, dancing, or painting. Over the last few decades, strategies of propaganda have been an integral part of war’s visual machine: Think, on the Iranian side, of women painting murals that depict Ayatollah Khomeini, and the next generation painting their missiles in pink. As Khoshnoudi digs through war’s remnants, her gaze does not focus on condemning those who produced such images and myths. Instead—and especially toward the film’s end—she tries to find the forgotten people who exist beyond propaganda, those who didn’t ask for war but were killed nevertheless. Mohanad Yaqubi’s Revolutionaries Never Die (2026) similarly (re)captures “the moment.” Structured chronologically, the film responds to an unanswered email from Jocelyne Saab, the Lebanese filmmaker known for documenting the ruins of war. Following her death in 2019, Yaqubi was entrusted with cataloguing and restoring archival material from the first part of Saab’s career. Spliced together from contact scans and digitized material, passages from her films are interposed with paragraphs of Yaqubi’s concise and personal musings on Saab’s work and his own life. Revolutionaries Never Die (Mohanad Yaqubi, 2026). Having followed Saab’s filmography with care, Yaqubi comments in the film on the multifaceted experiences detailed in Palestinian Women (1973), noting points of connection between the 1970s and today. He then parallels the destruction of Saab’s house in Beirut, My City (1983) with the bombing of his own house in Gaza in 2024. As Yaqubi establishes a dialogue between the personal and the historical, archives are, as he notes at the end of the film, "activated." In Revolutionaries Never Die , Saab’s archives are activated to work against a forgetting that erases recent struggles from collective memory, causing their needless repetition. Both Khoshnoudi and Yaqubi bring together different moments in time, then: Khoshnoudi resignifies propaganda media from the past and ties it to the phone recordings of the present; Yaqubi reactualizes Saab’s work through montage, but by adding personal notes, too. In their hands, the camera is a mode of self-preservation and self-defense. In the small Swiss town of Locarno, posters that feature white doves—that universal emblem of peace—are scattered on billboards, on buses and trains. Is Swiss neutrality still possible in the face of global conflict and militarization? Staying out of the moment is, it seems to me, the privilege of a place that does not need recordings as evidence of survival. Alex Petrescu *** Watching films at a festival produces a peculiar form of misremembering. By my third day in Locarno, the films I had seen were beginning to bleed into one another. Through the sheer density of images, a morning motif folded into an evening silhouette, and a line of dialogue acquired the phantom inflection of another film. In memory, the consecutive dissolves into the simultaneous. I found myself drawn to films that seemed to work with this instability—pulling experience apart, rearranging the debris, and holding those disparate fragments up to the light. Albert Serra’s hermetic concert film, Sixteen Moments of My Life (2026), does this with an almost perverse literalism. Across sixteen songs at Paris’s Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord, Ingrid Caven takes us through various phases of her life. While the lyrics move between themes of childhood, love, aging, and grief, the camera follows her body getting progressively spent with each song, punctuated by applause from an unseen audience. I noted the enthusiastic clapping after each song in my pocket notebook, trying to differentiate its textures, but there is little emotional variance in two hands coming together. Its function is structural: Applause confirms that one song is over. Onstage, magnetic reds and blues make way for magenta and white. Caven pauses, her exhaustion accumulating with everything that has come before: song, life, remembrance. But just when it seems as though the performance seems over, she descends into falsetto again. Between her shrieks and groans, and with a tight grasp on a red rose, Caven—while still singing—collapses onstage, her writhing form recalling the rattling backstage cough that opened the film. As one media scholar has noted , the concert film is traditionally structured by the temporal distance between the audience in the auditorium and the viewer watching the screen. However, with the venue’s crowd reduced to a sonic backdrop in Serra’s film, other defining tensions emerge. Equating the span of a concert with the span of a life, Serra and Caven not only explore the blurred line between performance and reality, but also insist upon the somatic toll of living and performing. An hour later, I watched François-Christophe Marzal’s Happiness Is So Close! (2026), which tells of another actor whose body has become an inconvenient archive. Jean-Luc, this tragicomic film’s protagonist, is preparing to play Don Quixote: the role of a lifetime, if only he could remember the lines. Again and again, he leans blankly on an alpenstock, waiting for the words to return. His inability to embody Don Quixote stood in stark contrast to Caven's rousing performance. Happiness Is So Close! (François-Christophe Marzal, 2026). Courtesy of Kyra Dowling. Jean-Luc’s paranoia crystallizes the moment the producers hire an understudy named Gilles. Convinced his position is precarious despite the team’s assurances, he stalks his nemesis across the city, at one point adopting a clown disguise. This erratic behavior exposes the core of his affliction: While Caven looks backward, gathering up a life that is already disappearing, Jean-Luc is frantically gripped by the terror of his own erasure, obsessing over an end that has not happened yet. After these meditations on the deliquescent past and the imminent future, there was then the uncomfortable present of Lê Bảo ’s Hearing (2026). Ninh, this film’s protagonist, is a technician whose clients have him install sound-level meters across a dystopian city that is consumed by noise. Swamps, houses, pubs, nightclubs: Everywhere, sound is something to be measured. There is little dialogue in the film, which instead makes a world out of ambience: chirping birds, fingernails peeling at an eggshell, a ladle scooping up custard. At night, the meters emit visual halos colored violet whenever the decibel limit set by clients is breached. The triggers range from the loud quarreling of monkeys to softer, quotidian conversations between estranged couples—the latter of which are, in this fictional realm, the source of the city’s most urgent complaints. Even this strange reticent world cannot resist a literal stage. As an unhappy couple rehearsed an ostensibly traditional opera before the film cut to their quiet bedroom, I found myself thinking of the silences that await Caven and Jean-Luc after they leave the stage. Quiet, silence, peace—Lê Bảo probes the thin, permeable boundaries between sounds and our understanding of them. In Hearing , the city’s men and women counteract their quiet days of labor with rowdy nights at the club; it is all about balancing the two extremes, they tell Ninh. Ultimately, the visceral impossibility of silence was what lingered with me most from this film. In the absence of pub chatter and dance music, a simple sigh can expand to fill an entire room. Hearing (Lê Bảo, 2026). Perhaps what makes the splice so unsettling is that it brings things together without necessarily reconciling them. Some cinephiles like to imagine criticism as an exercise in cool recollection. But is that possible at a festival? Sitting through a day’s fourth screening, eyes burning, reveals a more volatile truth: We do not always go to the cinema to encounter intact structures. Sometimes we go to inhabit the fault lines, to write about the exact moment the ground beneath us gives way. Manahil Tahira *** “Cut!” begs Noémie Merlant in the final moments of Bertrand Mandico’s Roma Elastica (2026). Kneeling before a camera and clutching at the yielding body of her costar Marion Cotillard, she insists on a premature end to the film’s delirious mise en abyme. Roma Elastica opens on a movie set, somewhere in dusty California. Merlant is Valentina, a makeup artist and confidante to Cotillard’s leading lady, a Hollywood actress whose name, Eddie Mars, is borrowed from the villain in Raymond Chandler’s The Big Sleep . The pair are taking their time in the dressing room, holding up the shoot. Valentina regales her glamorpuss superior with gossipy stories of this and that as she leisurely applies Eddie’s makeup. Eddie, once primed, will shoot a scene in which she straddles and strangles a man in bed. In this struggle, she will be splattered with blood, but come out on top. Roma Elastica (Bertrand Mandico, 2026). Cut. Speaking at a Locarno masterclass about his infernal bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude (2024), Albert Serra boasted of creating images that had never been seen before with human eyes. According to him, even the matador, who faces the beast head-on, is subject to the clutter of his peripheral vision. Only with the close-ups that Serra’s tight frames create can we see the bull, and the bull alone. Where Serra spotlights and isolates, Mandico looks at his subjects as if through a kaleidoscope. His characters are often shape-shifters, gender benders, artists, and freaks. With each new film, Mandico refines his use of traditional practical effects—double exposures, lens filters, handcrafted props—decorating each frame with extraordinary oddity. I want to call this approach anachronistic, but Roma Elastica feels like it was placed in the wrong world, as well as the wrong time. After learning from her doctor that she has a tumor on her brain, Eddie agrees to take a job she otherwise wouldn’t. She must keep working; after all, the movies, even B-rate movies, are her ticket to immortality. It’s a career move that could be likened to Elizabeth Taylor’s secondment in Italy—not in 1961, when she famously resumed the filming of Cleopatra (1963), but a decade later when she found herself in Rome shooting The Driver’s Seat (1974). Then at her nadir, this was a last resort for Taylor. Like Cotillard’s Eddie, her character in this film is strangely motivated by death, and Rome is the final stop on her manic goodbye tour. Speaking about The Driver’s Seat , Taylor reputedly said, “It takes one day to die, another to be reborn.” In Roma Elastica , Eddie hears the same sentiment almost word for word, and it's this logic, drenched in cliché, that helps justify her crossing the pond. The Driver's Seat (Giuseppe Patroni Griffi, 1974). Accompanied by her so-called “guard dog” Valentina—seen in one moment to bite a man who gets too close to the actress on the plane—Eddie heads to Italy to star in a project titled “Roma Elastica.” The two are greeted at the airport by the Cavalli sisters, the eccentric directing duo of this film within a film, one of whom can see the future. While Mandico’s film is set in an imaginary 1982, “Roma Elastica” is set in our present day. Like the movie we’re watching, it’s an overly stylish, often incoherent European art film losing a wrestling match against its own high-minded ideas about creation and destruction. Eddie is to play Rowina, an avant-garde sculptress who, in the year 2026, will be assassinated by neofascists for being too ahead of her time. “People like women who suffer, they even win awards,” Eddie is told by way of reassurance. This much was true for Cotillard when she was awarded the Best Actress Oscar for her starring role as Edith Piaf in La Vie en Rose (2007). Piaf suffered great tragedies: childhood neglect, substance addiction. In Olivier Dahan’s hoarse biopic, there was as much kicking and screaming as there was singing. Cut. As another chanteuse, Peggy Lee, sings “and it's me and my shadow” on the soundtrack, Eddie discovers what she believes to be a wound on the back of her head. Approaching the mirror, she finds that it is in fact a second face. She is horrified by her own reflection, screaming and writhing in pain. Eddie has taken the form of Janus: an actress in Rome turned Roman myth. With her two faces, she is simultaneously looking forward to the future and backward to the past. Cut. During a Locarno press screening, I watched as a woman walked backward down the aisle, her eyes still fixed on the projection, her desire to continue watching the film contending with her desire to leave. Cut. After threatening to leave Rome, Valentina abandons Eddie, who has become reckless, falling in with a crowd of drug-addled greasers squatting in the room next to her suite. Eddie, distressed, searches far and wide for her handler—and here Cotillard, with an almost dancerly theatricality, backs away from Mandico’s camera, walking into a horde of people. She is being led by another force, her other face. Roma Elastica (Bertrand Mandico, 2026). With its fascination for dualism, Roma Elastica takes pains to contemplate itself. The most overtly self-conscious of Mandico’s works to date, the film imagines itself as an unmakeable movie. I was struck by a line from the Cavalli sisters, who—having lost sight of the guiding vision for their film—confess to having lost “the essence of the future.” At this point, Mandico also seems to have lost his grip. Cutting between color and black-and-white with each faltering take, Roma Elastica and the film it houses take a wild, downward spiral. Before long, Mandico’s misfit objects and dreamlike sets, once charismatic, turn fulsome and immature. Take, for example, the bizarre intrusion of Rowina’s turd-shaped prop gun, a secret weapon she must make defecate in her fight against the neofascists. In her tailspin, Eddie encounters a man on set who has sadness in his eyes: “I do quality work too, you know,” he says under his breath. “Please don’t judge me for this.” On the defensive, the artists in “Roma Elastica” repeatedly refer to themselves as “martyrs in the postmodern world.” It feels as though Mandico would like us to think of Eddie as such; her death comes too soon, arrives even before her character Rowina can be killed off as planned. Wounded by its own creative misfires, Mandico’s film also meets an undignified end. Misquoting Greta Garbo in the film’s opening lines, Eddie’s costar declares, “One must know how to make a graceful exit.” I dare say—and dare say Garbo would agree—that one must know how to make a graceful cut. Charles Carrall

articles.description: Get in touch to send in cinephile news and discoveries. To keep up with our latest features, sign up for the Weekly Edit newsletter and follow us @mubinotebook on X and Instagram . NEWS Primtime (Lance Oppenheim, 2026). Meryl Streep and Laura Poitras have come aboard as executive producers on Julia Loktev’s upcoming documentary My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (2026) , the second part of Loktev’s profile of independent Russian journalists operating in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine, which recently had its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival. In a statement, Streep describes Loktev as “the Samuel Pepys of Putin’s Russia” and describes her films as a “blazing achievement.” Two surprises have recently happened on the festival circuit. The first is that Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial (2026), which was dropped by Amazon MGM Studios in June, will have its world premiere at the New York Film Festival followed by a Gala screening at the London Film Festival. Secondly, the Telluride Film Festival’s secret screening was revealed to be Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour documentary You Can See Everything (2026) about Elizabeth Holmes. AMC has launched its own distribution company, Leawood Films , which will focus on “small and mid-budget sized movies” from “emerging and established filmmakers.” This arrives on the heels of the success of Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour (2023), which AMC directly released into theaters after striking a deal with the eponymous popstar. Television presenter and YouTube personality Chris Hansen has purchased preshow advertising before every screening of Lance Oppenheim’s psychological thriller Primetime (2026) , which chronicles Hansen’s tenure hosting To Catch a Predator (2004–07). The ad reportedly directs viewers to Hansen’s streaming network TruBlu where he continues his predator investigations. DEVELOPING Sentimental Value (Joachim Trier, 2025). Lea Seydoux and Bill Murray are set to star in Ursula Meier’s The Quiet Land , which is reportedly influenced by the work of Swiss police photographer Arnold Odermatt, and will be lensed by Agnès Godard. Renate Reinsve is set to star as Mary Wollstonecraft in Mia Hansen-Løve’s If Love Should Die , which chronicles the last twelve years of the English writer and philosopher’s life amidst the French Revolution. REMEMBERING 9 to 5 (Colin Higgins, 1980). Dolly Parton has died at 80 . The American singer-songwriter and actress achieved initial success in country music by appearing on the weekly variety series The Porter Wagoner Show (1960–81) beginning in the late-1960s. She and Wagoner became a popular duo for nearly ten years before Parton pursued a thriving solo career. In between touring and releasing hit studio records, she starred in her own variety series Dolly! (1976–77), made frequent appearances on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson (1962–92) that boosted her popularity, and co-starred in many television specials headlined by Mac Davis and Cher. She made her feature film debut in 9 to 5 (1980) and wrote the film’s theme song, which was nominated for both an Oscar and a Grammy. She went on to star in a string of films over the next decade: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (1982), Rhinestone (1984), Steel Magnolias (1989), and Straight Talk (1992). Up until her death, she continued to regularly appear on television in made-for-TV films and sitcom cameos. Her final film was the Emmy-award winning musical drama Dolly Parton’s Christmas on the Square (2020), for which she produced and wrote the music. “I never knew anyone like her,” remembered former costar Jane Fonda. “She was simultaneously a naughty, playful southern gal from the hollows of Tennessee and a deep, soulful thinker who could see through people right down to their true selves.” Tim Curry has died at 80 . The English actor quickly garnered international recognition for his performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in both The Rocky Horror Show stage production and its 1975 film adaptation. Curry went on to have a prolific career on screen and stage, moving easily between live-action and voice roles. Some of his most memorable live-action film performances include Wadsworth in Clue (1985), Dr. Yevgeniy Petrov in The Hunt for Red October (1990), and Mr. Hector in Home Alone 2: Lost in New York . He also received praise for his turns as Pennywise the Clown in the two-part miniseries It (1990) and Nigel Thornberry in the animated series The Wild Thornberrys (1998–2004). Along with regularly performing on stage, racking up accolades for playing Mozart in Amadeus and King Arthur in Spamalot , he also released three rock albums, voiced numerous audiobooks, and continued to reprise Dr. Frank-N-Furter for various charity and anniversary events. “I don’t fear death,” Curry said a year prior. “I try to avoid it, as I think we all do. But, I suspect that in the end, I will welcome it.” RECOMMENDED READING One Night Only (Will Gluck, 2026). “The category is a capacious one, encompassing reclusive geniuses, thwarted iconoclasts, and tragic shooting stars. Some of these artists make only one movie. Some make more but resist the temptations of a prolific career, because of their own exacting standards, the challenge of raising money to make films, or forces beyond their control … In all cases, though, the scarcity of the films combines with the often distinctive nature of the work to capture our collective imagination, giving the reticent auteur a magnetism that, while not exactly unearned, also speaks to our own attitudes toward the creative act.” For The Yale Review , Bilge Ebiri examines various “reticent auteurs,” including Charles Laughton, Barbara Loden, and Víctor Erice, and their unique value in an increasingly algorithm-driven economy. “The Chronovisor is a hauntological invention, and in her research, Dr. Courte has cause to bring dead tech back to life. In one case she reassembles a video, detangling and manually winding a snarl of magnetic tape. She also watches a segment of the French-Canadian TV newsmagazine Camera ’89 profiling François Brune, a French priest and collaborator of Ernetti, who made his own attempts to use technology to rouse the dead. The media is the medium, though the message is garbled: When Camera ’89 plays a tape of Brune’s, the speech is raspy, barking, an almost entirely incoherent squawk to match the quality of the tape itself. An aura of unreality grows around the subject as information becomes sparser; things that were once common knowledge fade into irrelevance and dispute.” For The Baffler , Mark Asch reviews Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s Chronovisor (2026) and how it fits within and exemplifies the “academic mystery movie.” “[Will] Gluck’s touch is very light, but the movie’s obsession with credibility means most characters we get to meet stop to point out their dislike for the law. Whoever supports this thing is kept carefully offscreen. At most, we get a drunken rockstar going into a ramble about maybe the conservatives had a point because this makes who you pick to spend the night with special, right before getting increasingly creepier and falling into his face. The most chilling moment comes early when Turner remarks that most of his friends got married the previous year, the implication being that they just settled into marriage for convenient intimacy. The real crime is the one against the romantic comedy promise: you are not supposed to marry to find a fuck buddy.” On his Substack, Filipe Furtado unpacks the recent high-concept rom-com One Night Only (2026) and how it embodies the fictions Hollywood loves to tell. “The pre-Hitler mood captured in M (1931) finds an echo in films like Civil War (2024) and One Battle After Another (2025). Conflict no longer appears as a temporary crisis but as a permanent condition; politics becomes an endless chain of confrontations rather than a system capable of resolution. Like M , these films imagine a world of eroding norms and ambient violence. Kracauer’s warning, reaching across decades, is not that such outcomes are inevitable but that when a society begins to normalize this atmosphere, it grows more susceptible to the promises of demagogues—and to the conflicts that follow.” For The New Republic , Jimmy So looks back at Siegfried Kracauer’s landmark text From Caligari to Hitler and how the author’s diagnostician lens can be deployed in a contemporary context. RECOMMENDED EVENTS Import/Export (Ulrich Seidl, 2007). Berlin, through September 24: The Arsenal Institute for Film and Video Art presents Here and Now – The Films of Christoph Hochhäusler , a retrospective of the German filmmaker’s films tied to an exhibition of his materials at the Neuer Berliner Kunstverein . Turin, through October 5: The National Museum of Cinema presents My Name Is Orson Welles , which features more than four hundred items across many public and private collections dedicated to the auteur that retrace his unique life and career. New York, September 17 through October 13: The Museum of Modern Art presents Yuen Woo-ping: The Number One Martial Arts Director Under the Sky , a retrospective of the filmmaker and action choreographer’s work, from Drunken Master (1978) through Ip Man 4: The Finale (2019). Amsterdam, September 19 through January 31: Eye Filmmuseum presents Ulrich Seidl – On Life, Love, and Death , the first exhibition, and a complete retrospective, of the Austrian director’s work in the Netherlands. RECOMMENDED VIEWING A24 presents a surprise teaser for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new documentary You Can See Everything (2026), which follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares to go to prison. data-height="natural"> Neon presents a trailer for Fjord (2026), Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or-winning legal thriller starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as a couple fighting for the custody of their children after their behavior comes under scrutiny by the government. data-height="natural"> Magnolia Pictures presents a trailer for The History of Concrete (2026), John Wilson’s feature-length debut about the documentarian’s efforts to make a documentary about concrete using a Hallmark-approved commercial formula. data-height="natural"> Neon presents a trailer for Once Upon a Time in Harlem (2026), a documentary about a 1972 gathering of the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance at Duke Ellington’s townhouse, originally shot by William Greaves and completed by his son David. data-height="natural"> RECENTLY ON NOTEBOOK The Samurai and the Prisoner (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 2026). “Markopoulos wrote that ending a film is like tying an intricate surgical knot. One must make ‘the best knot for each work; and it is completed forever.’ It must be clean. It is somewhere near three in the morning when the projection cuts off and, though abrupt, there is a sense of finality. Before the screening, Beavers had asked that when the Temenos ends, we hold a moment of silence. These few minutes of quiet are like a canopy. In the dark, in the absence of the projector’s hum, true silence takes on a thick feeling in the air. The screen loses its violet wash as eyes readjust. We wait, until Beavers releases a thunderous ‘Thank you.’” Emma Fuchs reports on the screening of the final four cycles of Gregory J. Markopoulos’s Eniaios (1948–90 ), the culmination of the Greek-American experimental filmmaker's magnum opus. “The launch of Video Home System (VHS) in the mid-1970s therefore came at the perfect time for Northern Ireland’s cinema lovers, who desired entertainment and escapism but were less willing than ever to leave the comfort and relative safety of their own homes … For the time, the power to control when audiences watched films began to shift from the exhibitors to the audience. Power shifted, too, from producers to consumers, and for the first time people could directly record films or television programs onto blank tapes and play, pause, or rewind at their own leisure.” Sam Manning explores the VHS boom in Northern Ireland during the Troubles , when cinemagoing “became less of a social habit and more of an occasional activity that carried a level of potential risk.” “ The Samurai and the Prisoner (2026) is set apart from these other works by virtue of its assertive and imperative qualities. Whereas Kurosawa’s past filmography has sought to elucidate, The Samurai and the Prisoner seeks to prescribe—a shift perhaps commensurate with advancing age and stature (an impulse that finds more satirical expression in the coda of Cloud [2024], which ends with a character offering advice). Murashige is seemingly a self-portrait of sorts for Kurosawa, and after decades of diagnosing the ills of a modern world defined by alienation—and putting his observations in literally or figuratively scarifying terms—the filmmaker now wishes to push, calmly but urgently, for a fundamental, structural change.” Alexis Moon examines The Samurai and the Prisoner in the context of Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s career and how the Japanese director has charted a new path with his latest period drama. “The contrast with General Muhammad Zia-ul Haq, who overthrew Bhutto in a 1977 military coup and later executed him, has often produced a simplified narrative: of a liberal cultural sphere abruptly replaced by sweeping repression under his ‘Islamization’ drive. Yet Aina (1977) remained in cinemas for a record 401 weeks, well into the Zia period. Censorship until Zia’s death in 1988 undoubtedly affected filmmakers and narrowed the visual grammar of romance, but the shift was uneven rather than absolute: While romancing in an elevator became increasingly unlikely, lovers still had their duets. Far from a total and lasting capture by moral conservatism, post-Zia cinema in the 1990s often turned to overt sexualization to draw audiences back into a struggling exhibition economy.” Manahil Tahira unpacks the legacy of Nazrul Islam’s Aina and the history of erotic depictions within Pakistani culture. WISH LIST The Testament of Ann Lee (Mona Fastvold, 2025). The Philosophy of Time Travel: The Epic Sequel to the Motion Picture Donnie Darko , Richard Kelly’s literary follow-up to his 2001 debut feature is available to preorder. Rachel Antonoff presents a “Second Coming” T-shirt inspired by Mona Fastvold’s musical drama The Testament of Ann Lee (2025). EXTRAS Hail, Caesar! (Joel and Ethan Coen, 2016). Screen Slate compiled a list of the 100 most-screened films in New York City across the last fifteen years , sorted by the number of individual screenings, including a column for showtimes.
