articles.title: It Was Once Fire: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
articles.author: Rafaela Bassili
articles.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year's participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this first installment, letters exchanged between three critics contour what was on screen—broken relations, recalcitrant presences—with their experiences of Locarno beyond the frame. Photo by Alyssandra Maxine. Dear Vedant and Max, I’m writing you from the real world, which is to say, from my desk in my apartment in Brooklyn. The first few days of the festival seem very far away now, as they did even when I last saw you only five days ago. During a festival, time tends to go by like that: very quickly and also very slowly, so that ten days actually seem like two months that went by in the span of half an hour. To think back to the beginning of our time in Locarno is not unlike remembering a movie, all those images frozen in time. For a couple of weeks, reality suspended and gave way to a fantasy world contained within three or four hilly streets in a valley. This world revolved in large part around the GranRex theater, where we watched several films written, directed, or performed by Hollywood figures who got in trouble with Joe McCarthy for flirting with communism. At the start of the festival, I was struck by how, in some of these films, the male protagonists’ thirst for power and control manifested in their relationships with the women who get caught in their schemes. Take Edgar G. Ulmer’s Ruthless (1948), which opens on a stunning close-up of Diana Lynn’s face. Here, she’s playing Mallory, though she appears in the film mostly as the coveted Martha, the object of desire of childhood pals Vic Lambdin (Louis Hayward) and Horace Vendig (Zachary Scott). Martha rejects Vic in favor of the sultrier, sexier, taller Horace, who only reciprocates her love inasmuch as her father is willing to pay for his Harvard education. Ruthless (Edgar G. Ulmer, 1948). Martha may be half-blinded by love, but she is no fool. However broken-hearted, she doesn’t pine for Horace once his insincerity becomes clear. She is guided by self-respect: Stung by Horace’s selfishness, she never shows up in the story again, at least not as herself. It’s a kind of self-preservation, the same instinct that, in Horace, translates as—what else?—ruthlessness. I have nothing but admiration for women who save themselves. But as a fan of hardboiled noirs, I was itching for a cunning, glamorous dame. I got my femme fatale in Joseph Losey’s The Intimate Stranger (1956) , in which Reggie Wilson (Richard Basehart) is hounded by one Evelyn Stewart (played with pep by Mary Murphy). The film kicks into gear once Evelyn—whose mischievous position in relation to Reggie is the polar opposite to Martha’s sensible approach toward Horace—is allowed to be openly self-serving, manipulating Reggie’s indiscretions to her own benefit. Outside of the retrospective, Max and I watched a film that directly addresses the broken relations between men and women; or, more specifically, the broken relations between boys and girls. Like Ruthless, Wayne Wapeemukwa’s Manhunt (2026) orbits a pair of childhood buddies whose relationship is strained by the presence of a woman—in this case, a girl, one of two Austrian sisters that Joey (sensitively played by Harris Lowe) and Kit (Landon Tunold) meet on a hiking trip through Canada. Joey becomes involved with Dani (Dilara Foscht), which angers Kit, who may or may not be in love with his friend. Wapeemukwa foregrounds the fact that Joey and Kit’s closeness is forged at the expense of their ability to relate to girls in any humane way. Joey tries, but ultimately capitulates when what Kit had been trying to convince him of turns out, in his eyes, to be true: Girls are evil liars. Manhunt (Wayne Wapeemukwa, 2026). Dani is, obviously, not an evil liar in any sense, least of all in that irresistible Barbara-Stanwyck-in- Double Indemnity way. Instead, she serves a pretty straightforward narrative function, which is to reflect Joey’s brokenness. The same goes for her sister, Becca (Bianca Foscht), who bears the brunt of Kit’s gun-slinging, slur-spewing, manifesto-writing anger. Max and I talked it out on the walk back into town. Surely there is value in Wapeemukwa’s honest portrayal of apathetic boys who have lost the ability to relate to the wider world. But rather than explore the conditions that pushed these young men to incorrigibility, the film is content to simply identify them as “bad.” That doesn’t tell us anything much—not about the characters, and not about the world from which they come. It’s not cinema’s responsibility to cure any social ill, or to provide us with definitive answers, but what it can and must do is attempt to understand the people it sets out to depict. The opening line of Joan Didion’s novel Play It As It Lays rattled around in my head as I made my way back to my room: “What makes Iago evil? Some people ask. I never ask.” I can’t help myself—I always do. Max and Vedant, I can’t wait to hear from you. Warmly, Rafaela *** Dear Max and Rafaela, I too am slowly fumbling my way into what we might call the real world. As you rightly point out, Rafaela, time both stretches and contracts when I think of the last two weeks: Memories seemingly frozen in time also lilt and sway in my mind. I suppose my way of getting to know Locarno was similar to how I’ve befriended most cities: through long saunters, which I’d embark on each night after a busy day of screenings and talks. And yet, I was far from the romanticized figure of the flâneur. Bundled over with exhaustion and surviving on Coop sandwiches, with muscle cramps and a spreading shoe bite on my foot, my walks were imprinted with an uncomfortable profusion of sensations. The U-shaped promenade surrounding Lake Maggiore, with its cool breeze at night, was easier to maneuver than the cobbled pavement of the Piazza, stuffy with bodies huddled in front of the enormous outdoor screen. Midway into the festival, I attended a talk by the artist Ishita Chakraborty, who touched on how basil—the wonderful gelato flavor introduced to us all by Max—had a long history of travel from Asia to Europe. Though basil has been wrested away from its original habitats, domesticated to new surroundings and estranged from its earlier religious and medicinal purposes, Ishita imagined it as endowed with an agency of its own. Something of this disorientation stayed with me as I watched Albert Serra’s Sixteen Moments of My Life (2026). The film revolves around a live performance of sixteen ballads by the screen legend Ingrid Caven, who is accompanied here by The Molforts, Serra’s longtime musical collaborators. Shot mostly in undulating close-ups, and framed against incarnadine reds and velvety blues, Caven assumes an otherworldly persona, looking almost reminiscent of a Francis Bacon painting. Sixteen Moments of My Life (Albert Serra, 2026). I hadn’t heard much of Caven’s singing before. There was such force, such brute intensity in the guttural atonality of the music that I was, in a flash, struck by a vision of her iridescent onscreen history. Erika Balsom perhaps captures it best, referring to Caven as a “celestial creature of glorious artifice and terrible glamor: a rupture, a fantasy, a visitant.” Walking out from the screening, I found myself thinking of Serra’s 2018 installation piece, Roi Soleil , in which a writhing and moaning Lluís Serrat Masanellas—one of the great visages in cinema history—enacts Louis XIV’s agonizing death. There is something about a live performance that seems to echo Serra’s own alchemical style of filmmaking. It’s less about narrative than about capturing a continuous, live unfolding of energies and vibrations, movements and textures. His works—as Serra himself alluded to during a masterclass— activate a reality continually slipping beyond realism. A few days later, I encountered a similar slippage in Umair Bilal’s As Light as Air (2026). Bilal spent months attempting to capture the reality of Sehwan, a town in Pakistan renowned for its Sufi shrine, and yet something resisted that ethnographic gaze. It was only when he surrendered to the logic of the place—to the extent that the team began to shoot in streets they felt were “calling” them—that the film began to acquire its singular shape. As Light as Air eschews plot and exposition in favor of synesthetic immersion: music, lamps, and incense, collective prayers and the rapture of dhamaal (a ritualized form of devotional dance) are less subjects to be explained than materials through which the film discovers its own rhythm. Its arabesque form, meanwhile, leaps from color to monochrome, from freeze-frames to pans and tilts, from slow dissolves to elliptical cuts, progressing through emotional states and affective terrains. While the title invokes a transcendental state, it also recalls Lal Shahbaz Qalandar’s miraculous ability to fly (the saint’s name translates quite literally to “red royal falcon”). The metaphor extends equally to the viewing experience: Watching it, I felt myself gradually entering a state of willing surrender, attuned to invisible longings and unions, ecstatic thresholds and crescendos—all viscerally felt before being rationally understood. As Light as Air (Umair Bilal, 2026). Reading your letter, Rafaela, I kept returning to the question of possession: of women by men, of places by filmmakers, and of subjects by the camera. What struck me was how differently that question plays out in these two films than in those you mention. Sehwan resists Bilal’s vision until the filmmaker stops trying to impose one; Caven’s persona, similarly, resists reduction to any single image. Perhaps this is something we are both circling: a cinema that gives itself over only on its own recalcitrant terms. In retrospect, I understand something of the pull these works had on me. I too belong to a tradition of music—Indian classical—that is highly intricate and prone to improvisation. But beyond their evident musicality, how these two works reveled in the epidermal pleasures of the surface, and, through the very thickness and grime of film matter, transposed their shifting realities onto the nervous system, mirrored my own beleaguered and at times transfixed state during the festival. As I write this letter, I am reminded of Danièle Huillet and Jean-Marie Straub’s Cézanne films, and how fond the duo were of Cézanne’s famous quip on Mont Sainte-Victoire: “Look at this mountain—it was once fire.” Here then is perhaps an apt summation of my Locarno experience: Look at this film—it was once matter. Warmly, vedant *** Dear Rafaela and Vedant, Look at this woman—she was once beautiful. “ Yes, I always knew that life could be beautiful with you ,” croons Ken Conway (Lee Bowman) in the beginning of Smash-Up: The Story of a Woman (1947). Cowboy hat discarded, Ken is singing live in a radio station’s recording booth, accompanied by his ride-or-die pianist Steve Anderson (Eddie Albert). The pair dedicate their first original ballad to Ken’s wife, Angie Evans (Susan Hayward), currently in labor. Because the public loves an incorrigible husband graced with a velvet baritone, Ken catapults to stardom, while Angie spirals to the bottom of bourbon bottles. She’s unable to find her place in Ken’s new life or fulfillment in her own career, having surrendered warbling herself to marry the love of her life…the one now disgusted with her deterioration, unable to parse her trajectory. If love can come any time, then it may also depart at its own discretion. Smash-Up: The Story of a Woman (Stuart Heisler, 1947). Hungover Angie cups her face in her hands, teetering towards another woman (Martha Gray) at a house party. Perhaps we could program this film someday with Manhunt , Rafaela. Alienations of different genders. Two eras, decades apart. Discounting the heart you gave it on Letterboxd, I think you admired Smash-Up for how thoroughly it depicted a wayward, vulnerable soul. Did you? This is an uncouth way to start a letter. Salutations and inquiries to your healths have been excised. ¿Cómo estás? My circadian rhythm’s stuck in Zurich time. I write this letter at 2:40 a.m., consummating madness within this bonfire of words. 1 I have yet to go on a bender or set tenements aflame. I shall if nothing substantial emerges in 800 words (or more; sorry, Laura). One of our Academy peers joked about how I was among the final stragglers back to bed each night but the earliest at breakfast. I’m rarely that gung ho. An olla podrida of insecurity and the exhilaration of being in Locarno subsidized my quota for sleep. Having received a local grant to attend the Critics Academy yet not writing anything beyond our assignments—I considered pitching too late with a death in my immediate family—I felt stirrings of shame whenever I’d see Rafaela grinding away on a laptop, or Vedant declining lunch to prep for interviews. What was I here for if not to work my ass off? Who knew when I’d return to Europe, let alone expensive Switzerland? And why, seven days into the festival, was I declining impromptu meetings with editors to swim in Ponte Brolla? Talk about the indolent Filipino . After Smash-Up , our Critics Academy colleague Dylan and I reunited at Caffè Verbano to interview Ana Vaz for Variety . Before the publicist knocked on the door to remind us of the time, the three of us discussed the crepuscular sunset that appears midway through Hanabi (2026), her lysergic antinuclear feature premiering at the festival. “We need moments in the film that allow us to come out of this enormous anxiety of different events that succeed one after the other,” said Vaz, without missing a beat, “in order for us to tune into a different temporality.” Ten minutes later, we’re out and about, tottering toward Ehsan Khoshbakht’s talk on his retrospectives. Then, out of nowhere, Dylan brought up the tentative plans I had proposed to our group that morning: to join the Filmmakers Academy and Basecampers for a viewing of the partial eclipse—the second time it had happened during the Locarno Film Festival since the 1990s. “My girlfriend would kill me if I didn’t do one cool thing,” Dylan admitted. Alas, Rafaela and Vedant, you had your own plans. Meanwhile, my cowriter and I ran up the hill to reach Castello and left for Cardada, where everyone who didn’t want to hike for three hours awaited the six-minute ski lift. Critics Pierre and George tagged along, both toting eclipse glasses purchased in town for 10 Swiss Francs. I chatted with JT, the other Pinoy in the Locarno Academies, alternating their eclipse glasses with Pierre’s to squint at the penumbratic sky. The sun squeezed through a concave dip in the clouds, looking a tinge more orange than the red sun in Hanabi . My attention drifted. A donkey who looked like Balthazar’s understudy lingered by the fence until too many people petting it drove it off. Breeze sifted through the hillside, cooling the sweat tattooed onto my skin. It was like the best kind of durational cinema. We sat there for three hours until sunset. Photo by Alyssandra Maxine. After the group hiked down to the parking lot, I approached Dylan and asked if he wanted to work on the interview now. “Nah, that would be too antisocial,” he said. “Let’s talk in the hostel.” He would regret this decision after the winding, nausea-inducing drive back into town, though he would still write 500 words more than I did that night. I also bemoaned my decision the next morning, waking at nine o’clock for the press screening of Hong Sang-soo’s Nowhere to Lay My Eyes (2026) and another retrospective film on my watchlist, He Who Must Die (1957). You had walked with me from PalaCinema to GranRex, Vedant, after the discussion with other tenured critics about “How to Survive a Film Festival.” (And you raised a question on the tip of my tongue, too: “You’re not going to get commissions from any major publications that are willing to pay you decent money back home. So how do you translate what you learn here?”) Fatigue and irritation sweltered within. The Variety copy emerged turgid until the nth hour of the deadline, cobbled together with Dylan’s aid. Our draft landed in the editor’s inbox, and then our final day together unfurled: the last talk; the last lunch; the last film, Frankenstein Unbound (1990); the last swim by the rocks; and the last drink at the bar. You left the hostel early morning, Rafaela. We never said goodbye. The final stragglers were Catherine, Vedant, and me. Before I left, I caught you, Vedant, lounging by the garden with your elusive electric mandolin that you brandished upon request. “When are we going to see each other again?” you had asked. “In the next few months,” I promised. We ended up drinking together days later, on my last night in Milan. Then I chased the bus that dropped me off at a ghost town, its inhabitants all caught up in the throes of Ferragosto; I was forced back to Locarno for something affordable that wasn’t pasta (an impossibility). Nowhere to Lay My Eyes (Hong Sang-soo, 2026). Jeonwonsa Film Co. Afterward, I walked slower than the father-in-law in Nowhere to Lay My Eyes around the city. I knew that the moment I’d hit the sheets, I’d have a dreamless rest and then arise, caffeinated by checklists: this letter, the grant paperwork, other commissions, more pitches, a Sisyphean slog of emails…this time without the company of new friends. I write about films because the world moves too fast to remember all the interesting stories. Locarno had offered that holy grail I had been crusading for: doing something meaningful while enjoying the process. On the bus stop at Gordevio stood an open library. Its bottommost shelf cradled the last two entries of a series on Virginia Woolf’s letters in their 1980s editions, one entitled “Leave the Letters Till We’re Dead.” Indignant at my bleak inner monologue, I plucked them from the shelves and fluttered back to Manila. I’m fascinated by how much yet how little one reveals about themselves in lifelong correspondences with others. Will you tell us about whatever you watch next when you’re 65, Rafaela? Will you send pictures of your walks two scores later, Vedant? Even if you both never do, my memories of you and the films we watched together have melted like happy lemon drops on my tongue. Celine Nguyen’s essay on taste closes with this: “Our tastes are how we understand ourselves—and communicating them is how we understand each other.” If words precede thoughts, then your sentences conjoined with mine engulf dark rooms with projections as shimmering as Lake Maggiore. Look at this letter—it was once blank. Look…We were…alpha, bravo, charlie, matter, glad I’m not alone— Belatedly, Max 1. As Virginia Woolf puts it in one of her letters: “I know much of it is sketchy and wants working out; but I had not time. … But if it stirs up thought, that is what I wrote it for. And if someone like yourself feels that there is some scattered truth flying about in it then perhaps it won’t be, as I so often feel writing to be, a mere bonfire of words.”

articles.title: The Final Temenos
articles.author: Emma Fuchs
articles.description: Photo by Emma Fuchs. At sunset we move like a herd. Arms laden with blankets, we snake down the gravel path, as signs in blue spray paint warn “ΠΡΟΣΟΧΗ! Use Caution!” Halfway there, the trees that bracket us part like curtains. Below, stark against the green-gold valley, we can make out a small white square—the projection screen. At a fork in the path, there is a small sign with a blue arrow on it, and the word “Temenos.” From here, the path narrows until suddenly it opens onto a clearing. In a small field, like a basin, rows of red beanbag chairs dot the ground in front of the screen, and behind them, a crescent of pink cushioned benches and a projector wait. The restoration of Eniaios (1948–1990),the magnum opus of Greek-American experimental filmmaker Gregory J. Markopoulos, has been a gradually revealed 25-year process. The experimental film comprises 168 reels organized into 22 cycles—each composed of meticulously spliced black film leader, clear leader, and brief bursting footage from Markopoulos’s early films—and is 80 hours long. Segments of Eniaios ’s restoration have been screened in the same field in the Greek village of Lyssarea at Olympic intervals since 2004. This June, over the course of four nights , the final four cycles ( XIX – XXII ) were screened, marking the completion of the Temenos. This name, originally meaning “a place set apart or a sacred precinct,” has come to signify both Eniaios and the open-air cinema dedicated to it—it has become an event inseparable from its home. 1 This was my induction into the cult of Markopoulos. As I climbed onto the bus which would bring spectators from Karaiskaki Square, a hectic roundabout in the center of Athens, to the shrublands of Arcadia, I was asked if I considered myself “a Marko-head” too. I shrugged. I had found my way here by word of mouth. To undertake a pilgrimage requires both boldness and suppleness. One needs an openness to strangers, and the strangeness encountered along the way, as well as a willingness to transform. Markopoulos conceived of the Temenos not only as a screening but also as a “sanctuary where one may approach Understanding.” 2 This summer, I am approaching the idea that the goal is not to have completed something, but to have seen something through to the end. Photo by Emma Fuchs. When Markopoulos first sought a site for the Temenos, highways hadn’t yet been carved into Arcadia. Lyssarea, his father’s ancestral village, was six hours from Athens by car. According to Markopoulos, “Here was a location upon which a dream could be built. It was never forgotten, and it was believed to be inaccessible.” 3 Now, as two cream-colored coaches carry a hundred cinephiles across mountainous switchbacks to the lush and remote municipality of Gortynia, pilgrimage takes on a new form. While the site of the Temenos is not easily accessible, with certain organizational skills, it is reachable. Before this summer, my sole exposure to Markopoulos had been the film Through a Lens Brightly: Mark Turbyfill (1967), a portrait richly saturated in warm tones and overlaid images. In a cinema in New York, I had found the short film dense, dizzying, and claustrophobic. However, Markopoulos believed that every film deserves an architect that understands its needs. Cinemas, lacking specificity, fail. In 1967, he withdrew his entire filmography from distribution, from his first short of 1940 to his completed but unprinted projects. He envisioned the Temenos as an amphitheater of screens , a projection site that would allow his work to exist in its purest form—not as entertainment, but as “film as film.” I was innocent as to the distance I would have to travel as a spectator. I was unprepared for the ethereality of Eniaios. Photo by Micah Newberger. The film is composed mainly of varying brightnesses. Segments of clear leader create a total and stinging white. Pale moths in these projector beams become bright as stars. Black leader conjures a dark screen, but as the sun sets and the sky darkens, it takes on a violet quality against the true black of night. Brief and sharp between these two modes, excerpts of Markopoulos’s early films arrive stripped of their narrative qualities. Creases in the bent elbow of a man’s tweed jacket. A strange tool. A balding head. A nude body in a shabby apartment. An arm drawn back, hand curled and brushing the jaw, as if pulling an arrow taut against a bow string. Movements barely flicker and that which moves is always gestural, sensual. When black leader follows an image, it creates a lingering, silhouetted after-image. White clears the slate, cleanses the eye, and, when it precedes an image, distills the light into a sudden form, a figurative beauty. Photo by Emma Fuchs. The reels spin these contrasts in rapid cycles. I imagine looking down from the hilltops surrounding the screening site and mistaking the screen for a strobe light. Each image rarely exceeds six seconds, and this length itself is a delicacy. Something to be savored. Most images are even more fleeting, as brief as one frame. Nearly fifteen hours of footage were screened this year—yet endurance felt easy. Suspended between images, time condenses. Each night, extremes of duration and speed combined “subdue the common meaning of Time.” 4 Though the film is silent, dogs in the distance, the granular shift of the beanbag chairs, crickets, and the motoring projector score and texturize the night. On occasion, the rhythm of the film is interrupted by a loud clunk and a true dark screen. When the projector glitches on the second and fourth nights, the projectionist reveals a palm-sized flashlight and sets to fixing the machine with stoicism. Silence and bated breath, and then the reel picks up as if nothing had happened. There is simultaneously much and little more to say, for, as Italo Calvino has written, “any interpretation impoverishes the myth and suffocates it.” 5 The myth, in this case, refers to both the inspiration for Markopoulos’s early works, for he was obsessed with the tales of Asclepius and Prometheus, the Old Masters and Andy Warhol, and his tendency to mythologize and idolize himself and Robert Beavers, his muse and collaborator. Since Markopoulos’s death in 1992, Beavers, alongside his own filmmaking, has spent much of his life succeeding Markopoulos in his stewardship of their archives, the restorations of Eniaios , and their steadfast vision of the Temenos. As per Calvino again: “With myths, one should not be in a hurry. It is better to let them settle into the memory, to stop and dwell on every detail, to reflect on them without losing touch with their language of images.” 6 Where I find Markopoulos’s work the most remarkable, however, is in its value of lightness, not only in the form of brilliance, but also in relation to weightlessness. How does one make a colossal, 80-hour film without creating something stone-heavy? I have turned to Calvino’s essay “On Lightness” to try and make sense of this, since he shares Markopoulos’s view that the “intensively ascetic and isolated” process of creation is a calling to “remove weight from the structure.” 7 Calvino writes: Were I to choose an auspicious image for the new millennium, I would choose… the sudden agile leap of the poet philosopher who raises himself above the weight of the world, showing that with all his gravity he has the secret of lightness, and that what many consider to be the vitality of the times noisy, aggressive, revving and roaring-belongs to the realm of death, like a cemetery for rusty old cars. 8 Markopoulos viewed the world in similar conjunctions, whose hyphenated roles and merged ideologies allow one to view the world in a minuscule and modular manner, with greater attention paid to the illuminations of an image beyond language. For Markopoulos, his role was one of the filmmaker-physician. Anatomical delicacy, to Markopoulos, was the ideal approach to filmmaking, the approach that would result in the greatest clarity of his ideas. By counting the seconds of footage and meticulously measuring and suturing lengths of film, Markopoulos makes a science of his own. By reducing his filmography to brief illuminations, time itself seems to evaporate into light beams. Photo by Micah Newberger. P. Adams Sitney, the late historian of American avant-garde cinema, in his reflections on the earliest Temenos, 9 referred to his friendship with Markopoulos as “clouded.” Nonetheless, he had attended every Temenos between 2004 and his passing in the summer of 2025. At the annual welcome dinner, I sat with his son, who was attending the Temenos, carrying his father’s spirit. He gestured vaguely, explaining this, and the word spirit seemed to exist on the threshold of corporeal and atmospheric. On the third night of screenings, Beavers hosted a town hall of sorts in concentric circles of plastic lawn chairs. He sat alone in the center, and in a soft voice addressed the finality of the event while also joking that the Temenos is yet to be realized, and that the next iteration will occur in a field arranged with alabaster chairs. 10 On this penultimate night, Eniaios XXI felt particularly sparse. But, vibrant against the sparsity, there was an image on the screen of a glittering fountain. The total shock of this moment’s beauty reverberated long after the image had ended. After the last reel, as we walked uphill with flashlights casting halos around our feet, there seemed to be a thread woven through the crowd, euphoric whispers of “fountain!” In the murkiness of the bus ride home, faces obscured, I heard the word “fountain!” float past me again and again. Photo by Micah Newberger. On our final descent into the field on that fourth night, walking down the hill to endure hours of flashing lights felt both absurd and familiar. The air was charged with a heaviness of anticipation. Cycle XXII has a runtime of four hours and 43 minutes, with five reel changes. Alongside dinners and town halls, it is tradition to release large-format folios relating to each year’s Temenos. This year, embossed with a grasshopper on the cover and unfolding like a newspaper, Markopoulos’s 1992 essay “The Future of the Temenos and its Boundaries” is reprinted alongside its Greek translation in green ink. The folio also includes “Poverty & Need and Abundance & Ingenuity” in which Beavers further reflects on the Temenos’s totality, and Markopoulos’s own sparsely annotated list of the films from which he salvaged footage to build Eniaios XIX – XXII. Those who are familiar with Markopoulos’s oeuvre use this bibliography-like list as an archeological guide to the films. To the uninitiated spectator, these notes feel as sparse as the Eniaios , like loose threads that must be pulled taut in order to locate their origin. The final image of the film is attributed to figalea , a work that never circulated. In the folio, its naming is preceded by the note: “[morning, phosphorous / the light bearer, the morning star].” 11 Photo by Micah Newberger. Markopoulos wrote that ending a film is like tying an intricate surgical knot. One must make “the best knot for each work; and it is completed forever.” 12 It must be clean. It is somewhere near three in the morning when the projection cuts off and, though abrupt, there is a sense of finality. Before the screening, Beavers had asked that when the Temenos ends, we hold a moment of silence. These few minutes of quiet are like a canopy. In the dark, in the absence of the projector’s hum, true silence takes on a thick feeling in the air. The screen loses its violet wash as eyes readjust. We wait, until Beavers releases a thunderous “Thank you.” It is not yet light, but it will be soon. We march uphill in pairs and small clusters. At the top, the two coaches wait, patient and grave. Next to them is a folding table with sherbet-colored shot glasses and a large bottle of tsipouro, a Greek pomace brandy. Hands clink in the dark, and I make hazy eye contact as I toast. The rosy fingers of dawn stretch out across the sky. The exuberant birds are already waking. We toy with the idea of not sleeping, and then we drag our bags slowly through the village streets to meet the bus one last time and complete our own cycle, which ends in Athens, at Karaiskaki Square. 1. articles.title: The Armchair Answer to the Troubles
articles.author: Sam Manning
articles.description: Illustration by Danny Ische. The 1970s was a difficult decade for cinemas across Britain and Ireland as attendances continued their long postwar decline. Most of the glamorous art deco picture palaces built during the 1930s had either closed or fallen into disrepair and comparatively few new cinemas were opened after World War II until the arrival of the multiplexes in the 1980s. While these challenges were facing exhibitors in many other countries around the world, Northern Ireland’s experience of the downturn was unique. The outbreak of violent sectarian conflict in the late 1960s, euphemistically known as the Troubles, created an environment that actively discouraged cinema attendance. Queues still formed for blockbusters such as The Godfather (1972), The Exorcist (1973), and Jaws (1975), but ongoing violence and nightly curfews made it more difficult to justify a cinema trip for more run-of-the-mill fare, with many people retreating into private spaces. This meant that cinemagoing became less of a social habit and more of an occasional activity that carried a level of potential risk. In Belfast, bomb and fire damage in the early 1970s led to the permanent closure of the Classic and the Broadway cinemas, and in 1977, IRA firebombs damaged three venues: the ABC, the New Vic, and the Curzon. Cinemas were no longer safe spaces immune from what was happening in the outside world. The launch of Video Home System (VHS) in the mid-1970s therefore came at the perfect time for Northern Ireland’s cinema lovers, who desired entertainment and escapism but were less willing than ever to leave the comfort and relative safety of their own homes. JVC’s new VHS technology eventually beat the competition of Sony’s rival Betamax format and revolutionized the way in which people watched and consumed visual media. For the time, the power to control when audiences watched films began to shift from the exhibitors to the audience. Power shifted, too, from producers to consumers, and for the first time people could directly record films or television programs onto blank tapes and play, pause, or rewind at their own leisure. This power still had a barrier, which was the large expense of videocassette recorders (VCRs).Yet many people purchased them in spite of difficult economic circumstances and high levels of unemployment in Northern Ireland. In 1980, for instance, an electronics shop in the Country Antrim town of Ballymena advertised a Philips VCR for the hefty sum of £495, equivalent to £2,165 in today’s money. Renting a machine was a popular alternative for those who couldn’t afford to buy a VCR outright, with the shop hiring out the same device for £18.50 per month, still a considerable expense at a time when the average gross weekly household income was £119. By 1981, VCR ownership had spread so quickly across Northern Ireland that one newspaper report asked if home video was the “armchair answer to the Ulster Troubles,” providing an easy means of accessing the latest films without having to leave the house. 1 To compete, cinemas that were already struggling financially were forced to lower prices, improve their offer to patrons, and in some cases convert a single auditorium into a multiscreen cinema. Television channels responded by programming a broader range of films to compete with the appeal of home video. By 1983, reports suggested that Northern Ireland had a higher concentration of VCRs than in any other part of the UK. The video boom provided an extra source of income for the corner shops, newsagents, and electronic stores who rented videos to consumers. And soon after, specialist independent video shops sprung up on streets across Northern Ireland. For around £1.50 a night, film lovers could rent and take home one of the latest video releases from around the world, some of which had not previously been shown in local cinemas. American films generally dominated the rental market, but a 1982 list of the most popular rented videos in Northern Ireland also included British crime drama McVicar (1980)and the Israeli sex-comedy Hot Bubblegum (1981). Long before the streaming age, some video shops even offered subscription services, where people could pay a monthly or annual fee to rent multiple videos. Until later in the 1980s, very few people purchased videos outright, and a single VHS retailed for as much as £60. The distributors wanted to protect their product and were largely reluctant to “sell through” to the market. For a small investment, the video boom provided local entrepreneurs with the opportunity to earn a living by investing in a video rental library. But the same technology that allowed people to record films directly from the television also meant there were money-making opportunities for those willing to flout the law by copying and selling pirate or counterfeit videos. Why spend thousands investing in a legitimate video library when you could just as easily buy a bank of video recorders and flood the market with easily copied pirate or counterfeit videos? Before John Badham’s Saturday Night Fever (1977) was first shown at Belfast’s Avenue Cinema in 1978, pirated VHS copies of the film were shown in hotels, pubs, and clubs across Northern Ireland. In some parts of the province there was still a strong appetite for public entertainment, especially for those unable to purchase an expensive VCR. Kelly’s Golf Links Hotel in the north coast town of Portrush brazenly advertised the “first time showing in Northern Ireland” on a 10 ft screen. 2 For £1.50, the same price as renting a video, people could watch the film followed by a disco. This incident led a High Court judge to ban further screenings until the film’s official release and order that all pirate copies be returned to the distributor. 3 By 1981, the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC), Northern Ireland’s then police force, was starting to crack down on what they called “illegal video shows.” The police wanted to counter the public perception that pirating videos was a permissible and victimless crime, and the force’s anti-racketeering squad confiscated over four thousand illegal video tapes, including pornographic material, during a four-day operation. A police spokesperson said that “video piracy is not only a means whereby paramilitary organizations and criminal opportunists are able to make money, but members of the public are being conned into accepting and paying for something that is not the genuine article.” 4 By 1982, the UK video black market was reportedly worth £100 million. In Northern Ireland, legitimate distributors responded to piracy by grouping together to form the Northern Ireland Video Library and Trades Association. But if the RUC were able to stop illegal public screenings of Saturday Night Fever , they found it even more difficult to counter the spread of pirate and counterfeit videos on the streets and in people’s homes. The pirate hit of 1982 was Steven Spielberg’s E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (with an estimated ten thousand illegal copies available in the UK in mid-August, four months before the film was released in Belfast cinemas in December 1982. In September, one reporter found copies easily available in the town of Ballymena for £5, with a source saying, “I can get you any film you want—from the class like E.T. down to the blue movies.” 5 But the premature release did not dampen people’s enthusiasm to see Spielberg’s film on the big screen. It was still a massive success when it screened at Belfast’s ABC, which had reopened in 1980 as a four-screen cinema. The film then played at venues across Northern Ireland, at a time when overall cinema attendance continued to decline. Shortly after its cinema release, a magazine poll revealed E.T. as one of the top ten videos of 1982, despite not being legally available to rent or buy until 1988. The potent impact of piracy led the RUC in February 1983 to seize up to 35,000 videos from 25 suspected pirate and counterfeit dealers across Northern Ireland in the biggest raid of its type in the UK. Prosecutions were reported from 1985 onwards, and even though this took a few dealers out of the market, it didn’t seem to act as a widespread deterrent given the high demand and relative ease of copying video cassettes. Soon after the raid, Ulster Television’s Counterpoint program dedicated an episode to video pirates , showing how they were easily able to set up backstreet factories with multiple VCRs and make thousands of duplicate copies. It claimed that the market was flooded with illegal copies, and even legitimate dealers were unable to tell if they were selling counterfeit copies. In the episode, one video dealer, who denies stocking pirates videos, dons an E.T. hat, picks up an acoustic guitar and sings the following words: “ I’m a video pirate in the true Ulster way, and I make my living legitimately. I copy the soft porn on Sundays and leave all the hard stuff till Mondays. I’m good at the Disneys, the First Bloods, the E.T.s and I’ve copied the Rockys as well. I’ve closed 20 cinemas but now I’m on the Valium. Warner Bros. they scare me like hell. My machines are well hidden in a mountain in the bracken where fraud squads can’t dwell. And if anyone copies this ballad, sure they’ll be an old pirate as well, they’ll be an old pirate as well. ” Given the ease and profitability of video piracy, it’s not surprising that in Northern Ireland paramilitaries also got into the business. In 1990, one newspaper report alleged that video piracy earned the IRA almost £1 million a year, one third of its racketeering income alongside earnings from construction and cross-border smuggling. 6 Democratic Unionist Party Alderman Jack McKee warned that paramilitary organizations may be profiting from video piracy and said that “unwittingly, people could be buying tapes and helping to fill the coffers of organizations like the IRA. The money they’re paying could be used to buy bullets and explosives to kill soldiers and policemen.” 7 By the 1990s, attempts to clamp down on video piracy reportedly led the paramilitaries to seek funds from elsewhere. A 1993 newspaper article claimed that the RUC Anti-Racketeering Squad’s success in cutting off funding from video piracy had led to a recent increase in armed robberies. 8 The first video shops were independents with unique names, such as Toppers Video Shack in Lurgan or Zodys in Comber. In the mid-1980s these were joined by small local chains such as Star Video and Valley Video Co. Irish chain Xtra-vision first opened shops in Northern Ireland in 1989 and quickly became the largest video retailer in the region. In 1990, there were 248 “video libraries” in Northern Ireland, 72 of which were branches of Xtra-vision. Paramilitaries of all persuasions, having been clearly attracted to the money that could be made from the black market, began to target these shops. In 1990, one newspaper article claimed that “Loyalist paramilitary groups were responsible for three recent bomb attacks on Northern shops owned by the Dublin-based Xtra-Vision video chain,” with a hand grenade thrown into a Belfast shop, followed by bomb damage at branches in Belfast and Portadown. The violence that had turned some people away from the cinema was now encroaching on this alternative space. Loyalist sources were concerned that “addresses of loyalists and security force members may be in the firm’s computerised subscriber system.” A spokesman for Xtra-vision responded by blaming “loyalist racketeers irked at the loss of their lucrative illegal video copying scam because of the new competition.” 9 Later reports stated that after the fall of the USSR, Loyalist paramilitaries were using funds from video piracy to import arms from former eastern bloc countries. The arrival of purpose-built multiplexes in Northern Ireland from 1990 led to increased cinema attendance, with admissions rising from 2.3 million in 1991 to 4 million in 1998. But piracy continued throughout the decade, with films such as Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991), Jurassic Park (1993), and The Lion King (1994)reported as big pirate hits, copies being easily obtained from open-air markets. During this time, buying videos outright became a more affordable option. Distributors dropped prices for the “sell through” market, sales increased, and video purchases started to generate more revenue than rentals. Local independent video dealers also faced increased competition from new high street chains such as Virgin Megastore, whose prominence and high visibility made them less likely to deal counterfeit videos in the same fashion as the less scrupulous independent dealers. DVD entered the UK market in 1998, the same year as the signing of the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland. For several years, video shops fared well by adapting to the rise of this new format. But so did the pirates, who shifted from videotapes to counterfeit discs. By the 2010s, the legitimate dealers eventually succumbed to the ease and popularity of streaming. Northern Ireland’s last remaining Xtra-vision store closed its doors for the final time in 2016. As piracy shifted from physical copies to downloads and torrents, there was less of a direct connection between the pirates and their consumers. In the 1980s, physical copies needed to be bought from someone and somewhere, but by the 2000s a file could easily be downloaded from many places in the world. More recently, however, the rise of the so-called “dodgy box,” a colloquial term for an illegal or “rogue” streaming device, has reconnected the consumer with the people who install and distribute these devices. In its 2022/23 Annual Report, the Police Service of Northern Ireland’s Organised Crime Task force said that these and similar devices are now “one of the main intellectual property crime concerns in Northern Ireland.” 10 Though VHS and the video shop are things of the past, the home video boom which swept the province from the mid-1970s forever changed the way people paid for and watched movies, as well as redefining what cinemagoing meant in Northern Ireland. Home video was a global phenomenon, as was the rise of video piracy. But in Northern Ireland, the Troubles created both extra demand for home entertainment and led to cash-hungry paramilitaries who found that piracy was an easy way to partly fund their organizations. In preparation for the latest season of The Wonder Cinema podcast , which explores the history of VHS in Northern Ireland, I scoured the second-hand shops of Belfast looking for old VHS tapes. After one trip, I returned home to notice that something was a little off with my newly purchased copy of Crocodile Dundee (1986) . The front looked normal, but when I turned it over, there was no barcode, and when I opened the box, a shoddy silver label on the spine of the tape simply stated the title of the film. Thirty years after the film was first released, the pirate videos that had flooded the market in the 1980s were still available on the streets of Belfast. 1. articles.title: Inherit the Wind: Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s “The Samurai and the Prisoner”
articles.author: Alexis Moon
articles.description: The Samurai and the Prisoner (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 2026). Ever since he first broke into the Western cinephile consciousness with Cure (1997) and Pulse (2001), Kurosawa Kiyoshi has frequently been canonized as a horror auteur. This lens has been applied and reapplied to each of his films by distributors and critics alike, with the generic conventions of horror centralized as the key means of packaging and understanding a prolific body of work. Too often, though, this understandable but shallow view of Kurosawa’s filmography has missed the forest for the Charisma tree; the release of the director’s elegant new jidaigeki , The Samurai and the Prisoner (which boasts the scarifying title of “Black Prison Castle” in Japan), affords an opportunity to revisit and reframe a remarkable career. Kurosawa has regularly stated that he has never considered himself to be a “horror director,” and that he is entirely forward looking (whether the futures he perceives are bright is another matter). In a 2019 interview with Tokyo University of the Arts (where he is also a professor), Kurosawa stated, “I don’t much want to set my themes, my styles, etc., in stone, you know? I want to do lots of things. I’m often asked, ‘What do you want to do next?’ but the response that is easiest to understand is ‘I want to do something that isn’t what I’ve done up to now.’” Although Kurosawa has been lauded as an absolute master of the horror genre, granting him a privileged position even before the current boom of so-called “elevated horror”—and frequent name-checks from reviewers squinting for reference points in the low light of Obsession (2025)—it has come at a cost—specifically, how his work has been analyzed as a whole. The “horror master” designation has perhaps helped some of his other films attain a viewership, but this has sometimes come at a cost too—of how those films themselves are seen. This is especially infelicitous given that Kurosawa has long shown a desire to toy with generic conventions rather than find himself beholden to them. When observing his body of work as a whole, it is far more coherent to consider Kurosawa’s pictures in terms of themes and movements rather than genres. Kurosawa’s filmography can be coarsely divided into two epochs: his early works and his main body of films. These groupings are not absolute but they map the shifting perception of the director from craftsman to auteur. Between 1973 and 1997, Kurosawa’s feature-length cinema was primarily a scattershot mélange of gun-for-hire genre assignments, from “pink” comedies to yakuza crime pictures to traditional J-Horror; while certainly present on the festival circuit, he was not typically appraised as a master. The quality of these films varies, but the unevenness belies an accruing formal confidence (or, in the case of Sweet Home [1989], a lack of control over the finished work—Kurosawa sued Itami Productions in a failed attempt to prevent the film’s re-shot and re-edited form from being distributed). Kurosawa used this part of his career as a formal staging ground for experimentation; many early visual or structural ideas would notably be incorporated in his later, more famous projects. Rather famously, the Godardian experimentation in the “pink” film The Excitement of the Do-Re-Mi-Fa Girl (1985) was such that it was canned by the producers. The film is a mix of late-1960s Godard symbolism and aesthetic choices and a narrative on psychological research which mirrors David Cronenberg’s Stereo (Tile 3B of a CAEE Educational Mosaic) (1969), pleasing in its pop art frolicsomeness and use of Itami Juzo, but hardly the titillating and exploitative work the production company wanted. Cure (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 1997). The Excitement of the Do-Re-Mi-Fa Girl went unreleased until Kurosawa bought the completed work and released it himself. Kurosawa’s second period starts with Cure at the end of 1997, and it features increased consistency and authorial control—the latter quality embedded in this film’s deployment of a sinister hypnotist stage managing his prey, Caligari-style. Both periods share thematic concerns and stylistic flourishes: Excitement and Cure both revolve around psychology students, the most infamous sequence in Pulse —the “wobble walking” ghost—was already workshopped in Door III (1996), and the main thesis for much of Kurosawa’s career—as well as the comedic tones of both License to Live (1998) and Doppelgänger (2003) was articulated in the slapstick made-for-TV short Whirlpool of Joy (1992). This period contains all of Kurosawa’s most famous works—including Cannes-ratified titles like Bright Future (2003) and Tokyo Sonata (2008) as well as the occasional foray into V-Cinema and television, and some particularly experimental (and not always acclaimed) deep cuts. In order to best understand Kurosawa as an artist (and especially this second period of his career), it is important to consider the context of postwar Japan. The “economic miracle” of Japan (1955–1973) covers the first portion of Kurosawa’s life. Born in 1955, Kurosawa experienced its early years growing up in Kobe, a major center of heavy industry and manufacturing, land reclamation projects, and port development. Economic growth slowed in 1973 due to the oil-price shock, then rebounded, coinciding with a consumer electronics boom (although it did not re-enter a period of “miracle” growth). By the mid-1980s, Japan’s economy had slipped into recession. In the late 1980s, an asset price bubble began to grow, and was characterized by the rapid escalation of stock market and real-estate prices. Through what was later discovered to be wholesale corruption on virtually every level of Japanese society, the bubble proved unsustainable. When the bubble finally burst in 1991, it kicked off what macroeconomists refer to as the “Lost Decade.” The “Lost Decade” became “Lost Decades,” and Japan’s economy has yet to recover. As one might expect, the financial loss was felt most heavily by the average citizen. Retribution (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 2006). Various realist movements have had a strong influence on the films made during the second era of Kurosawa’s career. Although he eschews some of the typical conventions of neo-realism (such as non-professional actors and the use of documentary or documentary-like footage), his work (in line with his cinematic forebears such as Jean Renoir) self-consciously and authentically reflects the economic and social conditions of the day, even when the films skew toward the fantastical: Cloud (2024) is preoccupied with market forces; even a flatly supernatural tale like Retribution (2006) exists in a recognizably workaday world . Kurosawa has witnessed the economic ennui and social decline born from the various recessions of his lifetime,and the devastating impact of the asset price bubble burst and its social and economic fallout have greatly impacted his cinema. And yet, while Kurosawa’s films occasionally depict nihilism—the standard reading of the apocalyptic visions in Pulse , Charisma , (1999) and Cloud —they are anything but nihilistic. Instead, they seek an honest reckoning with their late capitalist moment—an unsentimental but humane moral clarity—that those living through the depicted conditions may miss because it cuts so close. This deep pathos, which accesses the emotional without wallowing in mawkishness, is part of what makes Kurosawa a phenomenal artist beyond his precise technique. However, this is also the aspect of his work which has been most often overlooked by Western commentators. Kurosawa’s work prior to The Samurai and the Prisoner has been grounded in explorations of a devastated national identity, ennui, and alienation. Cure , Eyes of the Spider , (1998) and Cloud are all informed, in whole or in part, by the effects of the “Lost Decades” recession in Japan: the angst is felt ambiently. He observes the total collapse of patriarchal order in the anti-Ozu film Tokyo Sonata centered on a family unit being pulled in several directions—kicked off by the father’s unemployment—and lugubrious devastation and misogyny in the supernatural thriller Loft (2005), which unfolds among a set of present-tense ruins. Films like Pulse , with its Y2K anxieties, isolation, and social failure, and Doppelgänger , which observes how technology can destroy human relationships as much as build them, portray technology-as-mediation of reality and each other. This is even better exemplified with the criminally underrated Real (2013), a film whose reputation has suffered from the expectation of Kurosawa as a horror director—something the film does not stick to (ditto Journey to the Shore [2015], a ghost story without scares). Each of these films paint a picture of a society trying to patch a communal hole with electronics, though it would be wrong to reduce the films’ worldview to simple technophobia. The existentialist meditation on the shifting conditions in pre- and post-bubble Japan in the zany, borderline-screwball License to Live tackles the need to create one’s own meaning and value. Even questions of national identity and sense of direction such as those in Charisma , Barren Illusion (1999), and the WWII-era espionage drama Wife of a Spy (2020) are contending with the experience of modern Japan. To the Ends of the Earth (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 2019). Kurosawa’s work has also taken him outside of the country, providing a kind of offbeat counterpoint to his usual setting. Both Daguerrotype (2016) and the 2024 Serpent’s Path remake are French productions, To the Ends of the Earth (2019) is an Uzbekistani-Japanese co-production, and Seventh Code (2013), while still a solely Japanese production, deals explicitly with experiences of Japanese immigrants in post-Soviet countries. Even setting these examples aside, it is not as though the perspicuity of Kurosawa’s other pictures is exclusive to a Japanese audience. Issues pertaining to technology, economic alienation, and national identity are also broadly digestible, even if the specifics pertain to Japan. Whether working within Japan, or in an international context, Kurosawa’s films are timely and prescient, and he has maintained a consistent thematic north star. This all changes with The Samurai and the Prisoner , perhaps Kurosawa’s most thematically ambitious film. Although it contains many formal and stylistic connections to Kurosawa’s past filmography, it charts new thematic and generic territory. Even Wife of a Spy , Kurosawa’s only other period piece, concerns itself foremost with questions of modernity—its eye is on the historical horizon. In fact, for a film which is so steeped in the legacy of Japanese cinema (not to mention culture, religion, and history), The Samurai and the Prisoner (which looks back without being reactionary) is his most cosmopolitan work. It is impossible to discuss every aspect of this epically scaled drama without disclosing critical plot details best left to a cinematic screening, but a short synopsis can still be suggestive of its scope and concerns. The film follows the actions of Lord Araki Murashige, a real historical figure, and his retinue of retainers during the second siege of Arioka Castle (1578–79). Murashige had previously rebelled against Lord Oda Nobunaga’s forces, and was awaiting the arrival of reinforcements from the Mori clan (a necessary condition of his eventual victory). The film begins with the arrival (and subsequent imprisonment) of Kuroda Kanbei (a man best remembered as one of the most brilliant strategists of the period), who was sent by Nobunaga in order to persuade Murashige to surrender. Instead of shooting the messenger, Murashige imprisons him, kicking off a battle of wills that spans a cycle of seasons. The Samurai and the Prisoner (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 2026). The Samurai and the Prisoner is set apart from these other works by virtue of its assertive and imperative qualities. Whereas Kurosawa’s past filmography has sought to elucidate, The Samurai and the Prisoner seeks to prescribe—a shift perhaps commensurate with advancing age and stature (an impulse that finds more satirical expression in the coda of Cloud , which ends with a character offering advice). Murashige is seemingly a self-portrait of sorts for Kurosawa, and after decades of diagnosing the ills of a modern world defined by alienation—and putting his observations in literally or figuratively scarifying terms—the filmmaker now wishes to push, calmly but urgently, for a fundamental, structural change. There is a lot of talk of strategy and victory in The Samurai and the Prisoner , both between clans and between individuals, and yet the stakes exist outside such frameworks. It is not a matter of winning or losing, but reorienting ourselves toward hope and abandoning the death cult of the status quo, first as an individual, and then by provoking collective action. Although this echoes the character arcs in Charisma and Bright Future , the context is quite different. In Charisma , Yakusho’s Yabuike rewrites the rules of the world, and in Bright Future , Odagiri’s Nimura decides to make his own moves to push society in some small way (to say nothing of Hagiwara’s hypnotist in Cure ). However, all of these are examples of characters responding to the social order of the day and taking action within that framework. The Samurai and the Prisoner takes a different tack, with Murashige opting to step outside of that framework entirely: The samurai refuses to be a prisoner of tradition (the English title is a germane reference to the protean and mercurial positions held by the cardinal characters). It is not sufficient to merely attempt to enact change, as Murashige does initially—his martial aims are comparable to those prior examples—instead, he takes an additional step, outside of the frame of the world itself. If you have seen the truth of the world through the lens of Kurosawa’s camera, you have no choice but to seek something different, as Murashige does; as Kurosawa himself does. Furthermore, in embracing the Sengoku period, The Samurai and the Prisoner is the first work where Kurosawa contends with the gargantuan legacy of Akira Kurosawa, particularly the films Throne of Blood (1957), an inescapable reference given the primacy of palace intrigue, and Kagemusha (1980), another self-portrait which manifests in the margins of Kiyoshi’s formal language, like annotations. Thus, it is the film of a dreamer, of an artist who has spent his life gently engaging with his audience in the hopes of helping them (and himself) recognize a broken world; now, he delineates a path toward a better one. In this respect (and several others), the film also has much in common with Kagemusha (if not 1990’s Dreams ). Like Kurosawa (Kiyoshi), Kurosawa (Akira) was 70 years old when he made that exceptional jidaigeki . Like The Samurai and the Prisoner , Kagemusha ’s narrative centers on a stand-in for the director, who aspires to a heroic, world-changing standard. But whereas Kurosawa (Akira) looks back at the samurai as a heroic ideal that he has failed to live up to (in a sense, failing to live up to the ideals of his samurai family ancestors), Kurosawa (Kiyoshi) idealizes a figure who is a sort of anti-samurai, someone who rejects custom and wishes to change the world. Much like in Kagemusha and Throne of Blood , most of The Samurai and the Prisoner ’s violence occurs offscreen, and that which doesn’t is not fetishized or glorified; instead it is portrayed as an ugly reality. Throne of Blood ’s Lady Asaji (Yamada Isuzu) is invoked in the way that characters contend with their guilty, violent consciences. The difference between the two directors is that Kurosawa (Kiyoshi) does not idolize the samurai, either as an ideal or a historical reality. This also sets Kurosawa’s adaptation apart from the best-selling novel upon which The Samurai and the Prisoner is based. Although still a relatively faithful adaptation (Kurosawa has spoken of the source text with admiration), it differs considerably from the original novel in its thematic purview. While the novel establishes Murashige as something of an anomaly, his strategies and overarching beliefs are firmly within the realm of the samurai. Kurosawa mythologizes Murashige differently, aiming to establish him as a subversive, revolutionary figure, one who seditiously disregards tradition to redefine the rules of engagement and the conditions of victory (“To win without killing,” as one character states). In a sense, Kurosawa (Kiyoshi) seeks to succeed where Kurosawa (Akira) failed, although not in a confrontational way. There is no point debating which auteur “gets it right” or which approach is superior. Kurosawa (Kiyoshi)’s aims are more subtle, and unlike those of Kurosawa (Akira), it is harder to gauge his artistic successes and failures. The Samurai and the Prisoner (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 2026). Irrespective of one’s evaluation of the legacy of Japanese cinema, The Samurai and the Prisoner stakes its most persuasive claim on the level of form. The spider that features in the plot (and the poster design) is an emblem of a narrative crafted as a web of intrigue and deceit. Scenes are staged and sutured together at a brisk pace; the frequent long takes have a rhythmic perfection which recalls Mizoguchi Kenji’s finest works. Motile subjects (and their motivations) are obscured and revealed by fusuma sliding doors, pillars, and walls, perpetually shifting in and out of sight; close-ups are at a premium. The titular prison is an expansive mass of shifting sands (and allegiances) which resemble the dunes in the ever-changing Zone of Stalker , in stark contrast to the novel’s historically accurate cell (also resembling any of Kurosawa’s cavernous warehouses without end). Masahiro Motoki is brilliant as Murashige, as is Arakawa Yoshitaka as Chiyoho, but it is Suda Masaaki, the sullen cyber-honey-badger of Cloud , who delivers a frankly astounding turn as Kuroda Kanbei, the titular prisoner. The centerpiece of the film takes the form of three consecutive scenes, one for each of the principal trio: moments of unveiling given the force of revelation. All three stand among the most formally perfect sequences in Kurosawa’s oeuvre, and as the conjoined emotional and philosophical core of the film, they are impeccable. The final sequence of The Samurai and the Prisoner is markedly different from previous Kurosawa films. While the endings of Cloud , Chime (2024), and the Serpent’s Path remake all mark an openness—a kind of forward progression—they are hardly optimistic about what could come next. To paraphrase the Buddhist koan at the center of The Samurai and the Prisoner , they are advances to Hell. Conversely (and critically), The Samurai and the Prisoner ’s ambiguous—but in its way, satisfying—ending paves the way for future optimism. The immediate outcomes are not necessarily what any of the characters involved wanted, but that is ultimately beside the point, for the filmmaker as well as the characters; we end on grace notes of solidarity, duty, and devotion (for the characters as well). Rather, the ending explores the conditions of the possibility of better outcomes for all of humanity, and how we can orient ourselves to them. The final scene’s focus on the wind in the trees recalls “impermanence” and the unseen reality in the Buddhist tradition; Murashige’s Zen philosophy and Kurosawa’s artistry converge on the breeze (another commonality with the other Kurosawa’s films). “I think this act of taking something that we cannot typically see and then, through its movement, being able to confirm its existence—to show us and reassure us that it’s actually there—is very much akin to cinematic expression itself,” Kurosawa told The Film Stage . “So wind, to me, is not so much something that is spiritual, but I think of cinema as something that is there for us to be able to capture the wind … [it is] almost like cinematic expression itself. The finale is divorced from that which came before, seemingly standing outside of both time and space, with an ascension for the characters who have abandoned their agendas in favour of responding appropriately to the way the wind blows.”
