articles.title: Songs for a Kiss: The Evolving Romance of Pakistani Cinema
articles.author: Manahil Tahira
articles.description: Lobby card for Aina (Nazrul Islam, 1977). In the song “Mujhe Dil Se” from Pakistani director Nazrul Islam’s Aina (1977), Rita (Shabnam) comes out of the shower still wet. Water beads on her forehead, runs down her bare arms, gathers in her hair. Instead of a towel, a red sari swathes her body, not yet disciplined into pleats. Her husband, Iqbal (Nadeem), just awake, rises from the bed and crosses toward her in a white kurta that mirrors the pale bathroom tiles she has stepped out from, as though he, too, belongs to the soft, steamy world she leaves behind. She smiles when he pulls her onto his lap. As Iqbal leans into Rita’s neck, the film cuts away before his lips can touch her skin. In the cinema of many countries, this moment would culminate in a kiss. But in Aina and its contemporaries, lovers never kiss. More than Muslim-majority sensibilities, this absence in Pakistani cinema can be attributed to cultural codes of respectability that date back to pre-Partition colonial India and continue to be reinforced by subsequent censor boards. If the kiss is cinema’s enduring initiation ritual for sex, Pakistani films offer a strange exhibit. Romantic duets replace kisses, whereas sex is displaced into a vocabulary of implication: flower-laden marital beds, dimming lamps, trembling vases on bedside tables, lovers dissolving discreetly offscreen before their bodies fully meet. By the time Aina arrived in theaters in 1977, these erotics were already a fixture. Hence, between Rita and Iqbal, texture becomes the terrain of erotic possibility: moisture, fabric, skin, waking intimacy. Nowhere is this more tangible than in the recurring image of the marital bed, an unmistakably erotic site housed within the romantic duet, “Mujhe Dil Se.” Upon release, Aina became an immediate blockbuster, winning 12 Nigar Awards—the country’s premier film honors at the time—including Best Film. Its place in Pakistan’s cinematic canon was so secure that it became one of the country’s few classics to be remade twice, once in 1998, titled Nikah , and later in 2013, as Aaina . Across the three films, the marital bed and its relationship to the duet become a barometer of the industry’s changing imagination of intimacy, tracing Pakistani cinema from its commercial zenith through its collapse and into its television-shaped revival. Lobby card for Aina (Nazrul Islam, 1977). Aina ’s appeal lies in its familiar premise. Rita, the daughter of a wealthy industrialist, falls in love with Iqbal, a hotel receptionist. Defying her family’s wishes, she marries him, but their domestic life is gradually undone by parental interference. Like much South Asian melodrama, the film relies on romantic duets and frontal address, but its distinctly Pakistani quality lies in the elaborate negotiation of the absent kiss and its attendant erotics. In what was a fundamentally paradoxical code in Pakistani cinema, bare midriffs were more acceptable than plunging necklines, while premarital sex could be depicted so long as “bad” women were punished. The opposite of a Shariah-compliant fantasy, Rita and Iqbal’s courtship is born out of these contradictions. Their first meeting arrives through a comic scandal: A drunk Rita floods her hotel room after slipping naked into the bathtub, and a mortified Iqbal must retrieve her with his eyes theatrically shut. A coincidental run-in at a film theater moves them toward romance proper, until a broken hotel elevator traps them together. Extreme close-ups isolate hands, hair, lips, and eyes before the camera finally reveals the lovers embracing. Set to “Haseen Wadion Se,” the song sequence exemplifies what Sangita Gopal identifies in her book Conjugations: Marriage and Form in New Bollywood Cinema as the romantic duet’s substitution for the kiss as the primary vehicle of couple formation. But Pakistani cinema extends this logic further through a subset of song, the marital duet, reserved for the wedding night, which merges the formation of the couple with that of the family. The wedding night is, thus, a license to begin a sexual relationship with the intent of procreation. Before “Mujhe Dil Se” begins, Rita and Iqbal lie flush against one another atop the phoolon ki sej —garlands of jasmine, marigold, and rose spilling across the marital bed—dressed in their wedding clothes. The camera tracks upward from their feet to their interlocked hands. Just as a kiss seems imminent, the frame cuts to a balcony overlooking a secluded beach. The montage moves from honeymoon fantasy, beaches and parks, to the rhythms of married life. The marital bed remains its central site—it is where the couple lies entwined, where Rita emerges from the shower in the scene at the outset, where the day begins with dressing for work and reluctant partings. A distracted, lovestruck Iqbal sits at the office while an equally lovestruck Rita drifts through household chores at home. A few shots later, the two cradle a child in their arms. “Were you having the same dream as I was?” Iqbal asks as we return to their wedding night. Rita nods shyly. This erotic openness is often folded into a broader mythology of the 1970s as a moment of modernity under Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s government and his promises of a socialist utopia. Nightclubs, liquor, and bell-bottoms are frequently invoked as shorthand for the era, even as they circulated within a regulated system of censorship and moral policing. The contrast with General Muhammad Zia-ul Haq, who overthrew Bhutto in a 1977 military coup and later executed him, has often produced a simplified narrative: of a liberal cultural sphere abruptly replaced by sweeping repression under his “Islamization” drive. Yet Aina remained in cinemas for a record 401 weeks, well into the Zia period. Censorship until Zia’s death in 1988 undoubtedly affected filmmakers and narrowed the visual grammar of romance, but the shift was uneven rather than absolute: While romancing in an elevator became increasingly unlikely, lovers still had their duets. Far from a total and lasting capture by moral conservatism, post-Zia cinema in the 1990s often turned to overt sexualization to draw audiences back into a struggling exhibition economy. Lobby card for Nikah (Sangeeta, 1998). This impulse is evident in Aina ’s loose remake, Nikah (1998). Directed by Sangeeta, the remake transposes Rita and Iqbal’s rebellious affair onto Bisma (Reema Khan) and Faraz (Shaan Shahid), replacing the original’s sensuality with raunchy comedy. Even a minor subplot turns lurid: a full song, “Saiyaan Ang Laga,” follows a lonely wife swiveling her hips beneath a wall poster reading “I am so hot for you.” Despite its departures, Nikah ’s “Main Yun Milun” is nearly identical in montage to “Mujhe Dil Se.” The song does not begin on the wedding night, but it still opens on the marital bed. In a wide, slightly tilted shot, Faraz leans over Bisma on a low bed crowded with oversized cushions, his white kurta glowing against the dim room. Beneath him, Bisma reclines in shimmering green satin as he cups her face. The two sink into an embrace before the camera cuts to a close-up; when Bisma turns away, her red lipstick is visibly smudged. Faraz’s lips brush her cheek, and the scene cuts again to a close shot of their toes curling. Faraz and Bisma share a familiar moment after she comes out of the shower—fully dressed—before sending him off to work with a kiss on her neck. Like Rita, Bisma waits for her husband’s return, though her day is spent grooming herself rather than attending to chores. At night, she brings him a glass of milk, their lips meeting at its rim as he leans in. If the child in Rita and Iqbal’s imagination only gestures toward futurity, Bisma’s pregnancy is rendered diegetically: a time-lapse cuts from a pregnant Bisma to an operating theater to a crying infant. This visibility of erotic life signals a moment distinct from both Bhutto’s and Zia’s Pakistan. Shortly after Nikah , Samina Peerzada’s Inteha was briefly recalled for sex and nudity until the producer obtained a court order to reinstate its release, even though the Central Board of Film Censors remained formally governed by the Motion Pictures Ordinance (1979) and the Censorship of Films Rules (1980), both instituted under Zia. Ironically, the smudged lipstick and curling toes arrive alongside a greater preoccupation with family values. Where Iqbal inhabits a small, orphaned apartment, Faraz lives with his mother and sister; Rita’s villainous father is refigured as Bisma’s conniving mother. Bisma herself is reimagined as a more abrasive figure—an acquisitive, embittered wife who abandons Faraz and their child, only to return when the boy falls terminally ill. “Main Yun Milun” also transforms Aina ’s romantic duet into Bisma’s solo address to Faraz, fitting the film’s conservative politics: Her insistence that Faraz abandon his mother and sister for a job promotion is shown as a desire for the material comfort of her own parental household, just as her mother’s fixation on status destabilizes her marriage. Where Aina frames conflict as mutual misunderstanding shaped by parental interference, Nikah blames only Bisma and her mother—a residue of Zia’s veneration of the patriarch. If 1970s films cleanly separated “good” and “bad” women, 1990s melodrama compels all women to err, but allows the good ones to be forgiven by men. Lobby card for Nikah (Sangeeta, 1998). Family is a far more televisual project in 2013, when Aina is remade yet again as a telefilm. Following the neoliberalization drive initiated under General Pervez Musharraf in 2002, the private network television boom absorbed a workforce of unemployed cinema personnel, TVC-makers, and veterans of the state-owned broadcaster Pakistan Television (PTV), producing serials that hybridized Indian soaps, PTV’s storytelling tropes, flashy advertising, and Pakistani cinema itself. The remarkably undifferentiated look of Aaina (2013) demonstrates this. Under Sarmad Khoosat’s direction, Rita and Iqbal become Aaliya (Saba Qamar) and Sameer (Faysal Quraishi), with “era-appropriate” revisions: Instead of a hotel receptionist, Sameer is a struggling writer who finds Aaliya unconscious outside a farmhouse party. Aaina was among six films remade under a partnership between Geo Films and Tarang Foods, primarily a tea whitener brand, in hopes of “reviving” Pakistani cinema. A revival increasingly steered not by auteurs but by television offshoots like Geo Films, ARY Films, and Hum Films, the new visual vocabulary began to suffer from a crisis of sameness whereby television, cinema, and advertisements all resembled each other. Khoosat’s formally uninventive Aaina is also structurally incapable of recreating the erotics of the original and Nikah . While the federal censor board is still susceptible to public outcry and moral hysteria from right-wing factions, films get away with far more than television, which is hawkishly surveilled by the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) in its drive to reorganize all media into “family entertainment.” PEMRA is also an accessible forum for the common citizen to air grievances: Its monthly catalogues of citizen complaints include, in June alone, a protest against the “portrayal of bold and intimate scenes… that are inappropriate for a family audience” and “vulgar” advertisements that preclude family viewing. Conversely, in cinema, similar scenes are greenlit all the time by the censor board and seldom prompt written complaints. Despite the wariness prompted by PEMRA, Aaina makes no effort to push boundaries. On their wedding night, Sameer and Aaliya stand in a bedroom lit by decorative candles and roses, embracing from a careful distance. The marital bed becomes a backdrop, shrouded in shadows, and the only suggestion of sex arrives through a close shot of flickering candles. The next morning, Aaliya makes tea with Tarang whitener before the couple leaves to visit Sameer’s parents’ graves. Of all places, it is in the graveyard that “Mujhe Dil Se” begins, severing the link between the marital bed and the marital duet. (Though Pakistani telefilms rarely contain song sequences, the Geo-Tarang remake retains them as gestures of homage.) A promotion image for Aina (Sarmad Khoosat, 2013). If the original duet subsumed family formation within erotic fantasy, this one folds it back into consumable domesticity. At times, the montage resembles an advertisement reel more than a romantic duet: Aaliya sprays perfume in slow motion beneath a flowing white sheet, Sameer teaches her to cook, they laugh in hammocks and throw popcorn at one another. By the duet’s end, her teary-eyed gaze brightens when Sameer walks in with two cups of chai. If it looked like a tea whitener ad before, this shot does little to change that. Insofar as television’s origins are bound up in ad revenue and what Raymond Williams called a “home-centred way of living,” a telefilm like Aaina is the perfect collusion of family and consumerism. The “selling logic” is not disguised; the Tarang logo colonizes Aaina ’s title card, its frames, and the commercial breaks around it. At the same time, the shopping mall emerges as the new frontier of romance, almost as if replacing the marital bed(room)—even Sameer and Aaliya’s courtship begins there. Barring a handful of beach shots, their romance unfolds largely through consumption: cocktails, escalators, perfumes, glossy restaurants, shopping bags. To some degree, this reflects the 2010s cultural scene: In a city riddled with street crime, gang wars, and police raids extorting couples, the mall was one of the few safe places in Karachi. However, the mall also prevents the romance from escalating through its cameras and onlookers. After brushing shoulders in the mall, Sameer and Aaliya glance briefly toward each other’s lips before awkwardly looking away. So pervasive is the respectability trafficked by Tarang and the mall that even a dripping wet Aaliya at the beach can only induce a wide, goofy smile out of Sameer, as he gives her a hand, like someone roughhousing with a friend, not a lover. Thirteen years after Aaina , Pakistani cinema’s “revival” still can’t shake the family-entertainment logic that shaped it. With the romantic duet now all but gone, new films remain afflicted by a crisis of imagination about how to circumvent decades-old censorship and cultural codes. The number of “social issue films” blocked by the censor board— Verna (2017), Zindagi Tamasha (2019), Javed Iqbal (2022)—suggests investors are willing to fund riskier projects, but only if justified as a cultural necessity. The question of how to show romance is itself incendiary, even though most audiences still flock to primetime television and cinemas for romance. As always, the kiss remains absent. Only now, so do the possibilities around it.

articles.title: Rushes | Mark Ruffalo vs. Paramount, Ilya Khrzhanovsky Defends “DAU,” Johnnie To Makes English-Language Debut
articles.author: Notebook
articles.description: Get in touch to send in cinephile news and discoveries. To keep up with our latest features, sign up for the Weekly Edit newsletter and follow us @mubinotebook on X and Instagram . NEWS Spotlight (Tom McCarthy, 2015). After Mark Ruffalo criticized the financial connections between Larry Ellison’s technology company Oracle, which has supplied software to the Israel Defense Forces, and Paramount Skydance amidst their impending merger with Warner Bros., Paramount released a rare statement condemning the actor for invoking “antisemitic tropes.” Ruffalo responded that their accusation is “appalling and fundamentally dishonest” and that scrutinizing the Ellisons and their business practices is “fair and necessary.” Director Ilya Khrzhanovsky has taken to Facebook to defend his upcoming film DAU (2026) against claims by the Ukraine government that it’s “linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence.” In a detailed response ahead of his film’s world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, Khrzhanovsky, who is no longer a citizen of the Russian Federation, insists that DAU is not a Russian film, has not been financed by Russia, and does not represent pro-Putin propaganda. Read Notebook’s Ella Bittencourt on the multidisciplinary project . More than two years after the killing of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in Gaza, Israel has announced that it will open an investigation into whether the Israel Defense Forces were in the area at the time of her death. Kaouther Ben Hania, director of docudrama The Voice of Hind Rajab (2025) about the event in question, has decried their efforts as a smokescreen. “What is needed now is not a public relations operation,” she says in a statement on Instagram. “What is needed is justice (delivered by an independent authority) for Hind and for all the victims of the genocide in Gaza.” The Walt Disney Company has sued the Federal Communications Commission , claiming that the agency’s decision to review ABC’s broadcast licenses two years ahead of schedule is part of a retaliatory campaign by the Trump administration. The FCC order comes on the heels of Trump’s criticism of late-night hosts, especially Jimmy Kimmel, who was briefly pulled off the air by FCC Chairman Brendan Carr for comments on the assassination of Charlie Kirk. DEVELOPING Ramy Youssef in Poor Things (Yorgos Lanthimos, 2023). Johnnie To is set to direct his English-language debut Two Gun Cohen , a “dim sum western” about grifter and conman Morris Cohen who became the aide-de-camp to Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen. Ramy Youssef is set to write and direct his feature debut , which chronicles a white widowed socialite (Sharon Stone) and her relationship with a young Muslim man (Youssef), for A24. REMEMBERING Scream 4 (Wes Craven, 2011). Hayden Panettiere has died at 36 . The American actress got her start on soap operas One Life to Live (1968–2012; 2013) and Guiding Light (1952–2009) before making her feature-film debut in A Bug’s Life (1998) as Princess Dot. As a child actress, she made supporting turns in Remember the Titans (2000), Raising Helen (2004), and Ice Princess (2005). Panettiere’s breakthrough was as Claire Bennet, a cheerleader with the power of cellular regeneration, on the NBC drama Heroes (2006–10), a role she played for four seasons. Following Heroes , she went on to star as up-and-coming country singer Juliette Barnes in the ABC/CMT musical drama series Nashville (2012–18), whose storylines often reflected Panettiere’s documented struggles with depression, addiction, and abuse. Panettiere also garnered recognition for her performance as highschooler and Ghostface-target Kirby Reed in Scream 4 (2011), a role she later reprised in Scream VI (2023) where her character has become an FBI agent. “I wish the world had more time with you,” said actress Viola Davis in tribute, “because I had a burning curiosity about who you were becoming. I saw this beautiful Phoenix rising from the ashes. Your tests became your testimony, and your testimony became your legacy. You will be remembered.” RECOMMENDED READING Late Fame (Kent Jones, 2025). “This confluence of consumer trends and changes in production workflow has effectively resulted in frames that strive less for innovation or beauty and more for a quick fix. The quickness and disposability here has infiltrated the set. This means that, outside direct-to-streaming films and the glut of plasticky Marvel and grim DC movies … the late 2010s and 2020s have seen the screen get grayer. Regardless of the quality of the movies, their visual identity is constricted by a notable lack of oomph, an absence of substantiality in their colors, highlights, and blackpoints.” For The A.V. Club, Kyle Turner unpacks the generally desaturated “look” of contemporary film by interviewing cinematographers, colorists, and camera operators. “She currently has five projects in development: ‘two treatments, three scripts. That’s because of Covid really; I wrote a lot.’ Stone Mattress is an adaptation of the Margaret Atwood short story about wealthy tourists on an Arctic cruise. Julianne Moore is attached to star as a passenger seeking to punish her high school rapist against the backdrop of melting icebergs. ‘It’s a revenge film, but it’s environmental,’ Lynne says. ‘The character uncovers the past, and the landscape is uncovering the past as well; it’s melting.’” For The Gentlewoman , Mark Smith profiles Lynne Ramsay about how she balances her artistically uncompromising career and her domestic responsibilities. “Even so, I was surprised to hear [Kent] Jones declare during an onstage interview at the film’s NYFF premiere that [Samy] Burch’s Late Fame (2025) screenplay was superior to [Arthur] Schnitzler’s novella. It is, frankly, an insane opinion … In the novella, Saxberger is obliviously narcissistic, childish, and ridiculous—an overlooked poet, in other words, exotic and prickly as a puffer fish. In the film, however, he has been thoroughly dulcified, reduced into a charmingly bashful and tender gentleman, as if the contemporary poet were an endangered species too sacrosanct to poke. In shielding him from the sharp needles of Schnitzler’s irony, the relentless sympathy for Saxberger actually flattens the most human part of the story: our embarrassing, blindly feckless need to be revered.” For The Baffler , Brittany Dennison examines the deficiencies in Late Fame , and how Jones and Burch’s adaptation misunderstands the source text. “Over the course of making The Bend in the River (2025), I was reading about the death of the Colorado River. I kept thinking that the river is running out of water as we’re running out of time. And, that the temporal frame of the river and the human frame of our mortality crosses for a moment … I couldn’t finish the film without acknowledging our relationship with this river and our love of it, and just being able to experience the river and then being on it again to have this experience, which is a representation of not being able to stay in the same river twice. It’s not the same river and you’re not the same person.” For Screen Slate, David Schwartz interviews documentarian Robb Moss , a pioneer of personal cinema whose latest film represents the culmination of his River Film Trilogy. RECOMMENDED EVENTS The Third Man (Carol Reed, 1949). New York, August 29: Film at Lincoln Center presents the Bibliomania Book Fair , a free public book fair tied to the literary-themed cinema series Bibliomania: A Preface to Chronovisor . Boston, through September 19: The Harvard Film Archive presents The Cold Heart is More Precious than Diamonds: The Cinema of Graham Greene , a program featuring films either written by or adapted from the works of English writer and film critic, including Confidential Agent (1945), The Third Man (1949), and Our Man in Havana (1959). London, through October 6: The BFI Southbank presents Claude Chabrol: Elements of Crime , a retrospective of wryly entertaining thrillers by the “French Hitchcock.” San Francisco, through October 31: The Yerba Buena Center for the Arts presents Through an Open Window , a film series inspired by the aesthetic and thematic elements embedded in the work of Korean painter GaHee Park. Seoul, through November 8: The Seo-Seoul Museum of Art presents Kim Heecheon: Moles , which features the video and game work by the eponymous contemporary South Korean media artist, the first of a series of solo exhibitions produced by the museum. It is a different kind of social proposition altogether. What happens when a community gathers to watch a film it has chosen together, in a space it has collectively claimed, cannot be replicated by watching the same film alone. The film becomes a shared reference point, a starting place for conversation, a way of recognizing something in each other. The room produces a temporary public, and that public, however briefly, understands itself as one.” Lena Mrachacz explores the idea of cinema as a commons , and cinemagoing as a radical act of communal formation. “Above all, 4Columns was a writer’s publication, a showcase for a vast array of styles, idiosyncrasies, points of view. It was the kind of forum in which turns of phrase such as “raging daughter of Bilitis that I am” and “lesberation”—deployed in my first 4Columns review, of Battle of the Sexes (2017), a staid Emma Stone-starring docudrama about the stunt 1973 tennis match between Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs—were left completely untouched, with no edits demanding explanation. (My 4Columns word cloud would likely feature “lesbian supremacy,” “misandry,” and “heterosexual depravity” in the largest font.)” Melissa Anderson reflects upon her tenure as film editor and critic at 4Columns , a weekly online arts-criticism site that recently published its final issue. “Wilson need not worry: Nolan’s dialogue, toggling between lyrical passages and more unadorned exchanges spiced with the occasional present-day expletive … is most definitely not culled from her work. And she may well be right about some of her points, too. I wouldn’t go as far as to call the script ‘abysmal,’ but the film is certainly not immune to its fair share of clunky, expository passages, and for an epic that features plenty of erotic interludes, Nolan’s chaste rendition can feel like a missed opportunity. Yet I cannot help but find it ironic that such scathing criticism should come from someone who—by trading the ornate vocabulary of previous Homeric translations for a simpler language—also sought to make the hallowed text more accessible to new audiences.” In the latest edition of The Current Debate, Leonardo Goi examines the conversation around The Odyssey (2026) , its depiction of PTSD, and the various strengths and pitfalls of Nolan’s idiosyncratic blockbuster-sized vision. “I always thought that The Swindle (1997) was one of his most autobiographical films, like a hidden self-portrait of himself and our relationship as a director and as an actress. It was easy for me to relate to Michel Serrault’s character. There was something in the complicity, in the connections between the two of us, in the film that was close to maybe what our complicity and connection was in reality. I think he was speaking about himself in that film and about the world of cinema, in a very fun and tender way. articles.title: Cinema as Commons: The Radical Act of Going to the Movies
articles.author: Lena Mrachacz
articles.description: Illustration by Nina Bachmann. “ We must develop film co-operatives by making and screening more films. We must help each other sincerely, by creating new standards of social awareness.” These are the first words of Report to Mother [ Amma Ariyan ] (1986), a film by the Malayalam director John Abraham. They are spoken in voiceover even before the first image shows up on the screen. The film follows a group of young activists traveling across the southwestern state of Kerala to inform the mother of a comrade of his suicide. It is a road movie structured around grief, solidarity, and the question of what political community actually means in practice. In its final moments, the camera turns away from the screen to show the community watching the film together, the same people who helped make it, now its audience. In May this year, a new 4K restoration was screened at the Cannes Film Festival, the world’s most prestigious and best-funded film event, a place built on glamour and industry, where the red carpet, the film market, and the award ceremony form a circuit of value that operates at a considerable distance from the communities most films claim to speak for. Report to Mother was part of the Cannes Classics section, 40 years after it was made and never commercially released. It received a standing ovation. That the film exists at all is something of an accident: No original negative survived, and the restoration had to be built painstakingly from two damaged prints. What makes that moment worth pausing on is that Report to Mother was never part of any distribution system at all. The Odessa Collective funded the film by traveling through Kerala asking people directly for money, collecting small amounts, village by village. The finished film was then shown for free in these same villages, outside any commercial structure. Even if Abraham himself understood his movies as his own, the model the Odessa Collective built around Report to Mother —how it was funded, how it was shown, who it was made with—is best described not as independent cinema or even political cinema, but by a word borrowed from a different tradition entirely: commoning. The term comes from the feminist theorist Silvia Federici, who uses it to describe the collective creation and management of shared resources outside market logic. A commons is not simply a public good; it is something actively produced and maintained by a community, for a community. The classic examples are land and water: resources that were once collectively managed, then enclosed and privatized. But Federici’s argument is not really about land. It is about what happens to social life when the things that sustain it, like the spaces, the knowledge, the practices of care and culture, are progressively handed over to the market in an ongoing process of enclosure. It is about what happens every time a community loses access to a resource it once held in common, every time a shared space becomes a private one, every time the logic of profit replaces the logic of participation. What commoning names, then, is the counter-movement: the active, collective practice of building and defending shared resources against that enclosure. Not a utopia or a finished state, but a verb, an action by many. Something that people do, together, continuously. Cinema seems like an unlikely commons. It is expensive to make, expensive to distribute and historically entangled with capital from its very beginnings. The Lumière brothers were industrialists, after all, and the Hollywood studio system was built on vertical integration long before streaming platforms relied on the algorithm to determine what gets watched. And yet the commercial form of cinema was never the only possibility. Nor has it gone unchallenged through history. In the Weimar Republic, Social Democrats, Communists, and independent leftists founded the Volksfilmverband as an explicit response to the monopolization of the commercial film industry: a membership organization that created its own screening network, using union halls, pub backrooms, and workers’ meeting spaces to build a counter-public sphere around cinema. It declared itself the property of the working class as a whole and was promptly contested by both parties involved, each wanting to use it as a vehicle for their own politics. What the Volksfilmverband shows is that shared spaces can also be contested ones. Who decides what gets shown, who gets to speak from the front of the room, whose politics frame the discussion? These questions don’t disappear just because the space has been removed from the market. If anything, they become more urgent. The Newsreel Collective in the United States ran into the same problem from a different direction. From 1967, they made and distributed 16mm films directly to civil rights organizations, trade unions, and community groups, explicitly describing themselves as the “propaganda arm of the New Left.” The language was honest, if uncomfortable: They knew they were making arguments, not documentaries in any neutral sense. But the collective’s own composition told another story. In 1973, African American, Latino, and Asian members confronted the group over its failure to represent communities of color, not just on screen, but in the room where decisions were made. They took over the New York chapter and renamed it Third World Newsreel. The lesson holds: The question of who gets to speak, and for whom, is not a problem to be solved but a practice to be sustained. It’s one that requires constant negotiation, and a genuine commitment to making participation as wide as possible. The history of cinema as commons is also, inevitably, a history of that negotiation failing, and being resumed. It is therefore all the more striking that the same impulse keeps returning and that the newest iterations seem more alert to that question than their predecessors were. SİNEMA TRANSTOPIA, run by the collective bi’bak, has been operating in Berlin since 2020 and is now based in Wedding, one of the city’s most densely postmigrant neighborhoods. Its name draws on migration researcher Erol Yıldız’s concept of “transtopia”: a place shaped by everywhere its community comes from, not just where it is located. Therefore the cinema is not a neutral container for content. Who is in the room, whose cultural memory is being tended to, whose gaze is being decentered: These are, first and foremost, political decisions. SİNEMA TRANSTOPIA is a place where postmigrant, transnational communities gather to define what a public can look like—in practice through an internationally drawn curatorial team, a program shaped partly by audience vote, and a communal space that extends beyond the screening itself. They are not alone. Kavaklıdere Cinema in Ankara, Turkey, sat empty for sixteen years before reopening in 2023 as Kült Kavaklıdere, a collectively run arts center that opens its spaces free of charge to nonprofit groups and theatre collectives, sustaining a public function without public funding. In Rwanda’s capital of Kigali, Imitana Productions revived Cine Mayaka, the oldest surviving cinema in the country, and regularly takes its screenings out of the building entirely, into public squares and open streets. Across different cities and very different contexts, the same basic claim repeats: that a room, a screen, and an audience are worth protecting. And that claim deserves more attention than it usually gets. A cinema as commons is not simply a different way of programming films. It is a different kind of social proposition altogether. What happens when a community gathers to watch a film it has chosen together, in a space it has collectively claimed, cannot be replicated by watching the same film alone. The film becomes a shared reference point, a starting place for conversation, a way of recognizing something in each other. The room produces a temporary public, and that public, however briefly, understands itself as one. People sit in the same room, encounter the same thing, and agree or disagree about what it means. That is very close to what democratic culture requires in order to function. It is also worth asking what those spaces are fighting against, or rather, what kind of relationship to cinema they are refusing. The dominant model of moving-image consumption today is not simply commercial; it is algorithmic. A small number of platforms now control not just distribution but also the conditions under which films get made, the data that determines what gets commissioned, the interface through which most people on earth encounter moving images. The logic is one of personalization: Every scroll, every pause, every abandoned film feeds a system designed to predict and preempt your next choice. What gets optimized, in the end, is your continued individual engagement with the platform. This is a form of enclosure of attention, of taste, of the very capacity to be surprised by something you didn’t already know you wanted. What gets lost is the condition of watching together in a room, with strangers and friends. This is why gathering matters. Streaming has made watching films easier, cheaper, and more solitary than at any point in cinema’s history. It has also made the act of gathering to watch something together feel, quietly, like a choice, one that requires a little more intention than it used to. But what the history of cinema as commons suggests is that this gathering was never incidental, that the room has always been part of the argument, as much as the film inside it. That idea is worth holding onto: a cinema that refuses to offer a service and insists on building a commons, and a public that understands itself as such. The cinemas carrying this impulse forward today are not simply alternatives to the multiplex but a response to a specific moment. It is not a coincidence that they are multiplying now, in a moment when public space is contracting, when political life feels increasingly managed from above, when the simple act of gathering together has started to feel like a position in itself. What these cinemas insist on, each in its own way, is that cinema can be more than entertainment delivered to an audience, that the room, and who fills it, and what happens after the lights come up, are themselves political questions worth taking seriously, and that those questions don’t resolve themselves once and for all. They have to be asked again and again, by every community. The cinema has always had the potential to function as a commons. In certain moments of political urgency, people have insisted on it. This is one of those moments.

articles.title: Movie Poster of the Week | The Film Posters of David Lance Goines
articles.author: Adrian Curry
articles.description: 1977 poster by David Lance Goines for Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror (F. W. Murnau, Germany, 1922) for the Pacific Film Archive. I recently came across two unusual film posters up for sale at Heritage Auctions, one featuring a winged beetle for F.W. Murnau’s Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror (1922) and the other featuring a woman at a table with a red rose for Max Ophüls’s Letter from an Unknown Woman (1948). Both are illustrated in what resembles the Arts and Crafts style of late nineteenth-century Britain and, while neither really capture the essence of either film (for example, the woman in the Ophüls poster looks nothing like Joan Fontaine nor does the rather austere poster reflect the florid style of that film), both are very distinctive and the Nosferatu in particular is a thing of beauty. The two posters are the work of David Lance Goines, an artist best known for being the graphic face of the celebrated farm-to-table restaurant Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, run by chef Alice Waters, who passed away in 2023 at the age of 77. Digging a little deeper, I discovered that between 1972 and 1983 Goines designed and printed 24 film posters for screenings at the Pacific Film Archive (PFA), at the University of California, Berkeley. The posters were commissioned by his friend Tom Luddy ,who was programming films at the PFA and who went on to co-found the Telluride Film Festival in 1974. (Luddy died in 2023, just six days before Goines). Goines wrote on his website in 1995, on the occasion of his poster celebrating the 25th anniversary of the University Art Museum and the Pacific Film Archive: My first poster for PFA was in 1972, on a handshake deal with Tom Luddy that continued through 1983. He never saw the designs until the posters were delivered. I'd tack up new ones upstairs at Chez Panisse, and at night we'd all of us sit around and drink wine and be pals. I’ve been a printer and graphic designer now for thirty years last April. Alice is looking at the restaurant's 25th anniversary next year in August. Tom's dream is alive and well after a quarter-century, and the Art Museum's roof still leaks in the rain. Born in Grants Pass, Oregon, in 1945, Goines’s father was an engineer and his mother was an artist and calligrapher whom he often named as his biggest creative influence. He studied classics at UC Berkeley but after being expelled for his involvement in the Free Speech Movement he apprenticed at the Berkeley Free Press, which was printing flyers and posters for the radical anti-war and civil rights groups that were springing up all over the city. It was through the print shop that he met Alice Waters, who was having flyers printed for a political campaign. They became a couple and, while living together, co-wrote a cooking column for the San Francisco Express Times . In 1970 he and Waters published a portfolio of prints titled “Thirty Recipes Suitable for Framing” for which Goines illustrated and hand-lettered Waters’s recipes. With the proceeds from the book, Goines bought the Berkeley Free Press and renamed it the Saint Hieronymus Press. When Chez Panisse opened in 1971, Goines and Waters were no longer a couple but they remained close friends and he illustrated the distinctive cookbooks, menus, and matchbooks for the restaurant for the next 50 years, and most notably made an annual poster for each anniversary. 1977 poster by Goines for Letter from an Unknown Woman (Max Ophüls, USA, 1948) for the Pacific Film Archive; 1980 poster by Goines for Café Chez Panisse. His 1980 poster for Chez Panisse is a self-portrait, though in later years Goines, who cut a distinctive figure in Berkeley with his bowler hats and three-piece suits, favored a large handlebar moustache. He made over 250 posters over the course of his life (255 to be exact, as assiduously catalogued on his website), many for Bay Area stores and organizations, or for exhibitions of his own work. His style remained very much indebted to the Arts and Crafts movement, and to the work and ideas of William Morris, though on his website he detailed a wide variety of influences for each individual poster, ranging from Albrecht Dürer to René Magritte, and from H. R. Giger to art deco cigarette lighters. His style was also quite indebted to the more sinuous and organic work of art nouveau, but it differed somewhat from the art nouveau-influenced look of the psychedelic music posters that defined San Francisco in the late 1960s. Goines pinpoints the origin of that style on his website: The old University Art Museum, now a fire station, was the site of one of the most important graphic events of the 1960s: a show of Jugendstil posters, organized and curated by Herschel Chipp. I can't quite remember the exact date: it was in 1965 or 1966. This exhibition was seen by all of the people in San Francisco and Berkeley who were doing posters for the rock ’n’ roll events of the time, and their very next posters were all but direct imitations of those of the Jugendstil, particularly reflecting the lettering of Ferdinand Andrei (President of the Vienna Secession in 1905), and Leopold Forstner of the Wiener Werkstätte, which were letters all made to fit into a square, or some other shape, and almost illegible. As a pressman, I printed some of the San Francisco artist’s psychedelic posters, and later became a poster designer myself. While in the same vein, Goines’s posters were less dense and more symmetrical and eschewed the swirly, cramped, nearly illegible lettering of his peers like Wes Wilson and Rick Griffin. Goines was a more traditional typographer whose 1982 book A Constructed Roman Alphabet: A Geometric Analysis of the Roman Alphabet Including the Greek Characters and the Arabic Numerals won the American Book Award for typography. Goines’s first film poster, made in 1972, was for Josef von Sternberg’s The Blue Angel (1930). 1972 posters for The Blue Angel (Josef von Sternberg, Germany, 1930) and Olympia (Leni Riefenstahl, Germany, 1938) for the Pacific Film Archive. I don’t know whether Goines chose which films he wanted to make posters for or whether the PFA or Luddy chose them for him, but his output would suggest that his taste in movies skewed toward European and American classics of the 1920s and ’30s. Letter from an Unknown Woman feels unusually modern for Goines (though a film steeped in the romanticism of the past) and the only contemporary film I can see in his oeuvre is Hans-Jürgen Syberberg’s Parsifal (1982). 1973 posters for Marcel Pagnol’s Marseilles Trilogy (1931–36) for the Pacific Film Archive. Three of my favorite film posters by Goines are his triptych for Marcel Pagnol’s Marseille Trilogy. (Alice Waters named her famed restaurant after one of the trilogy’s characters, Monsieur Panisse.) 1972 posters for The General (Buster Keaton, USA, 1926) and Ruggles of Red Gap (Leo McCarey, USA, 1935) for the Pacific Film Archive. Goines’s website includes a paragraph or two, written by the artist, about each film, some autobiographical and some quite abstract and philosophical. His poster for the horror film series Unpleasant Surprises leads to a reverie about collecting eggs as a boy growing up on a farm, while his poster for Buster Keaton’s The General (1926) inspires these thoughts: If you’re going to steal, steal big. If you're going to lie, tell a lie so big that, often enough repeated, it will come to be the truth. Do not pilfer, or tell fibs. You'll just get caught and you’ll be sorry afterwards. About the biggest thing you can steal is a man’s life. That takes everything he has. It doesn’t leave you with much, of course, except his dead flesh. Slavery steals his life also, except that the use of his days becomes the possession, for so long as he hangs on, of another person. The fratricidal war this film celebrates was about stealing, both big and small, and changing the rules about what was stealing and what wasn’t. Compared to stealing lives, and stealing days, stealing a locomotive scarcely seems worth discussion. While for Ruggles of Red Gap (1935) he wrote about signing his work: I’d done nineteen posters and a lot of other design work and I hadn’t signed any of it because I felt that my work was so derivative of the work of others that it would be presumptuous to claim any of it as my own. One day I walked past the gallery Dow and Frosini and there was a poster in the window that I really liked. It obviously had been done recently, but it wasn’t signed, so I couldn’t find out who had done it. This annoyed me greatly, and as I stood there being annoyed I realized that I was doing the exact same thing myself, and that there were probably plenty of people out there who were annoyed because I wasn’t signing my posters. So I started signing them. I liked the pattern of four squares arranged into a larger square, and had used that as a sort of signature before, so when I designed a signature I kept that basic idea and made it a square. This movie always makes me cry. Sometimes his descriptions about his thought process are more specific, as in this for his poster for Fritz Lang’s M : My six-year-old niece was given a camera to play with at a garden party. She spent a happy afternoon taking pictures of guests, most of whom were grown-ups. When the prints came back, the photographs were of people’s legs and feet. It seems obvious in retrospect that a small child sees the world of adults as a forest of trousers and stockings, but at the time it came to us as a surprise. People see the whole world from their own point of view, and are generally amazed that others see it differently. This film is about a murderer of children, and the poster presents a child’s-eye view. Below is the rest of Goines’s film oeuvre in roughly chronological order. 1972 poster for the film series Treasures from the Eastman House and 1975 poster for a series of films from the 1975 Cannes Film Festival, for the Pacific Film Archive. 1974 poster for Die Nibelungen (Fritz Lang, Germany, 1924) and 1975 poster for the series Music and the Movies . Both for the Pacific Film Archive. 1975 poster for Pandora's Box (G.W. Pabst, Germany, 1929) and 1978 poster for the horror film series Unpleasant Surprises for the Pacific Film Archive. 1977 poster for Faust (F.W. Murnau, Germany, 1926) and 1978 poster for The King of Kings (Cecil B. DeMille, USA, 1927) for the Pacific Film Archive. 1980 poster for Wings (William A. Wellmann, USA, 1927) for the Pacific Film Archive. 1982 poster for Double Suicide (Masahiro Shinoda, Japan, 1969) for the Pacific Film Archive. 1983 posters for Parsifal (Hans-Jürgen Syberberg, West Germany, 1982) and Frankenstein (James Whale, USA, 1931) for the Pacific Film Archive. 1995 poster for the 25th Anniversary of the University Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive. Goines’s final film poster, made some 21 years after his last poster for the PFA, was this typically eccentric and non-representational design for Ingmar Bergman’s The Seventh Seal (1957), which Goines lists as a piece of self-promotion, possibly anticipating the fan art poster phenomenon that began in the late 2000s. 2004 poster for The Seventh Seal (Ingmar Bergman, Sweden, 1957). On September 22, 2021, less than two years before his death, Goines wrote on the occasion of his Jubilee poster for Chez Panisse’s 50th anniversary: My mother called me on my birthday in 1995 and remarked, “I have no trouble being seventy-two years old, but I cannot believe that I have a son who is fifty.” That’s exactly how I feel about the Chez Panisse jubilee. The years have slipped past like water. Every one of those fifty years was jam-packed full of life, and growth and adventure and heartbreak and joy. Every day was one of living, work, eating, sleeping. Life went on at the steady pace of one second into the future per second, same as always. But when it’s past and over, it all seems to have happened at once. I am catapulted from the exciting, chaotic opening night fifty years ago to a muted celebration marred by pandemic with nothing, it seems, in the middle. Goines’s archive—consisting of over five thousand items—is now housed at UC Berkeley’s Bancroft Library .

Cannes-winning actor/filmmaker Riley Keough ( The Girlfriend Experience , 2016) is no stranger to the worlds of wealth or fashion, and in the bloody, bawdy new satire Rosebush Pruning (2026), she inhabits a larger-than-life character who is way too into both. articles.title: Artificial Intelligence: Ars Notoria and the Promise of Instant Knowledge
articles.description: Centuries before Neo instantly mastered Kung Fu in *The Matrix*, medieval scholars found a shortcut to years of difficult study: a magical manuscript that promised to fast-track advanced learning. Anne Lawrence-Mathers investigates the *Ars notoria*, its supposed powers, and the demonic influence it had upon some users.

articles.description: Pompous know-it-alls were once a mainstay of mockery on the Italian stage. Arnoud Visser investigates this stock character of the pedant and his association with individual superiority, social distinction, and sexual transgression, finding a form of satire that took aim at the Renaissance humanist’s erudition and lofty ideals.

articles.description: Arguably the first work of fiction to feature a *Tyrannosaurus rex*, Louis Pope Gratacap’s *The New Northland* (1915) is at once kaleidoscopic, mischievous, fascinating — and exhausting. Richard Fallon explores this “lost world” novel, finding a work as interested in cutting-edge science as it was in paying dues to its generic precursors.

A euphemism for culled fetal lambs? Or perhaps a medieval misapprehension of cotton? Thom Sliwowski traces the roots of this fabled zoophyte.

articles.description: The working class undergirds everything in this cartoon of capitalist society.

articles.title: Magic by Return of Post: How Mail Order Delivered the Occult
articles.description: What allowed occultism to blossom in the United States at the turn of the 20th century? Linotype machines, cheap pulp paper, and newly improved postal networks. Allan Johnson investigates the forgotten history and (still living) world of mail-order magic.

articles.title: Pulex irritans: The Attack of the Monster (1885)
articles.description: Lantern slide of man battling bug.

articles.title: “A Beautiful Purplish Hue”: Frank Dudley Beane’s Experience with Ergot and Cannabis Indica (1884)
articles.description: An early contribution to drug literature, in which a man came to be fashioned out of wood.

articles.title: Introducing PDR Press Minis
articles.description: Announcing an exciting new book series!

articles.title: Broken Ground: The Fall of the House of Usher (1928)
articles.description: A modernist adaptation of Edgar Allan Poe. One of the first avant-garde films from America.

articles.title: Songs from the Commons: A Q&A with Simon Close about the Public Song Project
articles.description: The creator of WNYC's Public Song Project on creativity, copyright, and the public domain.

articles.title: The Great Majority: Body Snatching and Burial Reform in 19th-Century Britain
articles.description: As populations flocked to city centres in the 19th century, church cemeteries began to overflow with the dead. Roger Luckhurst exhumes the history of this period, when anatomists fuelled a body-snatching trade led by “resurrection men” and reformers sought alternatives to the toxic urban graveyards and their pestilent fumes.

articles.title: Elizabeth I’s Manuscript Copy of Pierre Boaistuau’s Histoires Prodigieuses (1559)
articles.description: Marvels, wonders, and monstrosities: something between a medieval bestiary and a scientific treatise on birth defects.

articles.title: “Wretches, Speak Evil of Me”: Goethe and Schiller’s Xenions (1896 edition)
articles.description: One of the most elaborate works of literary insult ever written.

articles.title: Doing Impressions: Monet’s Early Caricatures (ca. late 1850s)
articles.description: Moneymaking caricatures by a teenage Monet, before he turned to Impressionism.

articles.title: Fear and Fragility: The Glass Delusion and Its History
articles.description: In early modern Europe, around the time when lenses began to bring the world (and heavens) into newfound focus, patients started appearing in medical records with a particular ailment: a firm belief that they were made of glass. Tamara Sanderson investigates the source and manifestation of this delusion, and finds a psychological idiom that once carried the weight of what could otherwise not be said.

articles.title: Calicornication: Postcards of Giant Produce (1909)
articles.description: "Tall-tale" or "exaggeration" postcards illustrating the bounties of California.

articles.title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s Herland (1915)
articles.description: A utopian novel where men are no longer necessary.

articles.title: Wayang Kulit: Raden Soelardi’s Illustrations of Javanese Puppets (1919)
articles.description: Illustrations of Javanese *wayang kulit* puppets with vivid colour and gilding.

articles.title: The Blinkered Flâneur: Walking with Franz Hessel in 1920s Berlin
articles.description: Does the flâneur , that curiously modern figure who wanders metropolitan streets, have a political consciousness? For Franz Hessel — author of Spazieren in Berlin , “a memorization while strolling” that Walter Benjamin called “thoroughly epic” — the answer seemed to be no. Paul Sullivan explores Hessel’s perambulations through Berlin and the achievements and limitations of his vision.

articles.title: Unbridled Passions: The Eight Horses of King Mu, Son of Heaven (ca. 1300)
articles.description: Unruly steeds from King Mu’s mythology, cavorting across a silk scroll.

articles.title: Pigeons Transmogrified: Hannah Glasse’s Art of Cookery (1751 edition)
articles.description: A bestselling 18th-century cookbook, containing the first recipe for curry in English.

articles.title: Snail Homes, Bog Bodies, and Mechanical Flies: Robert Testard’s Illustrations for Les secretz de l’histoire naturelle (ca. 1485)
articles.description: A wondrous illuminated manuscript, which gathers and illustrates the marvels of the world and beyond.

articles.title: Sekka Zusetsu: A Book of Snowflakes (1832)
articles.description: Observations of “snow flowers” made by microscope in Edo-era Japan.

articles.title: Typing for Love or Money: The Hidden Women’s Labor behind Modern Literary Masterpieces
articles.description: Taking dictation, revising manuscripts, typing copies, literary amanuenses often labour for little compensation and even less recognition. Christine Jacobson explores the neglected efforts of women like Theodora Bosanquet, Véra Nabokov, and Valerie Eliot, who — through their work as typists, editors, and champions — had a profound impact on modern literature.

articles.title: Sara Weiss’ Journeys to the Planet Mars (1903)
articles.description: A forgotten bridge between Spiritualism and UFO encounters.

articles.title: Autobiography of a “Jeep” (1943)
articles.description: A WWII propaganda film narrated as an "auto"-biography

articles.title: Cybernetic Attention: All Watched over by Machines We Learned to Watch
articles.description: Before the attention economy consumed our lives, “pursuit tests” devised by the US military coupled man to machine with the aim of assessing focus under pressure. D. Graham Burnett explores these devices for evaluating aviators, finding a pre-history of the laboratory research that has relentlessly worked to slice and dice the attentional powers of human beings.

articles.title: Flights of Fancy: The Nine Birds of Jacques de Fornazeris (1594)
articles.description: Etchings of birds in a somewhat theatrical style.

articles.title: A Prophet of the Weather: Lantern Slides by Clement Lindley Wragge (ca. 1900–22)
articles.description: Slides from twenty years of lecturing about the workings of the universe and the fate of the soul.

articles.title: Peter Kropotkin’s Memoirs of a Revolutionist (1899)
articles.description: The memoirs of an aristocratic man revolutionised into an anarchist communist.

articles.title: Happy Public Domain Day 2026!
articles.description: Each January 1st is Public Domain Day, when a new crop of works have their copyrights expire and become free to share and reuse for any purpose. Here's our highlights for 2026.

articles.title: Top 10 Most Read Pieces from 2025
articles.description: From sublime spheres to hungry cats, a rundown of the ten most read of what we published this year.

articles.title: A Thousand and One Nights in Italy: The Moorish Fantasias of Cesare Mattei and Ferdinando Panciatichi
articles.description: In mid-19th century Italy, two eccentric aristocrats set forth on parallel projects: constructing ostentatious castles in a Moorish Revival style. Iván Moure Pazos tours the psychedelic chambers of Rochetta Mattei, optimised for electrohomeopathic healing, and Castello di Sammezzano, an immersive, orientalist fever dream.

articles.title: Nature Morte: Chaïm Soutine’s Still Lifes (ca. 1920s)
articles.description: Still lifes by the artist who seemed to bridge expressionism with the baroque.

articles.title: Deceit and Disrobing: The Schefer Maqāmāt (BNF Arabe 5847, ca. 1237)
articles.description: Illustrations of Abū Zayd and his adventures in double meaning.

articles.title: Luke Howard’s Essay on the Modification of Clouds (1865)
articles.description: First cloud taxonomer and a poem by Goethe.

articles.title: The Launch of Our End-of-Year Fundraiser!
articles.description: Our End-of-Year Fundraiser is launched, and the new postcards theme will be Attention.

articles.title: “Quaint Dessert Dishes” in American Homes and Gardens (1911)
articles.description: Bizarre sweet treats that resemble human and animal forms.

articles.title: Henri Rivière’s Thirty-Six Views of the Eiffel Tower (1888–1902)
articles.description: French lithographs of the Eiffel Tower and its environs, in the style of Japanese woodblock prints.

articles.title: Art in Art: Cabinets of Curiosity and the Rise of the Gallery Painting
articles.description: In the 17th century, emanating from Antwerp, a new genre of artwork came on the scene: paintings of paintings, works populated by a lush array of meta-images. From its origins in picturing private curiosity cabinets to its later use in documenting increasingly public collections, Thea Applebaum Licht charts the course of this alluring aesthetic tradition.

articles.title: Too Computerised? Too Cold?: 1999 A.D. (1967)
articles.description: A past vision of the future. Domestic utopia? Or sanitised hell?

articles.title: New T-Shirts (Now in 100% Organic Cotton) and New Mugs in Our Shop!
articles.description: Adorn your body and coffee in PDR goodness! We’ve just added 8 new T-shirts and 13 new mugs to our online shop.

articles.title: Roma Lister, Aradia, and the Speculative Origins of a Witchcraft Revival
articles.description: In 1899, Charles Godfrey Leland published Aradia , “the gospel of the witches”, containing a goddess-orientated creation and saviour narrative, purported to descend from an ancient, hermetic tradition of witchcraft in Italy. A. D. Manns explores this text via an enchanting conjecture: that the writer, medium, and witch Roma Lister played a pivotal role in the formation of both Aradia and, therefore, a new form of paganism called Wicca.

articles.title: Last Order Dates for the Holiday Season - 2025
articles.description: The recommended cut-off dates to order from our shop by to ensure delivery in time for Dec 25th.

articles.title: Perverse, Grotesque, Sensuous, Inimitable: A Selection of Works by Aubrey Beardsley
articles.description: Selections from an artist whose phantasmagoric works defined an era.

articles.title: Animal Costumes from the 1862 Fairytale Ball of the Jung-München Artist’s Association
articles.description: Photographs from a costume ball featuring fairytale fables.

articles.title: PDR's Halloween Reader
articles.description: This Halloween week, a devilish dive into our archives to unearth some supernatural treats...

articles.title: “That’s Why We Become Witches”: Sylvia Townsend Warner’s Lolly Willowes (1926)
articles.description: A novel about a woman who throws off the yoke of patriarchy to become a witch.

articles.title: Hooked on Sonics: Experimenting with Sound in 19th-Century Popular Science
articles.description: Of all the senses cultivated throughout the 19th century, it was the sense of hearing that experienced the most dramatic transformation, as the science of sound underwent rapid advancement. Lucas Thompson delves into a particular genre of popular acoustics primers aimed at children and amateurs alike, which reveal the pedagogical, ludic, and transcendental strivings of Victorian society.

articles.title: A Treatise on the All-Healing Qualities of Earth Bathing (1790)
articles.description: A medical tract on the health effects of burying oneself alive in mud.

articles.title: Paramaribo and the Plantation: Gerrit Schouten’s Dioramas of Suriname (1810–30)
articles.description: Dioramas avant la lettre that depict local life in Suriname.

articles.title: The Nature of the Beast: Charles le Brun’s Human-Animal Hybrids (1806)
articles.description: Illustrations of supposed physiognomic affinities between humans and animals.

articles.title: The Adventures and Experiences of the First Slovak Novel
articles.description: Partially banned upon publication and translated into English for the first time this year, *René, or: A Young Man’s Adventures and Experiences* (1783–85) found new readers in the communist era thanks to its critiques of feudalism, capitalism, and the Catholic Church. Dobrota Pucherová introduces us to this hybrid work, which mixes the bildungsroman with the philosophical novel, the romance, the adventure story, the travelogue, the history book, and the orientalist fantasy.

articles.title: Vertiginous Accounts: Travels in the Air (1871 edition)
articles.description: Expedition accounts of aeronauts bravely venturing into the heavens on hot-air balloons.

articles.title: Birth of the Pearl (1901)
articles.description: A "living picture" film staging Botticelli’s *Birth of Venus* with a twist.

articles.title: The End of the World as We (Didn’t) Know It: Now and Then #5
articles.description: A Rapture that wasn’t, in 2025 and 1844.

articles.title: The Shadow of Desire: Painting the Origins of Art (ca. 1625–1850)
articles.description: Paintings illustrating Pliny the Elder’s account of the origins of art.

articles.title: “You Think Me a Bold Cheat”: Mary Carleton, Counterfeit Princess
articles.description: Accused of posing as foreign royalty to lure her young suitor into a bigamous marriage, Mary Carleton was the subject of dozens of pamphlets and broadsides published in the mid-17th century, including by Carleton herself. Investigating the fraudster’s life, Laura Kolb finds a self-fashioning figure who both influenced the emergence of the English novel and serves as a strange precursor to our modern-day fascination with conwomen and counterfeits, like the heiress manqué Anna Delvey.

articles.title: A Collection of Old English Customs, and Curious Bequests and Charities (1842)
articles.description: A compilation of historical gifting traditions in England, with a focus on the peculiar.

articles.title: Ivan Aivazovsky’s Miniature Seascapes (ca. 1887)
articles.description: Identical photographs of the artist, each with a unique miniature painting at the centre.

articles.title: The Cat’s Maew: Thai Treatise on Auspicious Felines (19th Century)
articles.description: A manuscript that pairs illustrations of cats with poetic descriptions and notes on what mystical benefits their owners might hope to accrue.

articles.title: Watching the World in a Dark Room: The Early Modern Camera Obscura
articles.description: Centuries before photography froze the world into neat frames, scientists, poets, and artists streamed transient images into dark interior spaces with the help of a camera obscura. Julie Park explores the early modern fascination with this quasi-spiritual technology and the magic, melancholy, and dream-like experiences it produced.

articles.title: Cannibal Modernity: Oswald de Andrade’s Manifesto Antropófago (1928)
articles.description: A modernist manifesto inspired (controversially) by the Tupi people of Brazil.

articles.title: Flowers of Fealty: Wilhelm Dilich’s Commemoration of the Christening of Elisabeth of Hesse (1598)
articles.description: Commemorative manuscript featuring illustrations of pageants, costumes, and fireworks, later further illustrated by a separate artist, with floral motifs.

articles.title: Breaking the Celestial Ceiling: Now and Then #4
articles.description: Female astronomical first, in 2025 and 1787.

articles.title: Through the Magnifying Glass: The Cheese Mites (1903)
articles.description: A trick film in the peepshow vein, involving magnification and mites on a block of cheese.

articles.title: Splitting Hairs: Chinese Immigrants, the Queue, and the Boundaries of Political Citizenship
articles.description: As Chinese immigration to California accelerated across the 19th century, the hairstyle known as the queue — a long, braided pony tail — became the subject of white Americans’ fascination, disgust, and legal regulation. Sarah Gold McBride explores why hair served as an index of political subjecthood, and how the queue exposed cracks in American norms regarding gender, economy, and citizenship.

articles.title: The Mowing-Devil (1678), or, the Earliest Known Depiction of a Crop Circle
articles.description: A crop circle sighting tinged with Christian morality.

articles.title: Perspiration, Bilocation, and Plagiarisation: “The Heat Wave” (1929)
articles.description: Time travel and murder during a New York heat wave.

articles.title: The “Private” Photographs of Bolette Berg and Marie Høeg (ca. 1895–1903)
articles.description: Excerpts from a dazzling image collection, discovered in a Norwegian barn in the 1980s, that experiments with the presentation of gender.

articles.title: Dancing Naked on the Head of a Pin: The Early History of Microphotography
articles.description: In 1853, John Benjamin Dancer achieved a feat of seemingly impossible scale: he shrunk an image to the size of a sharpened pencil tip. Anika Burgess explores the invention of microphotography and its influence on erotic paraphernalia and military communications.

articles.title: Trojan Pig: Tiny Cryptic #11
articles.description: Eleventh instalment in our series of extremely small and free-form cryptic crossword puzzles, themed on our latest essay.

articles.title: The Language of Form: Lothar Schreyer’s Kreuzigung (1920)
articles.description: The sole example of a Bauhaus workshop’s arcane theatrical scoring system, combining colours, words, and complex symbolic notation.

articles.title: Strings Attached: Helen Haiman Joseph’s A Book of Marionettes (1920)
articles.description: The first comprehensive history of marionette artistry in the English language.
